But in the discussion that follows this it will be necessary for us to mention certain other patients too who breathed great and rare, whom Hippocrates recorded in the subsequent books; yet this will not be for the confirmation of what is now proposed—for that is already clear—but for the explanation of certain other questions contained in the account concerning them, and incidentally the confirmation that many breathe in this way will also be increased. Of what condition, then, is such a dyspnoea diagnostic? Of no other than delirium.

[830] For what cause has been clearly demonstrated in the preceding discourse, but for the sake of reminder it will be stated now too in brief. For in truth it is a symptom peculiar to delirium to make the respiration great and rare, that is, at a long interval of time. For why should one breathe in more, when not in need of more? Or why at a long interval, when it is possible at a shorter one? And that those who breathe in great and rare do not need more air, the rarity testifies. For they would certainly be pressed to breathe in more continuously, if indeed they needed more; but remaining at rest for a long time is a sign of not needing much. But both of these seem to be affections, as it were, of one who is forgetting the activity. For to make the drawing of the breath immoderate, and the rest immoderate, belongs to one who knows neither where he ought to stop the activity nor when to begin it again, but who in both exceeds the measure through ignorance of what is fitting.

Just as, then, those who are delirious, having often asked for a chamber-pot in order to urinate, forgot in the meantime, and then would not urinate unless [831] someone reminded them, so, since breathing too is a psychic activity, and their reasoning has been impaired, they become more forgetful both regarding the activities themselves and regarding their intermissions. Doing both, then, over a long time, both the activities and the pauses, they thus produce largeness and rarity in the whole respiration. Is it, then, that we say so, but Hippocrates judged otherwise? Or did he too write in the Prognostic in this manner: 'breath drawn large and at long intervals signifies delirium'? For what he called 'rare' in the first book of the Epidemics, this he has called 'at long intervals' in the Prognostic, changing the word into a phrase. And indeed, in the case of those patients in whom he says the breath became large and rare, in addition to the other symptoms he also writes down delirium; in the case of the first of all, Philiscus, in this manner: 'During the night distressed, did not sleep, was delirious in every respect.' So in the account of the third day. And in that of the fifth again: 'short sleeps, talking, raving.'

In the case of the second [832] of the patients, whose name was Silenus, in the account of the second day he says, 'he was slightly delirious,' and in that of the third, 'much talking, laughter, singing; he could not restrain himself.' Then, adding to this, he will say, 'fourth day: through the same things.' That Philiscus and Silenus, then, were delirious, he recorded in this way. And in the case of the wife of Dromeades—for he says that she too breathed rare and large—he wrote in this manner: 'about midday she was much delirious, and again quickly she came a little to her senses.' So, then, on the fifth of the days. Then he adds: 'at night she slept somewhat; she was delirious.' And in the same manner, writing also what happened in the course of the sixth day, he says something like this: 'extremities cold; she was delirious.' Thus, then, in the first book of the Epidemics, where there is mention of large and rare breath, there he also mentions delirium; and in the same manner throughout the following books too he reminds us, nowhere mentioning large and rare breath where he does not mention great delirium.

[833] That, then, Hippocrates often observed in the sick this kind of dyspnoea arising in consequence of delirium, and that he made a universal pronouncement about it in the Prognostic — these points too I consider to stand sufficiently established, and they will be confirmed no less also through what is to be said next. For indeed it would have been right that not very much be said about it; but on account of those who have gone astray in their reasonings concerning the nature of respiration, and who then, out of contentiousness, behave shamelessly, we too have been compelled to say more than is fitting, in case we might somehow be able, at least now, to bring them over to the better. But there is, as it seems, no dye so fast as the attachment of those who, without reasoning, hold to bad doctrines. For it is not possible to persuade otherwise those who have been reared in them, inasmuch as they have neither been trained in the demonstrative methods nor have procured for themselves at all any criterion of things true and false, but — most of them, at any rate — do not even wish there to be one, and hate this very wisdom.

One of such men, then, once showed us a patient who was delirious, yet breathing neither large nor [834] rare, and, laughing — or rather guffawing shamelessly — and making sport of Hippocrates and of us, he went off, without granting us any discussion or enduring to listen to anything, although we promised to teach him that the phenomenon does not conflict either with what is said by us or with what has been written by Hippocrates. For he says that large and rare breath is a mark of delirium, not, however, that if someone is delirious, this person in every case breathes rare and large; and what is said by us professes this very same thing, since we neither counterfeit nor alter anything of what he wrote, but add only the exegeses and the demonstrations. But if, my good man, I said, you have now discovered that in all who are delirious the breath becomes rare and large, you clearly show that you have read none of the writings of Hippocrates, although you indeed pretend to condemn them, as having, I suppose, read them previously.

But that man went off before learning anything useful. You, however, who are engaging with these writings, if you truly love the truth, listen to Hippocrates, who in the third book of the Epidemics, in the case of a certain patient, [835] Pythion by name, writes as follows in the account of the seventh day: "At night much disturbance; he talked deliriously; he slept not at all." Then next, on the eighth day, thus: "Late he grew warm again; he was deranged." And after this again, on the ninth: "About sunset he was distressed; he talked deliriously." As, then, you have listened to these things, so listen in turn to what sort of form of dyspnoea occurred in this Pythion. For you will learn that he breathed neither large nor rare, although he was delirious. Now Hippocrates mentioned the dyspnoea that occurred in him twice in all throughout the whole account, on the second day and on the eighth. But I shall set out first the passage concerning the eighth, on which day he says the man both was deranged and breathed with difficulty, writing as follows: "Eighth day: in the morning he slept a little, but suddenly chilling, loss of voice, breath thin and diminished; late he grew warm again; he was deranged." Here, then, he has written one directly after the other that his breath was thin and diminished and that he was deranged, on one and the same day, this eighth.

Is it not then, by Zeus, already clear that Hippocrates does not say that in every [836] delirium the breath becomes rare and large? Unless, you there, you think that the diminished differs in no way from the large. For if that is so, it is clear that you do not even know what 'to diminish' is, and you think it the same as 'to increase'. Do not, then, learn such things from us, but go to those who teach the first letters. But just as the man who is ignorant of 'to diminish' did not learn these things, so neither has he read the writings of Hippocrates. For he would certainly have found in them countless times both 'to diminish' and 'to be diminished' and 'diminution', inflected everywhere in almost every number, gender and case, signifying the opposite of increase and of increasing, so that the diminished too would be the opposite of the increased. If, then, the increased is large, the diminished is small. So too, when he was narrating the second day of Pythion, he called him short-breathed. For short-breathing indicates that both the activity itself becomes short and also the rest; just as long-breathing, conversely, indicates that both are lengthened.

And yet, even if only one of the two were indicated, the point that the breathing does not become large and rare in all those who are delirious would even so have been conceded. For rare and large breathing is long in both respects, both in the activity and in the rest; whereas short-breathing is in every case short in at least one of the two, just as thin and diminished breath is in every case short. Hippocrates himself, then, clearly knows that large and rare breathing does not of necessity belong to all those who are delirious; yet this does not conflict with his pronouncement concerning this kind of dyspnoea. For rare and large breathing is proper to delirium, and for this reason it will of necessity indicate it; it is not the case, however, that if someone is delirious he of necessity breathes large and rare.

For we said that rare and large breathing is not an inseparable attribute of delirium, but a property of it, just as doing geometry, practising carpentry, philosophising, practising rhetoric, and countless other things, each of which belongs to none of the other animals except man alone, and for this reason is called a property of him, yet [838] not something inseparable, as the rational is. For not every property is straightaway also inseparable. And just as dialectic, which is reviled by them, taught us these things, so too it taught us that an axiom of this sort, 'if he breathes large and rare, he is delirious', is neither the same as 'if he is delirious, he breathes large and rare', nor is it necessary that they be true together. For these do not convert (ἀντιστρέφειν) with one another, but only invert (ἀναστρέφειν). So then, just as no one can win at the Olympic games without having trained long beforehand, so neither can anyone become a defender of the truth in arguments without having learned the wrestling-holds that exist in these too.

And just as those who are wholly ignorant of wrestling-holds do not even know how to fall gracefully, but sometimes, lying on their backs on the ground, keep their grip and throttle and do not let go, in the same way, I think, those who are ignorant of the art that concerns arguments, having often manifestly fallen a most shameful fall, are so far from feeling shame that they even think they have won; as indeed does the man who points to a deranged patient breathing small, and then thinks that by means of this [839] phenomenon the pronouncement of Hippocrates has been refuted. This man, at any rate, having fallen a most shameful fall, thought he had thrown his opponent. For how is it not most shameful, on the one hand to be found to have read nothing of the writings of Hippocrates, and for this reason to think that what was written by him elsewhere again was said emptily; and on the other hand not even to understand what is said, but to mishear and to think that the statement that large and rare breathing is a sign of derangement is the same as the statement that the aforesaid dyspnoea follows derangement in every case? Then what wonder is it that those who do not know even matters so small as these are blind in their reasonings about cures? But these small matters evidently depend on other matters, themselves also small, yet neglected by them. For not knowing which faculty governs the respiratory activity is the origin of such errors; and that was not known because it was not known beforehand whence one must procure the premises for demonstrations.

For it is in this wrestling-bout that those who have been left untrained, and those who are utterly ignorant, suffer falls of such magnitude; and it has been demonstrated by us elsewhere, and especially in the second book On the Movement of the Muscles, [840] that those who said that respiration is an involuntary activity happened to go astray because they were unable to derive the premises for the demonstration from the very essence of the matter, but followed the other things as accidents. But Hippocrates, who looked at the very nature of things and disregarded the others as accidents, in general pronounced firmly, through the Prognostic: 'breathing that is large and at long intervals signifies delirium'; and in particular, through what appears in diseases, he tested the statement with the most extreme tests for exactness, which, I think, one would marvel at, if one were willing to apply one's mind to what is said; for one will learn that upon all deliria there follows large and rare breath according to their own proper account, not however in all who are delirious, but only in those who do not, because of some other condition greater than the delirium, have their respiration altered in a different way.

But let him first allow me to add the account of one sick woman, recorded in the third book of the Epidemics, both for the demonstration of what has already been said and for the discovery [841] of what now lies before us. He begins his account of her in the following manner: 'In Thasos the wife of Dealces, who lay sick on the Leion, was seized by an acute fever with shivering, arising from grief; from the beginning she kept wrapping herself up, and throughout to the end, always silent, she groped about, plucked, scratched, picked at hairs; tears and again laughter; she did not sleep; irritation from the bowels, nothing passed; she drank small amounts when reminded; urines scanty, thin, having no sediment; fevers slight to the hand; coldness of the extremities. On the ninth day she raved much, and again settled down, silent.' So then, that from the beginning and throughout to the end this woman was delirious, we have learned; for not one single form of delirium befell her, nor a trivial one, but many and strong ones, some while she was silent, others while she was speaking, and some with tears, others indeed with laughter. Let us next hear Hippocrates too, as to what form of dyspnoea he says occurred in her. He writes thus: 'On the fourteenth day the breath was rare, large, at long intervals, and again she was short-breathed.'

Here, at any rate, "short-breathed" is clearly said once again by way of opposition to the woman who has great and rare [842] breath, and no one any longer, not even if he were altogether the most obtuse, would be in doubt that Hippocrates does not say that in all who are delirious the respiration becomes rare and great. At any rate, in the case of one and the same woman he mentions each of the two kinds of difficult breathing in succession, and proceeding a little further he writes somewhat as follows: "On the twentieth, much talking, and again she settled down, voiceless, short-breathed." Then, having said, "on the twenty-first she died," at the end of the whole account he has added the following: "In this woman throughout the breath was rare, great; she was insensible of everything; she kept wrapping herself up." It is clear, then, from everything we have cited, that Hippocrates knew that sometimes the great and rare breath occurs in those who are delirious, sometimes its opposite, and sometimes both, befalling the same person in turn. And I think I shall show you, if you apply your mind and do not listen carelessly to what is said, that in the very patients whom he described, the cause of each of the aforesaid differences is indicated by him.

I shall begin from the case of illness last [843] cited by us, that of the wife of Dealces, concerning which, having completed the whole account, and then, as is his custom, recapitulating briefly the chief points that hold it together, he writes as follows: "In this woman throughout the breath was rare, large; she was without perception of all things." For one among all these things is also the need for respiration, and this too she neglected for a longer time, because she perceived nothing; and as in this a long interval of rest was produced, the breath became rare, the choice setting out toward the activity only then for the first time, when it came near to destruction and suffocation. And just as this woman did not drink sufficiently—for she drank small amounts, he says, when people reminded her—so neither did she breathe before she was reminded by the force of being suffocated, which pricks and goads and rouses to the activity far more violently than those who remind one to drink. But having begun to breathe, she nonetheless recalled the whole previous deficit by the largeness of the activity, like those who sigh in griefs and in weeping.

But those people suffer this from a twofold cause: both because they are absorbed in the object of their concern, over which they grieve, [844] and on this account, having breathed more sparsely and more shallowly over many successive activities (ἐπὶ πολλαῖς ἐνεργείας), and then being forced by what is lacking, they have been compelled to make up the whole of it all at once; and, in addition, because in states of grief both the pneuma and the heat move inward, and in such conditions a great deal of heat, gathered imperceptibly and little by little in the depth, when it first distresses the person, necessarily makes him breathe more largely. But in the conditions of those who are delirious, the necessity arising from the first cause is similar, whereas that arising from the second no longer obtains. For in these people the heat certainly does not move inward more than outward, unless some other symptom happens by chance to supervene. Those who are deranged also differ from those who are grieving in the ordinary way by the fact that they have fever. And indeed Hippocrates himself is found using the term 'recalling' (ἀνάκλησις), as on another occasion also, when speaking about Philiscus: 'in this man the breathing throughout was as if he were recalling it.' What, then, 'at intervals' (διὰ χρόνου) means—this too it is right to explain.

For if 'much' (πολλοῦ) were omitted, the phrase 'at intervals' (διὰ χρόνου) could mean the same as what is said in the Prognostic: 'breath that is breathed large and at [845] long intervals signifies derangement.' But if this were so, the same thing would be said twice in succession in the case of the wife of Dealces and of the young man in Meliboea. For he writes in the same way concerning both: 'breath rare, large, at intervals.' If 'much' were added, what is said would become as follows: 'breath rare, large, at long intervals'; and 'rare' would then be said twice. Are we not, then, to suppose that 'much' is omitted—or rather, not omitted in the way we have just said, but otherwise and in another manner, so that what is said amounts to this: 'breath large and rare, not continuously nor in succession, but at longer intervals'? For if it happened that all the respirations continuously and in sequence became large and rare, we are to suppose that he does not add 'at intervals' to such cases, but writes simply 'breath large and rare'; whereas if the majority of the respirations did not become large and rare, but some few of that kind occurred intermittently, then he no longer calls it simply rare and large, but adds 'at intervals.'

Or does what is said about the wife of Dealces [846] at the end of the whole account conflict with this too? For he says this: "breathing throughout rare and great"; and yet higher up, at the fourteenth day, he said: "breathing rare and great, at intervals." For clearly what he here called "at intervals" (διὰ χρόνου), this in what follows he has called "throughout" (διὰ τέλεος). What, then, is "throughout"? Evidently that which occurs up to the end, through the whole of the disease. But with this what is said at the fourteenth day would seem to conflict: "breathing rare and great at intervals, and again short-breathed." For how, if through the whole time the breathing was great and rare, has "and again short-breathed" been added? For if there was any whole period when she was short-breathed, she was not long-breathed throughout. And indeed, that he meant her to have been long-breathed throughout, even if not through this expression at the fourteenth day, yet at least at the end, when he said "throughout," is clearly shown, and it will be agreed by all who are accustomed to listening to Hippocrates' diction.

For not once or twice but very many times is the expression 'through to the end' (dia teleos) found in him, and it is applied in [847] no other case than when he wishes to indicate 'throughout the whole time'. So this remains in every way a difficulty, whether we suppose that 'through to the end' itself indicates 'at intervals', or something else. And yet perhaps it is not even a difficulty, but we are vexing ourselves in vain. For what intervenes rarely does not, in any of the things so stated, interrupt the pronouncement made in universal terms—just as if we were also to speak thus: in this woman the breath was large and rare throughout the whole time, but occasionally, as a rare occurrence, short-breathing intervened. And that such a usage is customary with Hippocrates himself can be shown both from the other books and from the third book of the Epidemics itself, in which this patient too is recorded. For when narrating the pestilential constitution he began somewhat as follows: 'a year southerly, rainy, windlessness through to the end.' And proceeding a little further he says: 'the Etesian winds blew slight and intermittent.'

But he called the year windless for this very reason, that neither any other winds nor the so-called Etesian winds blew continuously and to any noteworthy degree, but slightly and in a scattered fashion. [848] And when writing of Apollonius at Abdera, the thirteenth case after this constitution, once he had discussed all his days during the disease, he added at the end of the whole account: "delirious dia teleos"; and yet a little above he had written about him in these very words: "About the twenty-fourth day, by way of alleviation; in other respects in the same condition, but he was in his senses for a little while." But his being in his senses for a little while was not sufficient to overturn the statement concerning the patient as a whole, and for this reason he rightly said "delirious dia teleos," that is, up to the end, which has the same force as "throughout the whole disease." Accordingly—for it is now necessary to put a head upon the argument—(it is established that) dia chronou is not the same as dia teleos.

And since this has been shown, let us next state the cause on account of which in some of those who are delirious the breath becomes rare and large throughout the whole disease, while in some it never does; and in some [it is so] for the greater part of the time, with either the breath that is simply different, or even the contrary one, intervening only rarely, whereas in others, conversely, the large and rare [breath occurs] rarely, [849] and frequently either the contrary one or the one that differs in whatever way; and in some, each equally. Let us here again recall what was demonstrated in the preceding book concerning the simple conditions. For pain alone, arising in one of the parts moved in the respirations, was shown to render the whole respiration small and frequent; delirium alone, the one contrary to it, the rare and large; increase of the heat, the large and frequent; and cooling, the contrary of this, the small and rare. If, then, the order of the respiration is confounded by delirium alone, the breath will be large and rare throughout; if by pain alone, small and frequent; but if both come together, then, when the pain prevails strongly, the alteration arising from the delirium is wholly imperceptible; but when the pain is moderate, it will come about that the respiration is altered either more from the pain and less from the delirium, or the reverse, or equally from both.

For derangement is not at all able completely to efface the alteration arising from pain, except if it itself should be [850] great and exceedingly vehement, while the pain is small and faint; pain, however, when it is strong, completely overcomes the dyspnoea arising from derangement, so that it does not appear at all. So too, if derangement is combined with some one of the other conditions, it will produce now one form of respiration, now another, according as it prevails, or is prevailed over, or is of equal strength, or now, as it may happen, prevails, and again at another time of the disease is prevailed over. We shall show, then, that in the books of the Epidemics too he teaches this very thing through the patients recorded in them. And it will be shown evidently and clearly once we have first said a little about the purpose of Hippocrates. For the ancients suppose that he writes down everything that happens to the sick, as Thucydides also does; but it is not so; rather, this very thing is what is most opposite in the writings of Hippocrates as compared with those of Thucydides.

For the one, Thucydides, writes everything that is known even to laymen, omitting none of it at all, whereas Hippocrates writes few of these things—only as many as make a difference to the whole condition in which the patient was in danger— [851] but a very great many other things, overlooked by laymen, yet furnishing a thoroughly technical and precise diagnosis, and often capable of escaping even the best physicians themselves. But this man, being brief in his manner of expression and thinking it right to write nothing that will not also be of great benefit, will seem to you, conversely, to have departed from his proper wits when he writes down things that did not happen at all to the sick man, indicating this very point, that it did not happen. For would not one who omits even most of the things that did happen seem to be raving when he dwells on things that did not happen? But if you understood that for the same cause he both omits the former and writes the latter, then I think you would admire him. For that man wrote nothing that is commonplace, nor anything that could occur to a commonplace physician. These matters too have been demonstrated by us both in many other works and in particular in those on the anatomy of Hippocrates, and not least also in those on the plague in Thucydides. Keeping these things in mind, then, you will perceive what is being said without difficulty.

For I am going to show, even if it will seem paradoxical to someone, that many of those written up in the Epidemics breathed with difficulty, yet that Hippocrates says nothing about their [852] dyspnoea, because it was clear and evident to all physicians. For if it happened that someone's sternum, or ribs, or the parts about the collarbones and the pharynx became inflamed, and on this account he of necessity breathed small and frequent, as was demonstrated in the preceding book, Hippocrates would not have thought it worth writing either the kind of the dyspnoea or, in the first place, that he became dyspnoeic. For such a kind of dyspnoea is very common, being seen almost every day in peripneumonic and pleuritic and synanchic patients, and in all, simply, in whom something in the thorax and the lung is inflamed. And upon inflammations of the liver too, and especially those at its convex parts, and those of the spleen, and those at its head, and those of the peritoneum, this kind of dyspnoea follows.

But also in those whose stomach is inflamed, and still more if its mouth and its gullet (stomachos) are, and in those in whom one of the membranes or of the muscles at the hypochondrium, or the diaphragm itself, is inflamed—in all these the breath becomes small and frequent; [853] and often too one of the small intestines, and especially those about the jejunum, and the upper parts of the colon, when inflamed to a greater degree, have compelled the person to breathe with difficulty in this way—"inflammation" (phlegmone) being understood here as the hard, hot and painful swelling, as Erasistratus is accustomed to call it and all the more recent physicians, since almost no one is unaware that the ancients used this name for the burning heat (phlogosis). It has also been shown in the book before this one that in dropsical patients and in those overfilled either with drink or with food, in pregnant women, and in the pot-bellied the breath becomes small and frequent, and, to speak generally, in all in whom any one of the respiratory organs is constricted. For thus also asthmatics and those with lung-disease (pneumonodeis) and empyics, and those whose spine is greatly distorted, and those in whom there is a formation of unconcocted tubercles either in the thorax or in the lung, and in general all in whom there is a scirrhus or some other considerable swelling of any whatsoever of all the aforementioned parts, must of necessity breathe small and frequent.

Neither, then, can these patients escape the notice [854] even of the ordinary run of physicians, nor can their conditions, upon which dyspnoea necessarily follows. For both the conditions are plain, and the form of the dyspnoea is evident, and it occurs in many people almost every day. But that Hippocrates writes down nothing that is so plain as this has been demonstrated many times. For Thucydides wrote the things that happened to the sick as a layman for laymen, but Hippocrates as a craftsman for craftsmen. Let us now, then, speak also of the patients themselves who suffered dyspnoea, in whose cases he did not see fit to state—not merely the form of the dyspnoea—but not even this one thing alone and simply, that they suffered dyspnoea.

But since the books of the Epidemics are seven in all, and of these the seventh seems to everyone to be clearly spurious, both later and put together by revision, while the fifth is not by the great Hippocrates, the son of Heraclides, but by the younger one, the son of Draco; and the second and the fourth and the sixth have seemed to some to be by the son of Hippocrates, to others to be by Hippocrates himself, not, however, as writings, nor as intended to be circulated among the Greeks, but rather as notes [855]; while to some, who indeed seem to me to have grasped the character of the books more accurately, the five seem to have been written by Thessalus, and two to be by the great Hippocrates, and for this reason, I suppose, to have been entitled "the things from the small tablet", evidently because Thessalus was eager to gather into one place everything that his father happened to have written, so that nothing should be lost; and it is agreed by almost everyone that the only remaining ones of these seven books that are by the great Hippocrates are the first and the third—it seemed reasonable to me first to take in hand the patients recorded in these books, and after that also those in the other books of the Epidemics, joining directly to them, according to the affinity of the discussions, also whatever has been said by him about difficulty of breathing in his other writings. And indeed, first of all let us mention Anaxion, whom, as he himself says, an acute fever seized; continuous pain of the right side; he coughed dry, and did not spit during the first days.

And first let us show this very thing: why it is that Hippocrates, although he is a man of few words, when it was possible to say it [856] in a single word, namely that Anaxion was pleuritic, nevertheless, having thus stated the symptoms belonging to this disease, chose rather to make his account of him by means of those. For such a thing is not his habit; on the contrary, it is his practice always to reduce the particulars to a single name and heading; nor indeed is it possible that one who writes not a single thing at random should now write in this way by chance. What, then, is the cause? To each of the diseases some symptoms belong of necessity, others for the most part. And of those that belong of necessity themselves there are several varieties: some are seen very frequently, and for this reason are believed to be proper to the nature of the disease; others very rarely, and on account of some peculiar and exceptional circumstance that has befallen.

Hippocrates, then, whenever the customary forms of the symptoms are present, is content at that point with the general name of the disease alone; but whenever one of the rare ones occurs, immediately after the general and common appellation of the whole disease he specifies that one; and if he should ever observe several forms of affections beyond the common and customary nature, each requiring its own proper determination, [857] at that point he passes over the general name and recounts straightaway each of the particulars, since from these the former too is made clear. To pleuritics, then, there occur of necessity the pain of the side, together with the fever, and the difficulty of breathing and the cough; for it is not possible for someone to be pleuritic and yet for all of these not to be present in him; but that something from the inflammation be brought up together with the coughs is not necessary, though it happens for the most part. So too the form of what is brought up is reddish, or yellowish, or frothy. And just as among the things mentioned one is customary and another unusual, so too among the very things that occur of necessity some forms are seen very frequently, others rarely. And so Hippocrates, in the case of the patient now before us, Anaxion, since the particular affections required determination, being of the rarer form, and since he knew that, once these were determined, the pleuritic concurrence would be clearly recognised, judged it superfluous to write what was in any case going to be understood even without being written down.

For, he says, an acute fever seized him, and a continuous pain of the right side, [858] and he coughed dry things, that is to say, dry little coughs (βηχία). So you have learned not only that there was fever, but also what kind of fever; for 'acute', he says. Nor only that there was pain of the side, but also what kind, namely continuous. Nor only that there were coughs, but also what sort and which, namely dry and without expectoration. And in this same statement you have also learned that this man was pleuritic; for in none of all diseases does the conjunction of the affections mentioned occur, except in pleurisy. Through a single statement, then, it has been shown both that the man was wrestling with pleurisy and with what kind of pleurisy. But since dyspnoea follows pleurisies of necessity, he omitted to write that he was also dyspnoeic. For if he had had anything strange and rare to say about this too, he would not have kept silent; but since, as it seems, it preserved its customary form, he reasonably omitted it. And just as he passed over these things, so he wrote in others, which neither belong to pleurisies of necessity, nor for the most part, nor can be inferred from what has been said. For what does he say? Thirsty, sleepless, and urines of good colour, copious, thin.

Then adding, [859] "on the sixth day delirious, and to the warm applications nothing gave way." None of these things belongs to pleurisies either of necessity or for the most part. And if you listen to him narrating also with regard to the seventh day, you will recognise more clearly the man's intention. It runs thus: "On the seventh day in distress; for the fever intensified, and the pains did not abate, and the coughs were troublesome, and he was dyspnoeic." Here he made mention of dyspnoea, when he was constructing an inference that the man was in a bad condition, enumerating it too among the others, those that had befallen him from the beginning and had neither ceased nor abated. For he says that the fevers even intensified further, while the remaining three—for four were found to be the things that complete the pleuritic syndrome—remained in the same state, he says: the pains, the coughs, the dyspnoeas; reasoning from the very essence of the disease that the man was in distress. For if, of the affections constituting it, which were four, three remained in the same condition while the fourth became worse, it is clear to everyone that the man was in a bad way.

You see clearly, then, that it was because he [860] needed it for the prognosis of the state of the disease that he mentioned the dyspnoea, and he would not otherwise have mentioned it. And for this reason I took up this patient first, before the others, in order to show that the dyspnoea about which he said nothing at the beginning, since he had no need of it at all, he now mentions not without good reason. For if you attend to the wording, you will find that it indicates this. On the seventh day, he says, in pain. For the fever, he says, intensified, and the pains did not remit, and the coughs were troublesome, and he was dyspnoeic. For here, as I said, he indicates that one thing has intensified, while the others remain the same. For what he indicated by saying 'did not remit', this one must understand as applying in common to the remaining ones as well, the coughs and the dyspnoea, such a mode of expression being most customary not only with Hippocrates but also with almost all the other ancients. For just as the pains did not remit at all, so too the coughs were troublesome, likewise, clearly, not remitting at all, and he was dyspnoeic, likewise, clearly, with the dyspnoea not remitting at all.

And the very word 'was' itself also [861] indicates the same thing as 'as before'. For he did not say 'he became dyspnoeic', although he could have said so—or rather, he would most certainly have said so, if this affection had supervened on the seventh day, not having been present before. But evidently it did not supervene, for it was altogether necessary that it should have been established from the beginning together with the other symptoms, and Hippocrates taught properly, omitting it at the beginning of the account but mentioning it afterwards. In the case of very many other patients, however, just as he omitted it at the beginning, so too he does not appear to mention dyspnoea even as the account proceeds. I shall set down all of them in order, both those written up in the first book of the Epidemics, as I said, and those in the third, having first added what remains of the exposition concerning the patient described above.

Just as, then, we would have known from the very nature of the disease that he was dyspnoeic, even if it had not been stated by Hippocrates afterwards, so too it is not unclear that the form of his dyspnoea was small and frequent, even if Hippocrates does not write it; for just as it is evident that pleuritic patients breathe with difficulty, [862] so too that they breathe small and frequent; and we said earlier that Hippocrates writes nothing of the things that are clearly known even to others. And yet this man also became deranged; at any rate he speaks thus about him: 'on the sixth day, delirious.' But this, not as a disease by nature productive of derangement but as an affection supervening upon strong pleurisies, was surely not going to prevail over the alteration arising from the pain, nor by itself to stamp the form of the dyspnoea; whereas the pain in the side, being strong, was in any case going to alter the respiration by itself. But if, by supposition, the pain had been faint and the derangement violent, the derangement would certainly have overcome the pain, either completely or for the most part; and thus such a patient would have breathed either throughout the whole disease large and rare, or for the most part thus, but occasionally small and frequent; and Hippocrates would certainly have indicated this beforehand, as in the case of the young man in Meliboea. For this man had indeed a certain tension in the hypochondrium, somewhat soft, but he also became greatly deranged.

At any rate he writes thus about the tension: [863] "tension of the hypochondrium, somewhat lax, oblong, on both sides"; and about the delirium thus: "on the tenth of the days he became delirious quietly, on the fourteenth he talked much nonsense, on the twentieth he went mad," he says. Now the word "went mad" alone would have been sufficient for him to indicate the magnitude of the delirium; but the fact that the young man was orderly and silent is also no small augmentation of its magnitude, if indeed in the Prorrhetic too he says that even bold answers, let alone the deliriums themselves, are bad in orderly persons. For it was certainly not for any other reason that in the narrative of the tenth day he added the remarks about the character of the young man. But so that we should not suppose, since it is written "he became delirious quietly," that the delirium was something simple and ordinary, for this reason he adds "but he was orderly and silent"; and from all these things, then, he indicated the vehemence of the delirium. As for the tension in the hypochondrium on both sides, someone might perhaps think that it would make the breath small and frequent; but through the very words he wrote about it he indicated that it was, with good reason, overcome by the delirium.

For he did not simply [864] say, "there was a tension in the hypochondrium," but added "somewhat slack" (ὑπολάπαρος), showing that it was not accompanied by a great swelling; for λαπαρόν means "empty." And by "elongated" he indicates the opposite of what he himself often calls "the drawn-up hypochondrium." For when it is stretched by the diaphragm, then it is drawn up and wholly hidden, being pulled into the thorax; but when by one of the parts below, then the tension appears elongated, for there is nothing in front to conceal it, as in the case of the thorax there are the spurious ribs and the sternum. Not only from these things, then, is it clear that the condition in the hypochondrium was altogether slight with respect to the generation of difficulty of breathing, but also from the very fact that Hippocrates added nothing about its pain. For he would not have kept silent, if it had been painful, since it is his custom not to pass over idly any of such things.

If, then, these things were altogether slight — for there was neither any great swelling in it nor pain, nor did it press upon the diaphragm, but it was stretched out over the whole belly — whereas the delirium lacked nothing [865] toward being greatest and most severe, it was reasonable that the condition in the hypochondrium was completely overcome by it, so that throughout the whole disease the respiration became rare and large. For this reason, then, Hippocrates also mentions both together, the form of the dyspnoea and the condition in the hypochondrium. The text runs thus: 'breath rare, large, at intervals; tension of the hypochondrium, somewhat slack' — so that no one should pass over the statement idly, but, having read one after the other two conditions which are by nature such as to produce opposite forms of dyspnoea, should investigate the cause of the delirium's completely prevailing and of the tension in the hypochondrium's being overcome. But we for our part have both stated the cause and explained the man's intention, and we must now pass on and go through the remaining part of the discussion proposed.

For when the delirium completely overcomes the opposite condition, this alone, according to its own power, alters the respiration, as has been written in the case of the young man described above, the one recorded last in the third book of the Epidemics; but indeed, that when the pain completely [866] prevails, nothing of the dyspnoea belonging to delirium shows itself at all, we have shown in the case of Anaxion, who is himself also recorded in the third book of the Epidemics, the eighth after the pestilential constitution; and in turn, in the case of the wife of Dealces, whom we also mentioned earlier, recorded as the eighth from this man and the fifteenth after the pestilential constitution, that for the most part the delirium prevails, but occasionally it is also overcome. But the passages I appended a little earlier, when I was explaining what sort of thing "at intervals" means; now, however, I shall also state the conflicting conditions themselves, following here too the wordings spoken by Hippocrates. Now no painful condition appears to have befallen this woman, but chilling prevailed, the innate heat withering away. For from what has been written about her—"fevers slight to the hand, coldness of the extremities"—this is shown, and from her wrapping herself up throughout the whole disease. For having said, "from the beginning she kept wrapping herself up," afterwards, at the end of the whole account, he says, "she kept wrapping herself up continually." But also the fact that it began from grief agrees with these things. For what does he say?

[867] "A fever with shivering seized her as a result of grief." But the shivering fever itself also came about through the same cause. And indeed the fact that what she drank passed straight through the belly, not being retained even for a short time, is the greatest evidence that the innate heat was being extinguished. And the skin that is καρφαλέον (parched) is skin that has been dried out; and together with such drynesses the innate heat perishes as well. And indeed that these things occurred in her case is shown by the following words. For "on the seventeenth day," he says, "disturbed irritations from the bowel; then the very drinks passed through, and nothing was retained; she was insensible to everything; a parched tension of the skin." With good reason, then, throughout the whole disease the large and rare breathing prevailed, while at times the short breathing, which follows upon states of chilling, also intervened. I shall remind you now as well of the passages, as I have already cited them earlier: "On the fourteenth day, breathing rare, large, at intervals, and again short-breathed. On the twentieth, much talking; again she became settled; voiceless, short-breathed. On the twenty-first she died. In her case throughout to the end the breathing was rare, large."

Here, then, the derangement prevailed over the cooling, [868] and for this reason the patient was observed to be short-breathed only rarely, but long-breathed throughout the whole disease. Conversely, in the case of Pythion, whom I also mentioned earlier, there was short-breathing throughout the whole disease, while long-breathing occurred only seldom on occasion—reasonably so, for two conditions, causes of short-breathing, were set in opposition to the derangement, pain and cooling, both of which are of a nature to make the respiration small, but the pain with density, the cooling with rarity. Now that he was deranged has been written many times in these very words by Hippocrates himself, so that this could escape no one; nor indeed the matter of the pain in the belly, for this too has been written clearly as follows: 'in the belly, heaviness with pain'; and that he had been cooled, and that the innate heat was wasting away, is clear from the following: 'on the second day, about midday, coldness of the extremities, more so in the parts about the hands and the head'; then next, in the account of the third day, 'late, about sunset, he became slightly cooled'; and indeed on the fourth day, not only that there was coldness, but also that he became warm again after a time, has been added in writing.

And more clearly, [869] when narrating the eighth day, he says: "In the morning he slept a little, but quickly a chill, and late in the day he was warmed again." And again, on the tenth day, "much chilling," he says. From these, then, it is clear that there was also chilling, and not only pain and delirium, in the case of Pythion. And that short-breathing prevailed, but that there was also some long-breathing, would become clear in the narration of the second day. For it is written thus: "short-breathed for a long time." For this phrase, "a long time," is indicative both of the fact that the short-breathing was not the only kind present, and of the fact that it predominated over the long-breathing. This Pythion too is written up in the third book of the Epidemics, the third after the pestilential constitution, so that it is open to each person on his own to dwell at greater length on the passages of the ancient, in order that we may not, by transcribing them all, make our discussion long. But also, that we deliberately omit no statement contrary to what is said by us, anyone who goes to the books themselves would be most fully persuaded.

And for this reason we ourselves indicate in which of the books the patient about whom we happen on each occasion to be speaking is recorded, [870] and what number he is, whether one counts from the beginning or from the constitution (katastasis), so that no one, on account of these matters, should delay and, shrinking from the search, either trust us without testing, which we do not want, or suspect that we too are tampering in our citations (παραγράφοντας), which indeed many of the commentators have done. But those men for this very reason keep silent about the books, and deliberately conceal those from which on each occasion they cite the passages, whereas we indicate not only these, but also the very places and the headings, so that what one wants may be found more easily; for we know that those who have read the whole section of the book from which we cite the passage will have a firmer confirmation of what we say. The sequence of the argument, then, compelled us to mention the aforesaid patients, since we wished to make clear in what manner sometimes delirium alone produces the dyspnoea, overcoming the contrary condition, and sometimes, being overcome, it becomes completely effaced; and at one time it prevails for the most part, the differing dyspnoea occurring only rarely, while at another time it is overpowered, itself showing through only as a rare occurrence.

And it is now clear, [871] as we said at the beginning, that whoever has the breath large and rare in every case has delirium as well, whereas whoever has delirium does not in every case have the breath large and rare. But let us add to the account what still remains of the matters proposed, going through all the patients recorded in the first and the third book of the Epidemics, from the first to the last of all, giving our account the same order which the written text itself also has. Now the first of all, Philiscus: that he both became delirious and had the breath large and rare we showed in the preceding discussions, setting out the passage of Hippocrates himself; but that he had no pain at all in any of the parts in whose affection we said the respiration becomes small and frequent, we shall show now, here too recalling the very wording of the ancient, which runs thus: "the spleen was raised up with a rounded swelling."

Therefore the spleen, as a viscus, is neither painful in other respects, nor does it press upon the diaphragm in the way the liver and the stomach do, unless at some time it should acquire a very great swelling at its head—which was not the case with Philiscus; and for this reason the spleen was not capable of overcoming the dyspnoea arising from the [872] delirium, since it was neither painful nor pressing upon the diaphragm. As for Silenus, who is written up next after him, and whom we also mentioned in the earlier discussions after Philiscus, that he too had rare and large breathing, and that he was delirious, we showed in those discussions; but that there was in him no disposition capable of overcoming the delirium will be shown here. For the account of the third day of the disease has this too written: 'tension of the hypochondrium, elongated on both sides, somewhat slack toward the navel.' So then the tension was receding toward the navel, and there was neither any pain nor any swelling worth mentioning. But also what is said at the end, 'palpitation of the hypochondrium', is not itself sufficient either to alter the dyspnoea arising from the delirium. For it has already been said countless times that there must either be pain in one of the parts moved in respiration, or one of the respiratory organs must be constricted, in order for the breathing to become small and frequent. Therefore neither did this Silenus, just as neither did the earlier one, Philiscus, have any other disposition capable of altering the respiration, except delirium.

[873] For there was neither pain nor compression of the respiratory organs, nor indeed was there any chilling, such as we showed in the third book of the Epidemics to have occurred in Pythion and in the wife of Dealces. The three, however, who are written up next after these, Herophon and the wife of Philinus and the wife of Epicrates, you would find, if you read through carefully the accounts concerning them, to have had a derangement too slight for the respiration to have been altered on account of it. But in Herophon the spleen was raised up, and there was, he says, tension of the hypochondrium, no longer adding somewhat slack, nor elongated, nor toward the navel, so that in him the parts about the diaphragm were inflamed, which was shown by us in the books On the Causes of Respiration to be the first and most principal organ of these. The wife of Philinus, he says, had pain in the cardia and the right hypochondrium; and the wife of Epicrates had not only the cardia, but also, he says, heaviness of the left side together with pain.

For this reason, then, he did not even add to any of these 'breath small and frequent', but was entirely silent, having the habit, as we also showed before, of omitting what is clearly [874] known to all. And most clear and familiar to all, as we also showed, was the dyspnoea consisting in smallness and frequency, with which the three patients described above of necessity breathed with difficulty. And indeed Cleanactides too, who is described after them, himself likewise of necessity breathed with difficulty on account of the pain of the left side; but not even in his case is anything written about dyspnoea, since it could be understood even without being written. This Cleanactides, however, certainly did not become delirious; whereas Meton, who is described after him, had neither a condition capable of causing pain nor one that narrowed any of the respiratory organs, nor indeed any morbid ground for delirium; but something paradoxical and not accustomed to occur befell him. For on the fifth of the days, having had a haemorrhage and having sweated, he reached a complete crisis. He was then still haemorrhaging even after the crisis while being sleepless, but he also rambled, he says, although before the crisis he had not become delirious at all. For this reason, therefore, we too said that no morbid condition of delirium came about in him.

[875] but he was talking wildly in the way that happens to those who are drunk, through a fullness of the head. And for this very reason the word 'was talking wildly' (parelegen) has been written by Hippocrates, who indicates the resemblance to drunkenness that arose in him from the fullness about the head. For there came to it, as one may infer from what happened, no small abundance of blood, upon which indeed the whole disease also reached its crisis, the head having received his entire condition. But of blood of this kind no small amount was straightway, on the fifth of the days, violently excreted together with sweat, yet a great deal more than what was evacuated remained in the head, weighing it down and compelling the man to talk wildly; whence Hippocrates used baths over the head, saying, 'he bled from the nose often after the crisis.' So that in the case of this patient he not only did not write any kind of dyspnoea, but did not even write whether he became dyspnoeic at all. For it is not in those who talk wildly in whatever manner, or in those who are drunk, but only in those who are delirious that the breath becomes great and rare.

And for this reason he says in the Prognostic: "breath drawn large and at long intervals signifies delirium." [876] But the patient after him, Erasinus, was of necessity dyspnoeic, yet the dyspnoea has been omitted for the reason often stated. For in general he nowhere appears, after first stating some condition that is painful or that compresses one of the respiratory organs, to write down next after it the dyspnoea that follows; rather he everywhere omits it, as being known to all. That Erasinus had such a condition he made clear by saying: "hypochondria raised, tension with pain"; for indeed a great inflammation is indicated, on account of which the man, even though he became delirious, did not suffer the dyspnoea proper to delirium—otherwise Hippocrates would certainly have mentioned this too. For just as he is found always omitting the dyspnoea that attends pains, the small and frequent one, because it is obvious, so, knowing that the one attending deliriums is disputed, he nowhere omitted it nor passed it over undetermined. For what is recorded in the case of Criton, who is written up next after him, has a clear cause.

For since he died on the second day most unexpectedly, [877] as one can learn from the account itself, Hippocrates reasonably omitted to say anything about dyspnoea, either because he did not observe the dyspnoea that occurred, or because he did not think it worth mentioning. For each of these is plausible: not observing it, both on account of the rapidity of the death and the astonishing character of the symptoms; for it is certainly no small marvel that a man who was going about and doing his customary activities, and then had violent pain in the great toe of his foot, should on the first day become slightly warmed and on the next day die. Since, then, there was no delay in the interval, but the man died quickly, and was not simply delirious but went raving mad, as he says, it was not possible to observe how he was breathing. For we do not even endure to come near those who have gone raving mad, but keep away from them in every way, fearing lest they inflict some harm upon us.

Either, then, he did not observe it, as we said, or he did not think it worth mentioning the kind of dyspnoea, on account of the paradoxical character of the whole concourse of symptoms, to which alone it is fitting that we direct our attention, [878] and not be drawn aside toward things that can be discovered through other patients. Next he writes about the Clazomenian, who, he says, had pain in the head and neck and loins from the beginning; but these are not sufficient to make the breathing small and frequent, except perhaps the neck. And there is also a place where this will be determined as the discussion proceeds; but the hypochondrium raised up with swelling is sufficient, so that even if this man became delirious, he did not breathe with the dyspnoea proper to delirium, since the painful affections mentioned prevailed. The wife of Dromeades, however, who comes after him, and whom I also cited right at the beginning of this book, not only became delirious but also had large and rare breathing, since no affection arose either about the thorax or in the hypochondrium of the kind that is of a nature to make respiration small and frequent.

For this reason, then, Hippocrates too, writing precisely everything that befell the woman, said: 'she began at first to have pain about the hypochondrium, nauseous, restless'; evidently because bad humours [879] there were biting the mouth of the stomach, though no inflammation was present, nor any other affection by which the breath becomes small and frequent. And indeed Hippocrates, having proceeded a little further in the account, then, having written 'pain of the hypochondrium', added 'nauseous', and then next again, 'thirsty'. Neither, then, was any of the things occurring in the hypochondrium or thorax sufficient to prevail over the delirium, nor yet was the innate heat being extinguished, as we showed happened thus in others; so that, reasonably, since no condition among those set in opposition to the delirium was able to alter the respiration, her breath became large and rare. But since there has been added 'straightway drawn up', I must note this now, so that no one may suppose that we are going to pass over it carelessly.

But now is not the time to explain it; rather, it will be examined in the book after this one, together with the other things said in a similar way. For the present we shall take in hand the three patients still remaining, who themselves also became delirious, yet did not suffer difficulty of breathing with the dyspnoea [880] proper to delirium. For this reason in the case of the first it is written: 'pain of the right hypochondrium, a somewhat slack inflammation from the inner part' — the part toward the diaphragm, evidently. In the case of the second: 'in the region of the hypochondrium a swelling with pain', and a little later, 'pain of the hypochondrium', and again in what follows, 'but around the left clavicle pain persisted'. In the case of the third of the patients — this was a woman, as was also the one before her — 'of the head', he says, 'and of the neck and of the chest strong pain', and a little later, 'the pains persisted'. These fourteen patients, then, are from the first book of the Epidemics, written in this way in succession by Hippocrates, just as we too have mentioned them; and in the third book of the Epidemics there are twelve before the pestilential constitution and sixteen after it, all of them agreeing with what we laid down from the beginning.

And I know clearly that, if I pass over them and leave it to those who wish to examine the agreement in all of them to read through privately and on their own the case-narratives written by the ancient, [881] I shall seem to do this not out of guarding against speaking at length, but because I am unable to preserve the suppositions laid down from the beginning throughout the whole discourse; but if I go through all of them in order, I shall seem to be some babbler and a prattler, myself pointlessly writing out those things which each person was capable of examining on his own. Nevertheless, if I must in any case submit to one or the other of the two unwelcome alternatives, either the suspicion of unsoundness in my doctrines, or prolixity, and I find certain mitigations for prolixity, but none for the suspicion, it is more reasonable to speak about all of them. What, then, are the mitigations of prolixity? The first is to run quickly through the patients in the discourse, no longer dwelling in the same way upon each one, but only reminding; the second is to urge those who cannot bear to listen even to things so brief to skip over them, regarding them as not even having been written. For just as at a splendid banquet, when many dishes have been prepared, one person chooses one thing and another another, the one as pleasant, the other as likely to be beneficial, so too in discourses the provision ought to be abundant, while the choice rests with those who make use of them.

[882] The first patient of all, then, whose name is Pythion, is clearly shown from the account itself to have had no basis for dyspnoea. The second, Hermocrates, began, he says, to have pain in the head and the loin; tension of the hypochondrium, somewhat slack. He did not, however, add further that the tension inclined downward and toward the navel, or that it was elongated; from which it is clear that the hypochondrium was drawn up by the inflamed diaphragm, and for this reason it also appeared somewhat slack, as having no inflammation of its own. This man, then, even if he was delirious, nevertheless the delirium was overcome by another, greater affection, just as indeed also in the case of the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth.

For in the case of the third, 'a somewhat slack tension of the right hypochondrium' is written; in the case of the fourth, 'the right hypochondrium was tense, it inclined inwards'; in the case of the fifth, 'he had pain in the neck'; and in the case of the sixth of the patients — this one was a woman — Hippocrates, having first said, 'at the beginning of the disease she had pain in the pharynx, and throughout she had redness, the uvula [883] drawn up, many fluxes, thin, small, acrid; she coughed, but brought up nothing concocted,' will a little later say, 'and there was also something congenitally consumptive'; so that in her case too the prevailing condition is clear, having formed in the respiratory organs. However, in narrating the patient after her, he begins in this manner: 'the woman with cynanche, the one at Aristion's'; and proceeding he says, 'breathing elevated' — which we too shall explain as the discussion proceeds, but for now what lies before us must be brought to completion. In the case of the eighth patient it is written: 'a somewhat slack tension of the hypochondrium on both sides'; in the case of the ninth, 'pains about the hypochondrium.' But this woman at least did not become delirious; and the next two women he says fell ill as a result of abortion, while their conditions, which he narrates, are, to state it in general, inflammations of the womb, and, in particular, all the affections that follow upon these.

And he says that one remaining woman still had pain in the heart (kardia), without adding "nauseous", but that she also sweated cold, and was shivering throughout the whole disease, and was greatly chilled, and [884] was with difficulty warmed up again, or not at all. So it is clear that she too was certainly short-breathed on account of both conditions, that of the pain and that of the chilling; yet not even in her case did Hippocrates think it worthwhile to speak about dyspnoea, as being quite obvious.

Next comes the pestilential constitution, after which again he writes as the first patient the Parian, in whose case, at the end of the account, where he writes the things that persisted continuously in the whole body, this too is added: 'sleepless with pains'; and as second the man in Thasos, about whom he says, 'coughs continuous, moist, many'; and third is Pythion, whom we have already explained, and fourth the phrenitic, and fifth the man who began suddenly to feel pain in the right thigh, and when the flux went back up to the parts about the head, straightway became delirious and straightway also died, similarly to the man in the first book of the Epidemics, who began — began from the pain at the great toe and died on the second day; so that in these cases too he wrote nothing at all about dyspnoea, for the [885] reasons we have already stated in the case of that man. The sixth neither became delirious nor had any other condition productive of dyspnoea. The seventh patient is the maiden, who because of the plethora of blood was troubled in her head in the same way as the seventh patient recorded in the first book of the Epidemics, who had a haemorrhage from the nostrils; so that whatever we have already said about him, let these things be transferred here too. The eighth patient is Anaxion, whom we explained in the foregoing. The ninth had the underlying basis of his whole disease similar to the maiden and to that man from the first book of the Epidemics who had the haemorrhage. The tenth, who is Nicodemus in Abdera, was deranged once on the sixth of the days; then, having reached a crisis on the twentieth day with a sweat, and having seemed to become free of fever, he again became feverish and again was slightly delirious. And he writes about him also the following: 'the paroxysms and the pains in his case continued to the end.' Pains of what? someone might perhaps ask. He said that he became cardialgic straightway at the beginning, and proceeding a little further he wrote 'pains of all [parts]'.

For this reason, then, the delirium too, being slight [886] and of short duration, did not alter the respiration. Next after this is the woman whose illness began from grief, concerning whom he writes: "great, continuous pains"; but also "many convulsions," he says. And in the Aphorisms he writes about convulsions thus: "In fevers, the breath stumbling is bad, for it signifies convulsion." And so, accordingly, the form of difficult breathing in this woman arose partly in consequence of the pains, partly in consequence of the convulsions; for this reason, then, although she became delirious, she did not have the large and rare [breathing], inasmuch as it was overcome by two other stronger conditions. After these there is the maiden in Larissa, written as the twelfth after the pestilential constitution, who fell ill through plethora of blood and was brought to crisis by the hemorrhage through the nostrils and by sweat and by the menses, which then appeared for the first time; she had no bodily constitution productive of any difficulty of breathing whatsoever.

As for Apollonius in Abdera, who comes after these, he says there was a swelling of the right hypochondrium with pain; but also that he was throughout large in the viscera and that pain about the hypochondrium was habitual for him, and this too [887] has been written at the beginning of the account. It is therefore nothing to wonder at if, even though he became delirious, he did not breathe with difficulty according to the form proper to delirium, possessing as he did so great a painful condition in the hypochondrium. Next after him is the woman in Cyzicus who gave birth to the twin daughters, about whom he wrote somewhat as follows: heaviness of the head and neck with pain, so that the dyspnoea too was in accordance with this. There remain after her two patients in the third book of the Epidemics, the wife of Dealces and the young man in Meliboea, both of whom became delirious and had large and rare breathing, about whom sufficient has been said earlier. But since this book of ours already has adequate size, we shall examine in the one following this all the remaining things that have been said by the ancient about dyspnoea.

[888] GALEN'S ON DIFFICULTY OF BREATHING, BOOK THREE. Having divided the discourse on difficulty of breathing into two courses of teaching, in the first of the commentaries we set forth what the physician must know about it, together with the demonstrations proper to it; while in the second, which precedes this one, and in this third itself we are making an exposition of what has been said by Hippocrates about difficulty of breathing in all his writings; so that those who aim only at the works of the art themselves, and who do not think it right, as they themselves put it, to busy themselves at all about what has been said by the ancients, have sufficiently from the first discourse everything they are eager for; whereas those who both desire and are able to learn in addition the opinion of Hippocrates may gather it from these [889] writings. Now the desire to know what has been said by the best men is common to all who are by nature lovers of what is fine; but also to be able to learn these things, which requires a longer time, no longer belongs to all alike; for many are deprived, by a great press of affairs, of the leisure for the finest things. Knowing this, then, we too went through what is urgent for the works of the art in the first of these commentaries, and separately, in sequence, we expound the opinion of Hippocrates through the remaining two writings, of which the one is the second and the other the third, according to the order from the beginning.

And anyone who intends to follow what is said in it must first have studied the second carefully, in which we showed, first, the whole purpose of Hippocrates, namely that he does not think fit to write down anything of what is commonplace, nor of what the majority of physicians know; and second, we also went through in detail all the patients in the first and third books of the Epidemics, demonstrating in the case of many of them that, even though it was necessary for the sufferers to breathe with difficulty, nevertheless he did not write it down, just as he also did not write many [890] other things which follow of necessity from what has been written—for the things which it is possible to discover even without learning them from him, if one sets out from what he has said, these he did not think it necessary to write—while in the case of many he also adds the form of the dyspnoea to the very narratives of the sick, whenever either it does not follow of necessity for the sick, or it is not readily apparent to those who read through his writings. Holding, then, to these aims now too, since we have expounded the first and the third books of the Epidemics in what precedes, we shall again make our beginning from the second, joining to it also the remaining writings of Hippocrates. And just as the first and the third are thought, by those who have judged best about these matters, not only to have been composed by Hippocrates, but also to be connected with one another by the affinity of their theory, in the same way, I think, it stands also with the contents of the second and the fourth and the sixth. For it is indeed already agreed that these too were put together by Thessalus the son of Hippocrates, who found the notes of his father himself on certain parchments or tablets, and also added not a few things himself.

The fifth and [891] seventh books of the Epidemics, however, no one, it seems to me, would judge worthy of being proper to the thought of Hippocrates; and in my own opinion not the fourth either, even if some have thought that this too was composed by Thessalus. But the Prognostic, the Aphorisms, On Waters, Places and Airs, and further On Regimen in Acute Diseases, which some entitle Against the Cnidian Sentences, are not unreasonably believed to be writings of Hippocrates himself. We shall therefore make mention of these books wherever need calls for it, and of all the others which they refer, some to Hippocrates himself, others to Euryphon, Thessalus and Polybus. We must now begin the exposition from the passage written in the second book of the Epidemics, which runs as follows: breath small, dense; large, rare; small, rare; large outward, small inward; the one drawn out, the other hurried. A double inward recall (ἐπανάκλησις), as in those who breathe in additionally; hot, cold. And this same passage is written more completely in the sixth book.

For to the three conjugations of dyspnoea itself the fourth is added there, [892] which has clearly been omitted in the second book of the Epidemics — not, in my opinion, by the writer himself; for he is evidently assembling the full number of the dyspnoeas not from some experience and memory, but from logical division; he was not, therefore, going to omit any dyspnoea. Rather, one of the ancient copyists erred; then the book, being in this condition, had already been published, and this very error was understandably preserved down to the present day, since some people engage carelessly with the books of the ancients, so as to recognise neither whether something is missing nor whether it has been expressed with a different letter, while some do recognise it but do not dare to add what is missing. For those of former times were not, like those of today, cavalier, nor ready to alter an ancient reading written in the same way in all the copies; rather, it was enough for them merely to note that here the division of the dyspnoeas is written incompletely, but in the sixth book of the Epidemics completely — the division according to greatness and smallness and frequency and rarity.

For Hippocrates is clearly interweaving these two oppositions with one another, the one according to greatness [893] and smallness and the one of rarity and frequency, and making four conjugations of dyspnoea: one in which the respiration becomes at once smaller and more frequent than that according to nature; another when it becomes at once greater and rarer; and in addition to these a third, in which it is smaller and rarer; and in addition to these a fourth, which we say has been omitted in the second book of the Epidemics, in which it becomes at once greater and more frequent. For it has been shown by me many times—even if indeed it is obvious to everyone without being shown—that two oppositions interwoven with one another produce four conjugations. And the passage in the sixth book of the Epidemics differs from the one in the second not only in this respect, but also insofar as, in what follows, when he compares the greatness of the inspiration with that of the expiration, the other conjugation has been altogether omitted in the second, the copyist here too clearly displaying either extreme negligence or rash tampering.

For if he skipped over whole phrases, he was careless in the extreme; but if, not knowing in what respect phrases that resemble one another differ, he supposed that both indicated one and the same thing, and then [894] removed the one of them, he had reached the very summit of officiousness, declaring himself a corrector of Hippocrates' writings, not a servant of them. This, indeed, it is useful to bear in mind with regard to many of the obscure passages, in which it is plausible that something has either been omitted or been miswritten. For nothing prevents us, in those passages, either by supplying what is lacking or by correcting what is erroneous, from rendering the statement complete and true. For just as rewriting the ancient passages is rash, so too, while preserving them as they are written, to resolve the difficulties by certain brief additions or alterations is the task of good exegetes. But concerning these matters I think I shall show a little later, through the actual practice, what one ought to do. For this must be done not simply, nor at random, but together with demonstrating both the truth of the matters themselves and, even before that, that the opinion of the ancient author himself is of this sort, and that both of these agree with the passage once it has been rearranged in its wording. Proceeding now to the matter before us, and setting out the more complete passage, the one in the sixth book of the Epidemics, let us see what sort of thing its meaning itself is.

For that [895] he attempts to discover all the differences of dyspnoeas from a logical division, this both seems so to those who have expounded his books, and I think it is altogether easy to infer; but whether he divides correctly, and whether he omits no kind of dyspnoea, this is no longer easy for everyone to discover; rather, the one who is to judge concerning these matters must be experienced in the method of division, and not unpractised in the doctrines of Hippocrates. Now the method says that one must look to the thing being divided, what sort of thing it is in its nature.
