For if it should be simple, one must examine the things that belong to it according to the account of its essence, how many they are and which and of what sort, and divide on the basis of these; but if it is composite, one must divide each of the two, or each of the parts, as has been said, and the whole on the basis of the manner of its composition.

The opinion of Hippocrates about the composition, whatever it may be, has been stated by us at very great length elsewhere, and has been stated also in what precedes, so that nothing prevents us, looking to these aims, from examining the passage of the Epidemics, which runs somewhat as follows: breaths small and frequent, large and rare; small and rare, [896] large and frequent; large outward, small inward; large inward, small outward; the one drawn out, the other hurried. A double inward recall, as in those who breathe in upon a breath; hot, cold. That, then, not only the fourth conjugation, that according to frequent and large, has been omitted in the second book of the Epidemics, but also that, of the two that follow, in which he compares expiration with inspiration, the second of these is written in the passage now set before us but has been omitted in the second book of the Epidemics, is easy to see. For in that book the words "large inward, small outward" are no longer added, but only the other species of dyspnoea is indicated, that in which a large breath is expired and a small one inspired. In many places, then, one can find this missing part written in as well, but in most and in the most trustworthy of the copies it has been omitted; and this at any rate makes no difference for the present purpose. For our task is to examine the more complete passage, the one now written out.

That, then, the activity of respiration as a whole is composite, made up of the inward and the outward movement of the breath, and that one of its parts is called inspiration and the other expiration, [897] has been stated in the first book right at the beginning; but even if it had not been said by us, there is hardly anyone who does not know it. And that speed and slowness are proper to nothing else among all things than motion, this too has already been said before, but let it be recalled now as well. Largeness and smallness, however, just as they are not proper to motion, so they are inseparable from everything that moves over an interval. And for this reason, in each of the two parts of respiration there will be two oppositions of differences, one according to speed and slowness, and a second according to largeness and smallness. And that of respiration as a whole there is a further opposition, constituted according to frequency and rarity, this too has been said before, as also that this opposition belongs to respiration not as a motion but as a composite thing, being made up of intervals (διαστάσεων).

So that all the differences of respiration must necessarily fall within these three genera: in speed and slowness, because these are proper to and inseparable from every motion; in largeness and smallness, because the motion of the respiratory organs is a motion over an interval; while density [898] and rarity, the third of the genera mentioned, is neither proper to nor inseparable from either of the proper and primary parts of respiration, but comes to belong to the whole as a part by a certain accident, since respiration is a composite thing made up of two contrary motions separated by rest. These, then, are the primary differences of the whole respiration. But because respiration is of a nature to act in some way and to be acted upon, there would also be another genus of differences in it, according as each of the two parts is accomplished evenly or unevenly; and indeed yet another again, belonging to the whole of it as composite, when the parts are compared with one another. This being so, one must know that the first four differences of dyspnoeas written down in the passage before us belong to the whole respiration; for density and rarity belong to neither of the parts, if indeed we remember what was said right at the beginning of the first of these commentaries.

And so too the two that follow them; for in these too the two parts of the whole respiration are compared with one another, and for this reason it has been written thus: "outward large, inward small; inward large, outward small" — breath, evidently, being understood. But the two differences that come next, [899] in which the one is called the "extended" (ἐκτεῖνον) and the other the "hurried" (κατεπεῖγον), must be considered to be proper to either one of the parts of respiration — that which, indeed, we said belongs most of all to the substance of respiration; for the "extended" is the slow, and the "hurried" is the rapid. And slowness and rapidity are inseparable from every motion.

What is said next—'double recall inward, as in those who breathe in additionally (ἐπεισπνέουσιν)'—is indeed indicative of uneven inspiration, but it demands the same antithesis in the case of expiration, which I am persuaded was omitted by the copyists who transcribed the text rather than by Hippocrates himself, if indeed he plainly mentions in other writings this kind of dyspnoea as well, as I shall show clearly in what follows. If, however, anyone thinks it was omitted by Hippocrates himself, that person chooses the worse over the better. For not to have mentioned unevenness at all in either of the two parts of respiration, but to have completely forgotten and omitted it—not even this would have been in keeping with the carefulness of Hippocrates; rather, for my part, even if what is now written about inspiration had not been written at all, [900] I would have ventured to say that this was a fault of the copyist rather than of Hippocrates—though in that case the view would at least have had some rationale for those who take the worse interpretation. But since he indicated the form of the inspiration so clearly that he not only said that the recall of the breath inward becomes double, but also added the phrase 'as in those who breathe in additionally', how could anyone still suppose that he forgot expiration? About these matters, then, more again later; but next there is added another antithesis of dyspnoeas, written at the end of the whole passage roughly as follows: 'hot, cold'—so that here too, evidently, we are to supply 'breath'. For just as the breath is breathed out great and small, and frequent and rare, so too it is breathed out hot and cold. And yet here too some, misunderstanding on the basis of what they themselves do not comprehend, 'correct' and venture to rewrite the wording, writing not 'cold and hot', as it has now been stated, but joining these words to what precedes and reading thus: 'as in those who breathe in cold upon hot' (οἷον ἐπεισπνέουσι θερμῷ ψυχρόν).

These men, then, in addition to making the text have no sense, [901] become manifest as not having even read the books of the ancient; for they would certainly have remembered what was written by him in other works about hot and cold expiration—and what reason he had either to write of these in those works or to omit them here, they would not be able to say. For if he did not consider hot and cold expiration to be among the dyspnoeas, he did not do well to mention them in other works as dyspnoeas; but if he acted rightly in those works, he did not rightly omit them now. But these matters do not stand thus: for both here they are rightly included in the division of the dyspnoeas, and what it is that they are of a nature to signify has been correctly stated in other works.

Leaving aside, then, now those who thus misunderstand the ancient and comprehend anything rather than his meaning, let us ourselves, on our own account, examine why it is that in the Prognostic treatise he writes somewhat as follows about dyspnoea: "breath that is frequent signifies pain or inflammation in the regions above the diaphragm; breathed large and at long intervals it signifies delirium; and breathed out cold [902] from the nostrils and the mouth it is already exceedingly deadly." For in this book he appears to mention only these three dyspnoeas; and yet, if there are only so many, why ever did he himself write of many more in the books of the Epidemics? But if they are so many, why ever did he mention the fewest of them in the Prognostic? Or did he think it useful to know their number, but not useful to know what sort of thing each is of a nature to indicate? Or is it that only those mentioned indicate something, while the others indicate nothing, but it is possible at some time to breathe contrary to nature while there is no condition contrary to nature in the animal? Or rather, is this so far from being true that it is altogether necessary that the condition contrary to nature in the animal itself become the cause of the dyspnoea? If, then, the condition stands in the relation of cause to the dyspnoea, it would thus be prior both in time and in order and in power. How, then, does Hippocrates appear to have passed over so great a number of dyspnoeas in the Prognostic?

For these reasons I for my part wished both to compare the exegetes with one another [903] and to investigate and to resolve the matter; but the situation is not so. For of those who expound him at present, whom would anyone even mention? And as for the earlier ones, those at least whose commentaries survive down to our time, it is possible to find many and lengthy ravings written down, but matters as essential as these have been completely omitted. But let us at any rate investigate them ourselves, even if we have no path toward their discovery handed down to us by those men.

It has indeed been stated both in the writings On the Best Sect and in those of the Therapeutic Method how one ought both to investigate and to discover all such things; but in the first of these commentaries too I showed a twofold path for the discovery of such matters, one setting out from the differences in dyspnoea, the other from the conditions in the respiratory organs, which I said was both easier and clearer; and whoever has read those writings carefully will not need many words for the solution of the present matters. But if he has either engaged with them carelessly, or is otherwise slow to learn, let the careless one, having read them through once more, come back again to these; and let the dull one do something else, knowing [904] that a small nature is not capable of learning thoroughly the thought of a great man, such as Hippocrates was. At any rate, what no one before has either proposed, or raised as a difficulty, or investigated, or discovered, I shall both propose and raise as a difficulty, and I shall say how one ought to investigate it, and with the gods' help I hope to discover it. The problem, then, has already been stated by me a little earlier: why ever did Hippocrates omit so many kinds of dyspnoea in the Prognostic? The difficulty will now be stated, after I have first recalled what was written in the first book. For in those discussions I reduced all the differences of the dyspnoeas to five genera in all, both of conditions and of dyspnoeas, so that the problem becomes still more perplexing, since the only hope still remaining has been removed.

For in all such cases, in which the differentiae of any existing thing whatsoever are said by one man or writing to be more numerous, and by another fewer, there is one sole hope of agreement: if someone could show that the one has remained at the first parts of the division, [905] while the other has gone on to subdivide. Now since this hope has been taken away from us (for it was shown in the first book that the genera neither of the conditions nor of the dyspnoeas can be reduced to a smaller number), what device for the solution of the matters now under inquiry could still be found? For, among other things, besides the fact that some of the primary genera have been left out, one might further find fault, in the Prognostic, with their having been torn apart, badly set off against one another in the division, and obscurely expressed—even though that book is clear if any other of Hippocrates' books is. And indeed what is said right at the beginning of the passage is at once unclear and undetermined: "Breath, when it is frequent, signifies pain or inflammation in the regions above the diaphragm."

For if frequent breath were not twofold, the one kind with largeness, the other with smallness, or if each of them were not the offspring of a different condition, Hippocrates would reasonably either have left it undivided, or would not have indicated the difference of what is signified in each case. But since he himself, in the books of the Epidemics, clearly recognizes the [906] frequent-and-small breath as one thing and the frequent-and-large as another, and we have demonstrated that these belong to the primary differences, he wrongly left the frequent undivided, and was content to say simply thus: "breath, when it is frequent, signifies pain or inflammation in the regions above the diaphragm." This, then, is one difficulty. Next, having mentioned the third difference in this way: "but breath drawn large and at long intervals signifies delirium" – and having stated this one alone clearly among the primary differences, he made no mention whatsoever of the dyspnoea lying next to it, the one that renders the breath rare and small; and yet, just as frequent breath was twofold, divided by largeness and smallness, so too the rare is of necessity twofold, divided by largeness and smallness. But in the Prognostic he mentioned only the one of the two, saying: "but breath drawn large and at long intervals signifies delirium"; the other, the rare-and-small together, appears to have been passed over.

So that, of the four conjugations which he wrote in the Epidemics, the first two have been stated indeterminately [907] and unclearly and confusedly, and only the third, as we said—both it itself and what is signified by it—has been written clearly. And not only in these matters would the account seem to be unclear and at the same time undetermined and to leave out the greater part, but also from what he says in what follows: "But breath exhaled cold from the nostrils and the mouth is by now very deadly." For why on earth, if he had decided to go through the differences with respect to hot and cold, did he mention the cold one alone? And further, why on earth, in the case of the other two—the one which he names indeterminately "frequent breath" and the one which, making a distinction, he names "rare and large"—did he write down only the conditions themselves, but did not indicate in what they will end, saying that pain and inflammation are signified by the frequent dyspnoea, and delirium by the dyspnoea that is at once rare and large?

But in the case of the difference according to cold he does say in what it will end; for he says that such breath is exceedingly destructive; the condition, however, from which they breathe with difficulty in this way, being the more obscure, he no longer states, although it would have been better, in the case of all the dyspnoeas, both to state the conditions themselves, [908] whatever they are, and to add to them their manner, distinguishing the mild from the malignant. He did not, then, do this, but in the case of the former dyspnoeas he indicated the conditions, in the case of the last only the manner. And what is the most inescapable of all the charges, that nothing whatever has been said about uneven dyspnoea, let this too now be added to the account. For the stretching-out and pressing breath, and that which is large outward and small inward, are indeed not themselves stated in the text of the Prognostic, but from what we went through in the first book they are found to be contained in the four conjugations of dyspnoeas; the fifth, however, the uneven, half of which he wrote in the books of the Epidemics, speaking of a double inward recall, but which in the Prognostic he omitted completely, it is not possible to find contained under any of the four conjugations in any manner whatever. The difficulties, then, are so many and of such a kind.

From this point on, however, we must not, like the majority of those who contradict Hippocrates, ourselves also readily discover the [909] difficulties while being at a loss in their solutions; rather we must first find some path toward resolution, and next confirm by demonstration the things found by means of it. What, then, is the path of resolution? For one must begin from here. One is the brevity of expression common to all the ancients and customary among them; a second is the high-mindedness of Hippocrates himself. For this man has often been shown by us to be formidable in passing over whatever is known also to the other physicians, as things that cannot be unknown to any of those who genuinely practise the art, while expounding carefully and at the same time clearly all the things that are unknown to such men. If, then, this is his custom, what wonder is it that the difference of dyspnoea in respect of greatness and rarity, which is disputed and unclear to most people, he attempted through his other writings to show to be peculiar to delirium (paraphrosyne), and in the Prognostic deemed worthy of clear teaching, whereas the differences of frequency, since these too cannot be unknown to physicians, he embraced under a single heading and indicated quickly?

For in pleurisies and peripneumonias and anginas and [910] orthopnoeas the breath becomes frequent and small; and even if there should be no pleurisy, but only pain in the region of the ribs, the breath will be frequent and small, just as also if [there is pain] about the mouth of the stomach, or the oesophagus, or the head of the spleen, or the convex parts of the liver. For indeed here too, when some pain is present, the breath must necessarily become small and frequent, and much more so if it should arise about the diaphragm and the part of it that joins the peritoneum and the muscles that lie around there. And indeed, even if the peritoneum has been affected more severely not only here but also lower down, the diaphragm perceives its injury and in this way makes the breath small and frequent. And the greater affections of the belly itself, those accompanied by pain and swelling, and [those of] the lower parts of the spleen and of the liver, no less make the breath, they too, frequent and small; and in general, whether there be some swelling pressing upon and constricting any whatsoever of the respiratory organs, or pain about some part so near to the respiratory organs that it is moved along with them when they move, the breath will be frequent and small.

The other causes [911] of these we went through in the first book, just as we also showed that, when much heat has been gathered in the respiratory organs, the breath will become frequent and large. And this too is seen almost every day in all burning fevers, so that it too could not escape anyone's notice. Moreover, that not Hippocrates alone but also nearly all the others before Erasistratus called the unnatural burning (phlogosis) 'phlegmone' has been demonstrated not by us alone but by practically all the exegetes of Hippocrates. These things, then, being laid down, it is no longer at all surprising that Hippocrates indicated both the aforesaid differentiae under a single heading, saying 'breath, when it is frequent, signifies pain or phlegmone in the regions above the phrenes', since we too are able to understand that the breath that is frequent together with smallness signifies pain, whereas that which is frequent together with largeness indicates phlegmone, that is, phlogosis; and that he reasonably added 'in the regions above the phrenes', that is, the respiratory regions, since immoderate heats below the diaphragm are unable to raise the respiration to largeness and frequency.

[912] This, then, is the way of discovery of the things under inquiry, at least as regards the primary differences; but it is necessary to add some demonstration as well to the argument. For at present it has been shown that it is not impossible that Hippocrates held this opinion; but it will be shown next that this is altogether the case. For why ever is it that in both books of the Epidemics, in the second and in the sixth, he is found dividing off these two differences of dyspnoea first of all, the former being small and frequent breath, the second frequent and large, whereas in the passage before us he is thought to be ignorant of them—in addition to the fact that immediately after these words, in the Prognostic, he writes 'rare and large'? Does he then know rare and large breath, but is ignorant of frequent and small?

And even if one of those who are zealous for the worse should say that he was able to know what in itself frequent and small breathing is, but was not able to know what the condition is that produces it, nevertheless, when he says 'frequent breathing signifies pain or inflammation in the regions above the diaphragm', he is clearly writing down the conditions as well [913] and omitting neither of them, but has indicated them in the same order which he also adopted in the two books of the Epidemics. It is clear, therefore, that he is joining pain to the frequent and small breathing, and burning heat (phlogosis) to the frequent and large. For neither is it possible to say this, that in the two books of the Epidemics he made mention of small and frequent and of large and frequent breathing, but nowhere else. For both in those very books, often, and in On Regimen in Acute Diseases, which they entitle On Ptisan, right at the beginning of the treatise he not only expressly names this kind of dyspnoea, but also the condition in which it arises and the manner in which it is of a nature to do harm; and yet, among those who out of contentiousness strike out many books as not genuine works of Hippocrates, no one has dared to take this treatise away from the man. For the parts at the end, those after the use of the bath, many remove, but the parts up to that point all preserve. If, then, we show not only in this book, but he is also found likewise throughout many others, to know both the differences of frequent breathing and the conditions, will anything seem to be lacking for the demonstration?

But if, in the [914] Prognostic itself as well, he should be found further on neither ignorant of the differences and also acquainted with the conditions, would you not believe still more that the matter proposed has been demonstrated? And indeed, that these things are so and that we are saying nothing false, one may examine from the passages themselves. I shall begin from On Regimen in Acute Diseases. In this book, right at the beginning, when making his discourse about the diseases of the lung and the thorax, he says somewhat as follows: "For in those in whom food has just been shut in, if one gives the gruel without first evacuating downward, one would further exacerbate the pain that is present, and if it is not present one would at once produce it, and the breathing would become more frequent; and this is bad, for it is drying to the lung and wearying to the hypochondria and the lower belly and the diaphragm." In this passage he has shown, first, that frequent breathing also comes about on account of pain, leaving it to us, I think, to conceive the manner of its genesis, which I think I have clearly gone through in the first of these commentaries.

For in the same way that, when we have pain in our legs, we cannot take a large step, in the same way, when any of the organs that are moved in respirations is in pain, we are compelled to breathe small [915] and we are eager to stop sooner. For since the pain is coextensive with the length of the time of the respiration, he who would sooner check the motion of the respiratory organs will sooner cease being in pain. But by as much as he has stopped earlier than he ought, by so much has the animal enjoyed the inspiration more deficiently. Just as, then, if someone takes in less food than his need, he will quickly require further food, so if someone should inspire less than his need, he will sooner require a further inspiration, and in this it will come about that the breathing becomes frequent. For the time during which the organs of respiration were at rest, reposing in the interval between the activities, this time the animal now does not permit them to rest. For inasmuch as it breathes each respiration deficiently, it draws ever and ever nearer to suffocation; and from fear of this very affection it hastens to breathe sooner, and moves the organs of respiration earlier than it ought, not permitting them to rest for as long as it rested when it was in accordance with nature.

When, therefore, Hippocrates says that the breath becomes more frequent on account of the pain, and the frequency is seen to be generated by way of smallness as the intermediate term, [916] it is surely clear to everyone that he also recognises the smallness. For who could know the third thing from the first while being ignorant of the middle, and especially when that middle is itself the cause of the third's coming to be? And indeed, going on a little further, in his own very words he outright assigns the smallness as the cause of the frequency, writing as follows: for the sputum itself, being held fast, prevents the breath from being carried inward, and compels it to be carried outward quickly. Here again he teaches the other cause of the generation of frequent breath, and he named it in the preceding discussions narrowness of the respiratory organs. What, then, in the case of pain he left for us to work out, this he himself here expounded. And what is this? When much sputum, he says, is contained in the arteries—those of the lung, evidently—and has already taken possession of the space belonging to the breath itself, the breath is prevented from arriving within during the activity of inspiration. Is, then, what is now being said anything other than a small inspiration?

Certainly not, if indeed one must measure the magnitude of respiration by the quantity of the substance inspired, as has been shown in the first [917] book. But if someone says that he (Hippocrates) states that the breath is compelled to be carried outward quickly for some other cause than the smallness of the inspiration, it is not possible to say this either, since the wording runs thus: for the sputum itself, being retained, prevents the breath from being carried inward, and compels it to be carried outward quickly. For because it has been deprived of the inward movement, it does not permit the animal, being in danger of suffocating, to remain at rest, and in this way it (the breath) becomes frequent. For to proceed quickly from the inspiration to the expiration is nothing other than to breathe frequently. For indeed one ought not to insist on hearing the very syllables of the words, when the statements as a whole are expressed clearly, nor to think that rushing quickly to expiration is one thing and breathing frequently another, nor that the inspiration's being prevented from taking place sufficiently is one thing and the respiration's being small another.

But here Hippocrates himself explained clearly how, in the case of sputum that is held back, the breathing becomes frequent by way of smallness as the intermediate step; but in the case of pain he left it out, inasmuch, I think, as he had himself said in many places that the activities [918] of the organs are hindered by pain, and as we too are able, even if we had not heard it from him, to discover this from what is evidently apparent. Accordingly, besides teaching us clearly both these things in this passage—that both pain and narrowness of space, by making the respiration small, immediately show it to be frequent as well—he further teaches this too, that these are not the only causes of frequent breathing. For first, in what he says—and it is put thus in the case of pain—he makes this evident, saying that the breathing, being already frequent on account of the other cause, becomes more frequent on account of the pain, inasmuch, I think, as here too we are able to reason out that the febrile heat in any case renders it frequent; and second, in saying that the sputum, made viscous in an unconcocted state by the frequent and abundant breath, as has already been said, prevents the return from taking place. For pain is the cause of the frequent breath, but of the abundant breath the cause is not pain but the febrile heat. And here too, quite clearly, he did not say 'great' breath but 'abundant'.

For 'great' is judged by the quantity in each respiration, whereas 'much' can sometimes be accumulated from many small ones. [919] And this is clearly seen to happen in pleuritics, who are unable to respire greatly at a single stroke because of the pain—although indeed they need more air because of the fever—but who by the continuity of the activity accumulate an amount of breath equal to that of great respirations. For what few great ones can do, many small ones can do. In the same way, in peripneumonics too the need is for much breath, but because of the narrowness little is inhaled; here too, then, the frequency, by making the small respirations many, brings them to equality with the few and great ones. Shall we, then, still need to find the syllables of the terms written in this book in just such a sequence—'small' and 'great respiration'—not being content with the things themselves so clearly demonstrated?

And indeed this was not the question at issue, whether Hippocrates knows the name of small and great respiration; for it is found written both in the books of the Epidemics and again in the Prognostic, in the passage where he said: "breathing that is great and at long intervals of [920] time signifies delirium"; but rather whether he knows the dense breath to be twofold, and says that one of them arises from pain, the other from much heat gathered in the respiratory organs. Since, then, these things have been demonstrated, it is superfluous still to long to hear the syllables of the names, since even with regard to this very statement in the Prognostic, which he wrote concerning delirium, it will be open to someone to say that the breath indicating it was not described as rare and great, and to put forward the wording as having the following form, "breathing that is great and at long intervals of time signifies delirium" — as if it were not merely the same thing to say either "rare" or "at long intervals of time", or as if we were now hunting names and not inquiring into the things themselves. But since some have arrived at such a degree of obtuseness as to wish to hear the very names themselves, let us remind them too, from the book On Regimen in Acute Diseases itself, of two passages which run roughly as follows: "breath stumbling in its upward movement, dense or great."

Here, then, you have, if you desire it, the word "great"; and the word "small" in turn, when he says: "and small breath [921] and a frequent and violent drawing-back of the breath supervenes." And again in the Prognostic itself he says that the patient bears the disease with difficulty and that the breath is great and frequent. This, then, he wrote outright in the very words, "great and frequent"; but the "small and frequent" in turn in the account of angina, when he said, "they produce very great distress and orthopnoea." For that in orthopnoeas the breath becomes small and frequent because of the narrowness of the respiratory organs, I do not know whether anyone is ignorant. And yet, even if we wish to learn such things from Hippocrates himself, in the Regimen in Acute Diseases, in the words I wrote out a little earlier, he taught us how small and frequent breath comes about in connection with the retention of the sputa.

But in On Joints, right at the beginning of his account of the spine, when he is describing the kyphoses that come about from swellings or diseases in the regions above the diaphragm, he says something like this (for I think it better to write out the whole passage): 'In those in whom the hump is above the diaphragm, the ribs are not inclined to grow in breadth, [922] but forwards, and the chest becomes pointed, but not broad, and they themselves become dyspnoeic and wheezing (kerchnōdeis); for the cavities that receive and send forth the breath have less straightness of direction. For indeed they are also compelled to hold the neck lordotic at the great vertebra, so that their head may not fall forward. They therefore produce much narrowing for the pharynx; and this contributes to the inward inclination. For even in those who are naturally straight this bone produces dyspnoea, if it inclines inward, until it is pressed back. On account of such a condition, then, such people appear more prominent-throated (exechembrochoi) than healthy people, and such people are for the most part subject to phymata in the lung, hard and unconcocted phymata. For indeed the cause of the kyphosis and the tension arise in most cases through such gatherings (systrophai), with which the tense cords (xyntonoi) may be in communication.' In this whole passage he says that the kyphosis comes about upon unconcocted and hard phymata in the lung, and the dyspnoea upon the narrowing; and he has called such a variety of it 'kerchnōdēs' (wheezing).

But in the [923] Regimen in Acute Diseases, when he made mention of those whose respiration turns to smallness and frequency, he both added this very name of orthopnoea and said that they snore (ῥέγχειν), so that also when, in the Prognostic, giving his account of angina, he said 'they cause very great pain and orthopnoea', he is naming in this way no other kind of difficulty of breathing than that of small and frequent breath. For all who because of narrowness are unable to breathe in sufficiently are in danger of being suffocated if they lie down. And for this reason they need to hold the whole thorax and the neck upright, since no small help comes to them from such a posture. For all the organs of respiration become at once both wider and longer, on the one hand being straightened out by the upright postures, and on the other being prevented from collapsing as much into themselves.

And Hippocrates himself is plainly of the same mind about these matters as we are now saying, from what he says in the books On Joints: 'and they themselves become dyspnoeic and rasping (kerchnōdees), for the cavities that receive and send [924] forth the breath have less straightness.' In all, then, who are dyspnoeic because of narrowness, the breath both becomes small and two symptoms follow of necessity: the rasping (kerchnōdes) kind of respiration, which is also named stertor (rhenchein), and the one mentioned a little earlier, orthopnoea. And indeed, as though deliberately dividing them, he writes of the one in the Prognostic, saying that it is present in the deadly anginas, and of the second in On Joints—in the Prognostic orthopnoea, in On Joints the rasping; but both he brought together into one in On Regimen in Acute Diseases, Hippocrates writing thus: 'those who have been suffocated by orthopnoea and stertor (rhenchos).' For what in On Joints he called kerchnos, this he here named rhenchos. And elsewhere too in his writings he uses both names as able to signify the same thing. Since, therefore, he himself went through so carefully in On Regimen every origin of frequent breath, it is no wonder if in the Prognostic he has written only the summary itself of the whole account.

But that he carefully [925] went through the whole account concerning frequent breath, I need say nothing further; rather, having recalled only this, that the breath becomes frequent either through pain, or through narrowness of space, or through an abundance of heat, I shall next set down the whole passage, which runs in the following manner: "For in those in whom food has just been shut in, if one gives the gruel without first evacuating somewhat, one would further exacerbate the pain if it is present, and if it is not present one would straightaway produce it, and the breath would become more frequent; and this is bad, for it is drying to the lung and wearying to the hypochondrium and the lower belly and the diaphragm. And if, the pain of the side being continuous and not relaxing under the fomentations, and the sputum not coming away but rather becoming viscous without concoction (ἀσαπέως), one does not release the pain, either by softening the belly or by cutting a vein, whichever of the two of these is indicated, and yet gives the ptisans to those in such a condition, the deaths of such patients come quickly."

On account of these causes, then, and others of this kind, those who use whole ptisan die even more readily on the seventh day or in fewer days, some having also been somewhat impaired in their mind [926], others suffocated by orthopnoea and rattling. The ancients very much called such persons 'struck' (blētoi), chiefly for this reason, and not least because, when they have died, the side is found livid, somewhat like a blow. The cause of this is that they die before the pain has been resolved. For they quickly become short of breath (pneumatiai), and by the frequent and copious breath, as has already been said, the sputum, becoming viscous in an uncocted state, prevents its return from taking place, but rather produces the rattling, being held fast in the bronchi of the lung. When it comes to this, it is for the most part deadly. For the sputum itself, being retained, prevents the breath from being carried inward, and compels it to be carried out quickly, and thus they assist one another toward the harm. For the retained sputum makes the breath frequent, and the breath, being frequent, makes the sputum more viscous and prevents it from slipping away. If anyone should attend carefully to this passage and read it over many times, I expect that he will readily be persuaded of what has been said.

For because the division of dense breathing into the differences within it did not [927] require great wisdom, and because he had already written it out completely in this book, for this reason in the Prognostic he ran over it very quickly, making as it were a kind of epitome of the account, as for people who already know the whole matter. Three conjugations of dyspnoeas, then, have now been discovered by us, and the fourth remains, in which the breath is small and rare. Why ever, then, did he omit it and write of cold expiration? Or is it because the breath that is at once small and rare is not one thing and the cold another? And this is clear. For we showed that its opposite, the breath that is at once large and dense, is the offspring of immoderate heat gathered in the respiratory organs. Of necessity, then, the small and rare breath will belong to these same organs when they have been cooled, and two difficulties are solved for us, in that neither the fourth conjugation of dyspnoea, the small and rare, has been omitted, nor the hot.

For we shall have that one included in the other part of the dense breath spoken of at the beginning, since it is the same as the dense and [928] large; and the rare and small, in turn, in the cold, for this one too does not differ from the cold. Why, then, did he write it not as rare and small but as cold? Because, first, he wished to indicate it from the more readily apparent symptom; second, to point out the cause on account of which he calls it deadly; and third, because he supposed that in this way we would most quickly understand both that this very one differs in no way from the rare and small, and that its opposite, the hot, differs in no way from the dense and large. For the cold breath is in every case both rare and small, as has also been shown in the second book; and as for the dense and large, that which is indicative of burning heat (phlogosis) of the respiratory organs, no one would even rightly speak of it as such unless it were also breathed out hot. And indeed, by adding, to the cold breath alone, that it 'now becomes exceedingly deadly', he clearly shows the opinion he holds concerning the three dyspnoeas spoken of before. For if he considered any of those too to be deadly, he would surely have added this somewhere. Did he then suppose them to be free of danger? By no means; rather, not deadly, yet not for that reason free of danger either.

For the respiratory [929] organs' being chilled is outright deadly, since the heart is situated there, which we know to be the origin and fount of the innate heat; but that there should be either much burning heat (phlogosis) in them, or pain, or delirium, is not necessarily deadly; for heat of this kind accompanies many of the acute fevers, and it has been stated before in how many and in which diseases pain is present. And indeed delirium, too, is among the things not necessarily deadly. That this is his judgement about them he showed clearly through the statement that follows, saying: "And one must consider that easy breathing has a very great power toward recovery in all the acute diseases which are accompanied by fevers and are decided within forty days." For if indeed he considered easy breathing to have great power toward recovery, clearly he did not suppose that the forms of difficult breathing were always free of danger; so that the other forms of difficult breathing are just this alone, not without danger, whereas the one mentioned last of all, besides being dangerous and deadly, indicates that the person will die before long.

For this reason, [930] then, he did not say simply that it is deadly, but also added the 'exceedingly', and, not content even with this, he further added the 'already', on the grounds that this dyspnoea alone indicates that death is imminent. For it is so deadly that it seems to me that Hippocrates would not even have written anything about it, had he not been going through the whole subject in order while speaking about the dyspnoeas. For the things that occur to those who are already dying have no great value in prognoses; and it is the task of good physicians to foreknow, not the things already evident to laymen, but all those which escape them and which appear while the patient seems to have nothing bad about him. But because he wished to write down all the kinds of dyspnoea in sequence, it seems to me that he mentioned this one too, and moreover on account of the opposition to the large and frequent (breathing). Let these matters, then, end here.

But why did he write nothing in the Prognostic about uneven dyspnoea, even though he recognised it not only in the second and the sixth books of the Epidemics, [931] but also in the first and the third, and further in the Regimen in Acute Diseases and in the Aphorisms, and in many other places in his writings? For in the second and the sixth he mentioned it in the passage written out above, saying: 'a double recall inwards, as if they breathe in a second time.' And further, in the second book of the Epidemics, in narrating what happened to the woman Lycie, he added: 'and the breath was doubled.' For this differs in no way from 'a double recall inwards, as if they breathe in a second time.' And in the sixth he says: 'if the breath is left behind within (ἐγκαταλείπηται).' For this too is the same as what is said in the Regimen: 'breath stumbling in its upward movement.' For just as some people, when breathing in, do not do this in a single act, but interrupt the activity with a pause, like children sobbing, so too when breathing out. But also in the passages after the account of baths he has spoken of 'stretchings-forth (προτάσεις) of breaths,' indicating the interrupted activity.

And in the first book of the Epidemics, in the case of Philiscus, he spoke in this manner: 'in this man [932] the breath throughout, as of one recalling it'; for here too 'recalling' is said in the same sense as 'double recall inwards'. Again, in the case of the wife of Dromeades, he said, 'breath rare, large, at once drawn up'; for this too has been said in the same way. And in the Aphorisms he also teaches what such breathing signifies, writing thus: 'in fevers, breath that stumbles is bad, for it signifies convulsion.' Accordingly, then, in the books of the Epidemics too he says that the wife of Dromeades died having been seized with convulsion—she of whom he had said beforehand, 'breath rare, large, at once drawn up'. And here indeed one may especially marvel at how each of the two dyspnoeas indicated the condition proper to it. For this woman was not only convulsed but also became delirious, inasmuch as she had not only the dyspnoea peculiar to convulsions but also that of delirium.

So that Hippocrates recognised this uneven dyspnoea has been clearly demonstrated; but that he reasonably omitted it in the Prognostic too, just as [933] he did also most of the prognostic signs, would have to be said next by him (αὐτῷ), after first recalling under chief points that he wrote nothing in the Prognostic about the matters pertaining to ages, or regions, or seasons, or epidemic constitutions—although a whole book, On Airs, Places and Waters, was written by him, and in the Aphorisms all these things are stated in epitome—nor, as regards the diagnosis of urines, did he go through in the Prognostic those things which he wrote in the Aphorisms, nor indeed did he transfer into the Prognostic what he wrote in the Aphorisms concerning women; and yet both these and many other things said in the Aphorisms belong to the prognostic part of medicine, as he himself indicates through his own words. For both in saying: "but if it be northerly, coughs, sore throats, dry bellies, dysurias with shivering, pains of the sides, of the chest; when this wind prevails, expect such things in illnesses."

and in saying: when the summer turns out like spring, expect many sweats in the fevers; [934] he is clearly indicating that such things belong to the prognostic part of the art. For 'to expect' and 'to anticipate' and 'to look for', and all verbs of this kind, are proper to prognosis. And indeed also in saying: if the winter is dry and northerly, and the spring rainy and southerly, it is necessary that in the summer acute fevers and ophthalmias and dysenteries arise; he clearly shows this same thing, and much more so when he writes somewhat as follows about urines: those in whom the urines are thick, clotted, and scanty, they not being free of fever, an abundance of thin urine coming after these is beneficial; and such urines come especially in those in whom from the beginning it quickly has a sediment. And again: those whose urines are stirred up turbid, like that of a beast of burden, in these headaches are either present or will be present. And again: in those who are judged on the seventh day, the urine has a red cloud on the fourth day, and the rest in proportion.

Similarly to these, the things that indicate the conditions of the bladder and of the kidneys have also been written in the Aphorisms, but have been left out in the Prognostic, as have a very great many other things as well, [935] such as the following: 'In whichever diseases black bile passes off, either upward or downward, at their beginning, it is deadly'; 'dysentery, if it begins from black bile, is deadly'; 'in those who in fevers haemorrhage copiously from whatever source, during the recoveries of such persons the bowels become loose.' And a very great many such things, belonging to the prognostic part of the art, one can find written in the Aphorisms. Why, then, did he go through none of these in the treatise Prognostic? Because in that work he had proposed to teach about acute diseases, as he himself explained both when beginning and when completing the book, saying at the beginning: 'One must observe as follows in acute diseases'; and at the end adding this: 'I say these things concerning acute diseases, and all those that arise from them.' And which are the ones that arise from them Hippocrates himself again goes through in the same book: 'The dropsies that come from acute diseases are all bad.'

And this again: 'One must consider that easy breathing has a very great power for safety in all acute [936] diseases which are accompanied by fevers and are judged within forty days.' Here too he makes mention of the acute diseases that arise from a shift, just as we also demonstrated in the books On Critical Days. He also indicated in many other places of the treatise that his discourse concerns either acute diseases or those which arise from them, as also in these words: 'Sweats are best in all acute diseases when they occur on critical days.' And why need one say much? For he himself clearly shows that he deliberately omits many of the prognostic signs in that book, at one point speaking somewhat as follows: 'But let it not deceive you if the bladder itself, having some disease, yields any of these urines; for this is not a sign of the whole, but of the bladder itself by itself.' Yet he does not add the distinguishing marks in the Prognostic, but writes them in the Aphorisms.

And again in turn he says: "One must also quickly consider the differences of the diseases that are epidemic, and not let the constitution of the season escape notice"—yet he does not teach us anything about this either in the [937] Prognostic. For he set out, as I said, to go through only the features peculiar to acute diseases, and to leave aside all the features peculiar to chronic ones, so that with good reason he left out here the irregular dyspnoea as well, since it belongs to another genus of disease. For if indeed it arises when the respiratory organs are convulsed, the affection would also attend chronic diseases, and in this respect at least it would be peculiar to neither acute nor chronic diseases; and it would also occur without fever, just as convulsions too do. But his purpose in the Prognostic is to make his account about the diseases properly named acute. And these are the ones that occur, for the most part, with continuous fevers, as he himself showed in On Regimen in Acute Diseases, writing roughly as follows: "These, then, are acute: such as the ancients named pleuritis and peripneumonia and phrenitis and causus, and the others that are akin to these, whose fevers are for the most part continuous."

Convulsions, then, are not of this class of diseases, which is why he did not go through the dyspnoea peculiar to them together with [938] these, just as he did not go through the urines, or the stools, or all the other things that he wrote about in the Aphorisms, because they were not peculiar to the acute diseases. But why he also taught nothing in the Prognostic about those dyspnoeas in which either only what is inhaled or only what is exhaled is large, I consider it superfluous to go over now, since I showed clearly in the first of these commentaries that it is sufficient to refer the other differences to these five dyspnoeas, about which I have just now finished speaking; for neither did he mention quick or slow respiration in the Prognostic. And by the same argument we showed that all the other differences happen to be contained in those previously mentioned, so that Hippocrates appears to have done each of the two correctly: in the books of the Epidemics setting out the division into all the particular dyspnoeas, and in the Prognostic and the Aphorisms what is pressing for practical use.

[939] Since, then, these things have been sufficiently demonstrated by us, it would still remain to expound the remaining passages from all his writings, beginning again from the second and the sixth books of the Epidemics. For in both these books, next after the passage stated first of all, the one that teaches the differences of dyspnoea as a whole, it is written somewhat as follows: 'Curative of continuous yawnings, long-breathed; in those who do not drink and drink with difficulty, short-breathed.' Here, whether he so named the man long-breathed, or the dyspnoea itself, that the breath which comes about over a long time, that is, the rare breath and in addition the large, is signified by this appellation, has been shown in the second book, just as also that the breath which comes about at a short interval, that is, the frequent, and in addition the small, is signified by 'short-breathed'.

Curative, then, of continuous yawnings—whether as a sign or as a cause, for either can be shown—is the breath that becomes great and rare: a sign, inasmuch as the condition is shifting over into its opposites; a cause, because the remedies of opposites are opposites. [940] For people yawn and stretch continuously when some vaporous and thick pneuma has been trapped in the muscular kind, as has been shown elsewhere; and those to whom this has happened straightaway also breathe out continuously, since such pneuma is being cleared out and evacuated in the expirations. But if someone no longer makes his expirations continuously, but now at a long interval, it is clear that the conditions previously present in him have ceased, and in this way long-breathing will be a curative sign of the yawning. And indeed that it is also possible to understand long-breathing as a cause curing continuous yawnings—this too seems to me no longer to require a long account. For holding the respiration for as long as possible, which is called retention of breath, will cure yawnings by the same reasoning by which it cures hiccups. And in fact all athletes also do this after their exercises, striving to force out by violence everything, whether of moistures or of vapours, that is held in the fine pores of the skin.

For these reasons, then, long-breathing is a sign, or a curative cause, of continuous yawnings; [941] and again, in those who are without thirst for drink and drink only with difficulty, short-breathing is so. But this is no longer stated clearly, but now rather more enigmatically. For should one suppose that the phrenitics are indicated by it here, because he also said elsewhere, "phrenitics are small drinkers, affected by noise, tremulous"? Or rather those in whom the parts about the lung and the heart have been chilled, so that they both breathe at long intervals and breathe out cold air? For short-breathing, when it comes to be present in both cases, is a curative sign; but in those who have been chilled it is not only a sign but also a cause. For just as the holding of the breath was able to evacuate the superfluities, and on this account we employed it in those who hiccup and yawn much and stretch themselves and have exercised strenuously, so continuous respiration will be able at once both to fan and to heat thoroughly the parts that have been chilled.

On this reasoning, then, in the second book of the Epidemics too he advised making it a practice to induce sharpness of temper, both for the sake of the recovery of complexion and for the sake of the diffusion of the humours (ἐκχύμωσις), since sharpness of temper too is able to rouse the innate [942] heat. But that sharpness of temper in any case makes respiration more frequent, no one is unaware. We shall therefore employ it in those who are chilled and ill-coloured and lean, at certain intermissions and at suitable occasions; for certainly not continuously, in such a way as to harm the faculty excessively, but just as we do not bid that the exercises which strengthen the innate heat be performed without measure, but employ them with due occasion and measure, so too short-breathing, whether we practise it on its own or together with sharpness of temper, we shall employ not without due occasion and measure. Here one must attend to the argument and not suppose that the condition in the Prognostic, concerning which he said, is the same as that which we are now indicating: "but cold breath exhaled from the nostrils and the mouth is by then very deadly."

For in those in acute diseases, about whom he makes his discussion in that book, dyspnoea of this kind indicates death; but in the other diseases, all those without fever, coldness takes hold of the whole habit of the [943] animal; it does not occur in these either without danger, yet not in every case destructively. Among these belong also the so-called hysterical suffocation and in general all the apnoeas, which befall women continually, and especially those who are barren, but rarely on occasion men as well. For in all such conditions the innate heat is weighed down by an abundance of cold matter, in the manner of a flame being choked by much wet wood, so that it is even possible at some point to rekindle it, once one has gained mastery over the matter; in those cases, however, in which, the matter having been consumed, the heat itself is of necessity extinguished together with it, as in those in acute diseases who breathe out in this way, no hope of safety is left.

One must therefore keep these things in mind, and also that in the apnoeas it is neither possible to suppose that the whole respiration has been completely lost, nor does what happens appear so to those who examine it carefully; rather, their breath becomes very small and at the same time occurs at very long intervals, and in this way it escapes the notice of most people. But if one applies one's [944] mind carefully, or even places one of one's fingers before the patient's nose, one will perceive the respiration. And if one also hangs a hair before it, or a fine piece of wool, thoroughly carded out, one will see these too being stirred. In such conditions, then, short-breathing, that is, the movement of the respiratory organs at short intervals of time, which indeed we also call frequent breath, is at once a cause and a remedial sign; and in the same way, in the case of continuous yawnings, not only the breathing at long intervals, that is, the rare one, is at once a remedial sign and cause, but also the large one. For this too is called, in a secondary sense, long-breathing. For primarily the breathing that occurs at a long interval of time, that is, the rare one, possesses this name, and secondarily the large one as well. This, then, is how matters stand regarding these. Let us now set out as well all the other things that have been written by him concerning difficulty of breathing.

In the second book of the Epidemics, then, in the case of the wife of Antigenes, having first said that she became asthmatic before childbirth, he adds after this: "then [945] together with the delivery she vomited up pus." So that this too agrees with what has been demonstrated by us; for those are asthmatic who breathe frequently and at the same time dilate the thorax to a great extent. This occurs sometimes in conditions that require much inspiration. At any rate, such a thing befalls those who have run or have exercised vigorously in any other way whatsoever, and all who have burning fevers. It also occurs, as was shown, when there is an obstruction, or compression, or some narrowing in the respiratory organs; and something of this sort appears to have happened also to the wife of Antigenes, as the pus made clear. This, then, is the first dyspnoea he mentions in the second book of the Epidemics; and after this, the one that befell Lycie, concerning whom, as I also said earlier, he wrote: "the breath was doubled, yet not great in proportion." For the nervous kind of her organs had been affected, so that a complete retention of the urine also occurred. For this reason, then, the doubled breathing came about; but why was it not great? Or was it because she had been chilled?

At any rate, he says, "she was contracted"; and he was shown to use this [946] word of those whose innate heat is being chilled away. Next, discussing also the cases of cynanche that occurred at that time, he writes as follows: "and the breath in these was not very elevated"—evidently on the ground that in those with cynanche the breath is for the most part elevated. It is his custom to call by this name the small breath, which, as it might seem to someone, enters only about as far as the pharynx and does not descend into the depth of the thorax. That the breath must necessarily be of this kind in those who suffer pain in any one whatever of the respiratory organs has been stated earlier. What, then, is the cause on account of which in those with cynanche the breath was not very elevated? Is it because the form of cynanche also did not occur in them in the accustomed manner? For first he will say: "the pharynx not inflamed, but lying [flat]" (κειμένη); then he says thus: "most of them not being choked, unless they attempted to swallow"; and in general the whole account of the cynanche that occurred at that time showed that the pharynx remained unaffected, while the parts neighbouring it, those continuous with the vertebrae of the neck, were affected.

For indeed he says that the vertebrae themselves were also displaced, [947] some only inward, others also toward the sides. Since, then, no other of the respiratory organs was affected, nor indeed the pharynx itself in its own right, except in so far as it shared in the affections through the community of its position, it was fitting that their breath was not very elevated; for if the pharynx had not been troubled at all, it would not have been elevated in any way whatsoever; but since it was troubled by suffering in sympathy with the adjacent parts, the breath acquired the condition intermediate between those mentioned, being moderately frequent. After this constitution he mentions another which occurred in Perinthus, beginning his account in this manner: "We came to Perinthus a little about the summer solstice." Then he describes the whole form of the diseases, which began from causus, became vomitous, and persisted for a very long time. But he also added this, that the causus fevers occurred in these patients without vomiting, and that their bowels passed a great deal.

So that from these and from all the other things it is quite evident that the basis of the constitution had come about in phlegms undergoing putrefaction, the respiratory [948] organs having remained unaffected, and also the mouth of the stomach, while the causus set out once more from the lower parts. Reasonably, then, for them the breath neither became large, as it did for those in whom a quantity of fiery heat had been gathered in the lung and the heart, nor was it small altogether, since they were neither in pain nor chilled. If, therefore, 'elevated' (μετέωρον) signifies nothing different from 'small', he says in accordance with reason that their breaths became elevated, though not very much so. After this constitution Hippocrates made mention of no dyspnoea in what follows, up to that passage which I cited first of all at the beginning of this book, which begins in this way: 'breaths frequent small, large rare.' And this I have already explained in its entirety. It would now, then, be the time to mention the dyspnoea written by him next, in the case of a certain patient whose name was Scopus; the wording of the ancient runs thus: 'breath somewhat frequent; he had pain in the hypochondrium, both when breathing and when turning.'

[949] This patient too, then, clearly bears witness to what has often been said by us before; for since the hypochondria are joined to the respiratory organs, for this reason, when these were in pain, the breathing was somewhat frequent. These, then, are the kinds of dyspnoea he wrote of in the second book of the Epidemics. In the fourth book he mentions first the wife of Nicostratus, the one in Cranon, who had small and frequent breathing; and second the wife of Antigenes, who had not become asthmatic recently at that time, but had been so from the beginning, so that she was also always coughing. Concerning the latter, then, there would be no question at all; but concerning the one in Cranon, the wife of Nicostratus, he seems to me to have added the small and frequent breathing for this reason, because she became delirious. For it has already been said many times that, on the contrary, rare and large breathing is proper to delirium; so that it is worth inquiring why this did not occur, but rather its opposite, that which is proper to pains, the small and frequent.

For neither did he add, in the account of the illness, that any pain occurred in any of the parts, nor indeed any notable swelling [950] either in the hypochondrium or in the thorax. What, then, is it that happened? To me it seems that a certain twofold form of disease was constituted in the woman from a twofold origin; for from her being delirious and from the neck and the mouth and the nose being drawn aside, it is clear that some basis of disease was present for her in the head; but from the fact that the food was shut up within until the tenth day and that the sediment in the urines became vetch-like (ὀροβοειδῆ), I think that no small inflammation arose in the liver, in consequence of which the condition from above, having been overcome, was not able to stamp the respiration with its own form. For indeed it has already been said many times before as well, that the form of the dyspnoea is shaped according to the prevailing condition. And the very wording of the ancient also shows, not least, the slightness of the delirium: at any rate, he said that she 'talked aside' (παραλέγειν); and he is accustomed to use such a word when he wishes to indicate a slight injury, as this too has been demonstrated many times.

It is therefore nothing to wonder at that, since she was delirious only to a slight degree but strongly inflamed in the liver, not [951] the dyspnoea proper to the delirium but that proper to the inflammation occurred. So, then, it stands with these matters as well. But when he says that someone became full of pneuma (pneumatōdēs), how ought one to take it? As the man whom in the Regimen in Acute Diseases he called pneumatias? Or as the man whose belly has been inflated with pneuma? What the pneumatias is, he himself explained most clearly in the Regimen in Acute Diseases. For having first said that they quickly become pneumatiai, he immediately adds in continuation: 'by much and frequent breath (pneuma)'. This indeed I explained right at the beginning in this book; but the passage in the fourth book of the Epidemics must be examined, once we have set down the statement itself, which runs as follows: 'The man from the mines: right hypochondrium tense, spleen large, belly tense, somewhat hard, full of pneuma, colourless.' For either is possible: both that he became dyspnoeic on account of the conditions in the hypochondria, and that his belly became inflated with pneuma.

[952] Much more unclear still is the next patient, who runs thus: "The son of Timaenes had something of pneuma, so as to be yellowish." For in this man too there was quite a serious malfunction of the liver, on account of which it was possible both that he had difficulty of breathing and that his belly was distended with wind; for the yellowish colour is a mark of a malfunctioning liver. But what is said next, thus: "The husband of the woman in childbed, the one at the house of Sitodocus, jaundiced, whom I visited on the seventh day, died on the eighth, neither passing urine nor passing stool; hypochondria large and hard, and breathing frequent"—this contains no problem at all. For when the hypochondria had become hard to no moderate degree and large, it is reasonable that his breathing was frequent. But wholly unclear is what follows on from this, said of the woman in childbed thus: "as the fever was lifting (διαίροντος), the breathing was not resolved." For what kind of difficulty of breathing she had, he neither himself showed clearly, nor did he write any other symptom of such a sort from which one might infer the condition that had come about in her.

And moreover, after this woman, having gone on not a little way, [953] he begins to narrate in the following manner: 'The wife of Timaenes, pneumatic (πνευματώδης).' For this can be understood as dyspnoeic, and it can also be taken, as most of the commentators think, as meaning that she had her hypochondria filled with pneuma; but it seems to me better, and perhaps even necessary, that it be the woman whose hypochondria were inflated with pneuma who is meant, rather than a dyspnoeic one. Then, having gone on a little in the account, he says, 'and in some degree breathing more easily,' as though he had already said beforehand of her that she was dyspnoeic. And that he is accustomed to call 'pneumatic' those whose breathing is frequent has been stated in what precedes, but it is clear now as well; for the symptoms of this woman turned once more for the worse, and he says that she died on the sixteenth day with her breathing frequent.

And that the one described after her also himself breathed rapidly on account of the condition of the hypochondria, the passage itself will make clear, which runs in this manner: "The boy, who belonged to the woman, the sister of Apoemantus: hypochondria [954] large, and spleen, pneuma, evacuation bilious (πικρόχολος)." For just as he sometimes calls those who breathe rapidly "pneumatic" (πνευματώδεις), so at times he also writes simply "pneuma." And it is nothing to wonder at if, the hypochondria being large, the breathing became rapid. For indeed, going on further in his account of this patient, he will say again: "The hypochondria were tense, and moreover there was a slight dry little cough (βηχίον), quietly." For in general, as we said, whenever either a swelling or some pain forms in the parts about the hypochondria, they of necessity breathe small and rapid. So that it is nothing to wonder at either when, in what follows these, having first said "hypochondrium somewhat slack," he adds, "but not very pneumatic." For if indeed "slack" (λαπαρόν) means empty, and "somewhat slack" (ὑπολάπαρον) means somewhat empty, they will have difficulty of breathing to the same degree as the parts about the hypochondrium are in a bad state for them.

When, therefore, these parts are moderately affected, they will be moderately dyspnoeic; just as again, in the lower portions of the book, he writes somewhat as follows: "For the female house-slave, whom I saw when she was newly bought, [955] in whom the hardening (sklerysma) in the right parts was large, not very painful"—he reasonably adds, "and not very dyspnoeic." For if indeed the hardening was not very painful, it was likely that the woman was also not very dyspnoeic. So too, now at the end of the book, in giving his account of the older man, after first saying, "he wandered in his mind in an orderly manner," he added, "not very dyspnoeic." For the magnitude of the dyspnoea always comes about in accordance with the magnitude of the cause that produces the dyspnoea. But these things, too, have been written in the fourth book of the Epidemics, and they agree with what has been demonstrated by us concerning dyspnoea.

In the fifth book of the Epidemics, in turn, the fourteenth patient is written up in the following way: 'In Larissa, Hipposthenes seemed to the physicians to be gripped by peripneumonia; but it was not so at all. The beginning: while wrestling he fell on his back on hard ground, and [his opponent] fell upon him; and he bathed in cold water, and remained so, and seemed to become heavier. On the following day he became feverish, and a rather dry cough took hold, and the [956] breathing was frequent.' Then, going on a little further, he says: 'whenever he coughed, he had pain in the chest and the back.' It is therefore not at all surprising that, with the parts in the thorax in such a condition, the breathing became frequent. And what is added at the end of the account, 'nor did he have stertor', is said as a demonstration that the man had not become peripneumonic, and it too agrees with what was said by us right at the beginning of this book, when we were explaining this passage in On Regimen in Acute Diseases: 'those who were suffocated by orthopnoea and stertor'. The thirty-ninth patient also is written up in the fifth book of the Epidemics, he too having frequent breathing. I shall quote here too the passage itself, which runs something like this: 'A child was struck by a mule in the belly and the liver; it died on the fourth day; it had frequent breathing, and was not in its senses, and fever held it.' It is not unclear in this case that the peritoneum and the diaphragm became inflamed together with the belly and the liver, and that for this reason the child also became delirious.

But it was not in accordance with the delirium [957] that he breathed with difficulty; for the greater condition, the one in the hypochondrium, by itself stamped the form of the respiration, while the lesser one was overcome. So much for what is in the fifth book. Passing again to the sixth, of which we have already earlier explained the passage it shares with the second, let us come to the remaining ones. And almost all of them are by now clear because of what has been said before. For when he writes 'breath' alone, simply in this way, in the concurrences of diseases, he has been shown to use it in place of the dyspnoea from which the breath becomes frequent; and this same thing, when it becomes frequent to a greater degree, it is his custom to call asthma. So that in the sixth book of the Epidemics, when he says 'breath is left behind within', we shall understand the dyspnoea accompanied by frequency. Likewise also in the case of the woman in Crannon, of whom he writes thus: 'spleen naturally large, burning fever, very red, breath' — the aforesaid dyspnoea is to be understood, in which the breath becomes frequent, as also in the case of the daughter of Agisis.

And that frequent breath [958] differs from asthma he showed clearly. The passage runs as follows: the daughter of Agisis, while she was a girl, was of frequent breath; but having become a woman, being in distress not long after childbirth, she carelessly lifted a great weight, and immediately there seemed to be a noise in her chest; on the following day she had asthma and had pain in the right hip. Then, in what follows, she spat up frothy matter, he says, and at the beginning she was florid. And it is clear from the whole syndrome that, an old and hard-to-concoct phyma in the respiratory organs having burst, she spat up these things, and that it was on account of these phymata that she was of frequent breath. And again in the lower parts of the book, in the constitution which he began in this way, 'coughs began about the winter solstice', he says, 'in whom also the breath was raised up together with them' (and that the raised breath is the small and frequent one, we explained in what went before); indeed he also said that anginas occurred in that constitution.

At any rate, those are mistaken who suppose that 'elevated' (μετέωρον) is said in place of 'great', on the ground that it lifts up the thorax, raising it to the greatest extent. [959] A little further on he names certain persons pneumatiai (πνευματίας); and it has been said about this too earlier, that he so calls either those who are filled with wind or those who are asthmatic. The 'unmarked breath' (ἄσημον πνεῦμα) spoken of in what follows is small, and for this reason imperceptible, such as also accompanies the so-called apnoeas and the hysterical suffocations. That he wishes to indicate something of this sort is clear from the wording itself, which runs thus: 'and in the consumptive, the unmarked breaths are bad, and in childless women; and whatever other such things arise from the same constitution.' For childless women—and these for the most part are those who are not well purged—are especially seized by apnoeas, just as, of course, are those who remain widowed for a very long time. So that whatever breaths are not clearly marked, nor manifest to us, these he has called 'unmarked'. Starting from these, one could discover even without me all the other things said about difficulty of breathing in both the genuine and the spurious books, although we have gone through nearly all the genuine ones in this treatise.

But since the writings of Thessalus his son and [960] those of Polybus his son-in-law also belong to the art of Hippocrates, and not far from them are also those which seem to be by Euryphon but are transmitted among the works of Hippocrates, if ever I come to have more leisure, I shall add another, fourth book, expounding what is said about dyspnoea in the remaining works inscribed with the name of Hippocrates. But for now, since other matters are pressing, I shall not pass over to those.

B.translation: [753] GALEN, ON DIFFICULTY OF BREATHING, BOOK ONE. That difficulty of breathing is a certain impairment of respiration, just as difficulty of sensation is an impairment of sensation and difficulty of motion an impairment of motion, the name itself is sufficient to show. But how many differentiae of the impairment there are, through what causes they come about, and how one ought to diagnose each of them, cannot at present be learned from the appellation; rather, the nature of respiration itself will indicate it.

That, indeed, is why knowledge of what is according to nature has been zealously pursued by all the ancient physicians, both for the sake of many other things [754] and not least for the sake of the indication it provides in matters contrary to nature. For since what is according to nature is something single, a kind of rule and measure, and like itself, whereas what is contrary to nature is varied, unlike and multiform in its deviations, so that it is liable to be infinite in number and indeterminable for the art, it seemed impossible to comprehend its infinity within any definite limits without knowledge of what is according to nature. For since this is single and serviceable to the animal, it is clear that it is also well-proportioned; and if this is well-proportioned, what is contrary to nature would be disproportionate; and if disproportionate, it is in every case twofold in genus: for it either falls short of what is according to nature or exceeds it. And within it, it will have as many particular differences as the thing is capable of admitting according to the excesses beyond the moderate and the deficiencies of it. The simple admits two, while that which is composed of several admits twice as many as the number of the things that compose it.

If, then, respiration is some one and simple thing, it will have twofold [755] disproportions, and the dyspnoeas will be twofold in genus; but if it is not one, it will have differences double the number of the things that compose it. If, then, this teaching is at once clear and concise, any teaching that departs from it is justly a long one. Now, since there are two primary and most principal parts of the whole respiration, inspiration and expiration, and two others which are parts incidentally, the pauses between these, the inquiry concerning dyspnoea would in this way take place in four things in all. So it will in every case be necessary that in some one of the things mentioned, or in some of them, or even in all of them at once, there be a fault and a corruption of the natural form, for dyspnoea to come into being.
