For the sake of clear teaching it would be no worse to name 'simple dyspnoea' that which on each occasion occupies a single part of the whole respiration, and 'compound' that which arises in several. But since the compound is always secondary to the simple, it would be reasonable to make our account first about the things that are prior by nature, and so to begin from the simple dyspnoeas.

And once [756] we have gone through these sufficiently, thereafter, by combining the movements and the rests both with one another and with themselves, we shall in this way discover the compound ones. What, then, are the natural causes of the inward and outward motion of the pneuma, and what are the causes of each of the two rests? For these, as was said, were all the parts of respiration. Since, of the parts we have mentioned, two are movements, namely the outward and inward motion of the pneuma, and two are quiescences that separate these, and since the movements have a compound genesis while the quiescences have a simple one, it is clear that the former will have more disproportions, whereas those of the rests will be twofold. For the latter, being simple, have their differences in the quantity of time alone; the movements, however, will differ not in this respect only, but also in the quantity of the distance over which they are carried.

So their immoderations will be twofold, just as are those of each of the pauses: being divided according to the quantity of time, and in respect of these they will be called either quick or slow. And there will be another twofold set, differing in the quantity of the dilatation of the respiratory organs, in respect of which people call them either [757] large or small. For if both the time in which the thing moved is moved and the distance over which it travels are inseparable from every motion in respect of place, then on account of the time we shall say that the motion takes place quickly and slowly, and on account of the distance much and little. But it is customary to call the dilatation of the respiratory organs not little and much but small and large, and likewise the contraction, for the same reasoning holds for both motions. And just as quickness and slowness are proper to motion, so sparseness and density are proper to the quantity of the intervals. At any rate we say that vines or olives or anything else of the kind are planted dense when we wish to indicate that the distance between them is very short, and likewise sparse when the space between the planted bodies is large. To speak generally, all things composed of several separated parts make use of these names.

Since, then, breathing too is composed of contrary motions separated by rests, the shortness of the rests makes it frequent, [758] and their length makes it infrequent. These, then, are all the simple differentiae of dyspnoea, and these are their names, customary both to the other ancients and to Hippocrates. But if anyone wishes to name them otherwise, as some of the more recent physicians already do, it makes no difference to us. Only let him know that he is using names that are neither those customary to Hippocrates, nor to the other ancients, nor at all to the other Greeks. And even if he should despise these, let him know that he is expressing himself neither in the proper sense nor clearly. For suppose he applies one name to both, to the motion and to the rest: either speed alone or frequency alone, and again, for the contraries, either slowness alone or infrequency alone, making no use whatever of the other terms. Such a man is plainly striving after obscurity.

For it is much clearer, I think, to assign one proper name to each of the two things and to call each by that name always, knowing that names held in common, since they indicate the one of these things no more than the other, confuse and disturb the hearer, so that he cannot know what is being said until the homonymy has been distinguished. [759] But if someone does apply one name to each of the two things, yet not as we have divided them but the other way round, speed and slowness for the pauses, and infrequency and frequency for the movements, I do not know what he can mean by using names that are improper and unaccustomed in preference to those that are proper and customary. For no one is unaware that all people now, and the ancients too, predicate slowness and speed of nothing other than things that move. What clever thing, then, will have been accomplished by one who transfers the use of names so far as to call the pauses by the names of the movements? And what is clever in his applying the names of the intervals to the activities? For just as we call vines and olive trees dense when they have little space between them, and name them sparse if it is greater, so we call those activities of animals that occur after a short time frequent, and those that occur after a long time infrequent.

But if someone, as I said, wishes to name things not in this way but otherwise, following neither Hippocrates nor the other ancients nor the Greeks at all, and [760] not even caring for clarity of expression, he must be allowed to win a Cadmean victory. With the others, however, who care about names only so far as they are useful for teaching, while their whole effort is to discover the truth in the things themselves, let us now discuss the matters about which we proposed from the beginning to write. Respiration is in genus a motion. It is composed of two parts contrary to one another, of which we call the one inspiration and the other expiration. But by some accident it also has two others which are not similar, the so-called rests and pauses. Its impairments therefore occur, in the motions, toward speed and slowness and largeness and smallness, and in the pauses toward infrequency and frequency. Besides these you would not find any other simple differentia of difficulty of breathing, for the method of division shows that this is so. It would remain, once we have found their causes, to turn again to the compound ones.

What, then, is the cause [761] of rapid breathing and of slow, and of each of the others? To me it seems that here too one must search for them by method, and not simply make pronouncements. What, then, is the method? Since each thing becomes worse or better through the very same things through which it naturally comes to be at all, if we know by what causes breathing comes about, we shall plainly also know the causes of the difficulties of breathing. What, then, are the causes of breathing? You have them written elsewhere, with demonstration; for now it is enough merely to recall the chief points. The psychic faculty moves the thorax, and the lung is moved together with it, and upon its movements there follow, when it is dilated, inspiration, and when it is contracted, expiration. It has also been shown in those works that the use of breathing, the greatest and most principal, is the preservation of the innate heat, and next to this also the nourishment of the psychic pneuma.

This being so, whenever the faculty, the use and each of the instruments fare well, the animal breathes according to the law of nature; but whenever any of them is affected, the breathing too must of necessity [762] be impeded in a manner corresponding to that affection. And so, just as in the treatises on the pulses we gave a twofold instruction, either seeking the causes for each of the pulses, or the alterations of the pulses for each of those causes, so here too one must train oneself in each of the two ways, so that when the cause has been put forward one is at once able to state the dyspnoea that follows, and when the dyspnoea has been stated one readily recalls the cause that produces it. We must therefore begin here too in the same manner from the simple dyspnoeas, as in those works we began from the simple pulses, and inquire what causes produce rapid inspiration. For we demonstrated that a rapid pulse comes about when the use is pressing, the faculty is strong, and the instruments are compliant. And it seems that here too we shall state the same causes, if indeed we were not wrong to show, in the work On the Use of Pulses, that the same benefit accrues from respiration to the heat in the heart, and from the pulses to the heat throughout the whole animal.

In that very discourse on the causes in the pulses, it has been sufficiently stated [763] also concerning Archigenes' counter-argument against Magnus, that the quick pulse comes about not from strength of the faculty but rather from weakness; and there is no need to speak twice about the same things, since the mode of demonstration will be one and the same. And if the more recent physicians had treated difficulty of breathing in the same way as they treated the pulses, and had not utterly neglected it, it would have been more fitting for the account of quick motion to be investigated here, since this subject of study is also the clearer one and for this reason ought to be taught first.

But I do not know how it is that, while they inquired at very great length about respiration itself, leaving unexamined neither the use for the sake of which it occurs nor the faculty by which it is brought about, and while they also busied themselves carefully with its organs themselves, how many and which they are and how they are moved, yet difficulty of breathing they passed over altogether idly, as though the account of it were not more necessary, or not more varied, or not harder to discover. Some said nothing whatsoever about it, not even the least thing; others touched on it quite briefly. And this although Hippocrates had written [764] in the books On Epidemics, like a kind of gadfly, the differences of the difficulties of breathing; stung by it, they ought at some point to have been roused from their deep sleep, and to have inquired what the affected place is in each of them, what the mode of the condition is, and what the cause is; and whether these things have been entirely omitted by Hippocrates, or some have been stated by him and others not; and where in his writings, and how: whether completely and clearly, or deficiently and, as it were, in seminal form. For no one has inquired into any of these things, and, of those who call themselves Hippocrateans and write exegetical commentaries on his writings, no one has gone through the account of difficulty of breathing completely and in a manner worthy of the subject itself. But let us gather together into one place everything that has been said in each of the books, and show that in these matters too the man far surpasses the others. This, however, is not to be done yet.

For it is my purpose not only to expound the opinion of Hippocrates, but also to add the proper demonstrations [765] of his doctrines, and to furnish to those who read them an exact grasp of the truth that is in them. For this purpose it is much better not to forestall the occasion with the opinion of the ancient. Accordingly, this first book of mine will be a teaching, with demonstration, of what is true; the second, which follows it, an exposition of what Hippocrates held concerning difficulty of breathing.

Let us, then, take up again the point at which we broke off our account, namely that the whole inquiry into speed of motion is carried through by us in the works on the pulses, because that treatise has been zealously pursued by most of the more recent physicians, whereas the one now before us has been neglected by almost all, although it is far clearer and no less useful than that one. But I myself might state the cause of this as the account proceeds. For now the sequel must be carried through: that in all cases quick motion comes about both through urgent need and, in addition, through the faculty being able to serve it, that is, being strong, and through none of the instruments [766] offering resistance; the demonstrations of these, we said, have been stated in the works on the pulses. It has also been stated in those works that it is possible, at times, when the need presses sufficiently, for the motion to become quick even if the faculty is moderately weaker; but if it should come to a greater degree of weakness, it is no longer possible for it to come about quickly, and then the activity becomes frequent rather than quick. For of all frequency of activities there is one cause: the deficiency of the preceding activity. For, since that presses, they are compelled no longer to remain at rest for longer. All these things have been demonstrated in those works, but the account of them is common to respiration as well: first, because it was stated universally, concerning all motion; and then also because respiration, almost in its entirety, stands in proportion to the analogy of the pulses. For it is composed of contrary motions separated by rests, and it comes about for the sake of the same need; and of its parts, inspiration, being similar to the diastole of the pulses, cools the innate heat, while expiration, like the systole of the pulses, excretes the smoky residue of the combustion.

[767] Moreover, that both activities contribute to the nourishment of the psychic pneuma, and that of the rests the one after the dilatation is shorter and the one after the contraction longer, are common to both. How speed comes to be added to the respiratory movements has now been stated. Next I shall go through magnitude. In this case too, then, the need must summon to the work, the faculty, being strong, must serve it, and readiness must be present in the instruments. For magnitude of breathing requires the same concurrence of causes as speed does. Their opposites, however, slowness and smallness, do not in every case require all the opposites together; rather, one of them must by all means be present, but more than one is not necessary.

For if the need is greatly relaxed, the speed of the movement and the size of the dilatation are relaxed along with it, even if the faculty is as well off in strength as can be; for it will hold this faculty idle so long as the animal has no need of its activity. So too if the need is great but the tone of the faculty is in some way relaxed, and so too if these are in order but some damage befalls [768] the instruments, of the kind we went through in our works on the pulses: for whichever of these it may be, the speed and the size of the breathing will be hindered. In these respects, then, the pulses wholly resemble the breathings. So if we first take up the causes and then examine the alterations of breathing that follow upon them, we shall find them closely similar. For example, suppose we inquire what form of dyspnoea there will be when the heat has been increased while the other causes of breathing remain unchanged. We shall find, as was also shown in the first book of The Causes in the Pulses, that when the heat is increased a little, the inspiration becomes clearly larger, but not also faster; but when it is increased to the greatest extent, the inspiration becomes very large, fast, and by now also frequent. In the same way, if the natural heat were diminished while the other causes remain unchanged, we shall find that the inspiration must then become small, slow and sparse, but smaller than the natural by only a little, much slower, and very much sparser.

For when the faculty is strong, [769] it is not possible for the dilatation to become much smaller. But if what pertains to the need is relaxed to a considerable degree, it is likely that it remains at rest for a very long time, yet not on this account that it moves altogether slowly either, so long as the faculty is strong. And the kinds of dyspnoea that occur when the heat increases will also be those that occur when the nourishment of the psychic pneuma is pressing, namely those that arise in connection with inspiration. So too the immoderate amount of the sooty combustion of the humours will produce the same dyspnoeas of expiration as those described in the case of inspiration. For they will be fast and large and frequent when much residue of this kind has accumulated, but slow and small and infrequent in the opposite conditions. Is it, then, that reason requires this, while something among the things that are evidently apparent conflicts with it? I for my part find all these things in agreement with the ages, the regions, and in general all the constitutions of the air that surrounds us; and not least the phenomena in all occupations and those in diseases bear witness to it.

[770] For where heat predominates, one can see the inspirations becoming fast, large and frequent; where, on the other hand, cold predominates, the opposite ones, slow, small and infrequent. Moreover, those in whom the psychic pneuma is being emptied, and who for this reason need its renourishment quickly, draw in breath not only large but also fast and frequent; for those in whom nothing is emptied, the form of inspiration is the opposite of these. But if both should concur, both an increase of heat and a consumption of pneuma, these have the largest, fastest and most frequent inspiration of all, and especially if each of the two should be increased vehemently; just as, when both are strongly diminished, the inspirations become smallest, slowest and most infrequent. And indeed the form of the expirations too, if many smoky residues should have been collected, is largest, fastest and most frequent; but if they should be altogether very few, smallest, slowest and most infrequent.

Among the ages, at any rate, we see that all those in growth breathe in large, fast and frequent, while those in decline [771] do the opposite, sparse, small and slow. This is because in the former the hot is greater and in the latter less, and because in the former the substance of the psychic pneuma must grow along with the body, while in the latter it must wither along with it. For both causes, then, the young differ greatly from the older in the forms of inspiration, and again for two other causes in their expirations. For in the growing ages a very great quantity of humours is consumed, both because of the strength of the innate heat and because of growth itself. In the declining ages only so much is consumed as serves for living itself, since they are no longer growing and are already being chilled. Accordingly, in the former the expiration appears fast, large and frequent, and in the latter disposed in every respect the opposite way. The pulses too are found to have this same form according to the differences of the ages, as we also went through in the third book of the causes in them.

As in the ages, so also in the seasons, in the regions, and in all the conditions of the air that surrounds us, the pulses are analogous to the respirations and the respirations to the pulses [772]: in the hot ones they turn towards largeness, quickness and frequency, and in the cold ones towards the opposites. All these matters have been discussed in those books, as indeed have the habitual pursuits. For when we run and wrestle, or exert ourselves vigorously in any other way, we breathe large, quick and frequent; but when we are at rest we breathe small, slow and sparse. This is because with intense movements the heat is increased and the psychic pneuma is used up, whereas when people are quiet and remain motionless the heat dies down, and pneuma is consumed either not at all or in very small quantity. So too with baths: hot ones make the respiration quick, large and frequent, and cold ones the opposite. In sleep one must pay very close attention to what happens. For expiration exceeds inspiration both in size and in quickness of movement, at the time when the working-up of the foods and of all the humours, and above all the digestions, take place. It is therefore likely that the smoky residue also accumulates in the greatest quantity during sleep.

[773] And as regards diseases too (for we must now speak about these as well): in all the febrile ones, and especially in those in which some great quantity of heat has collected about one of the respiratory organs or the heart, the breathing as a whole is seen to become large, quick and frequent; but in those in which the heat has been chilled, the opposite, so that to some it has even seemed to have been lost completely; and the breathing which Heraclides of Pontus wrote about as 'the breathless [woman]' (apnous) is this one. For it seems that breathing and pulse stand in proportion to each other in this case, just as in all the others. For neither of them can be lost entirely so long as the animal survives; that it should seem to have been lost on account of its smallness, however, is nothing remarkable. For escaping the senses is common not to these alone, but to all other things that are extremely small. But since enough has been said about the respects in which breathing and pulse are alike, we shall now investigate also how much in them is not alike.

For the peculiarity in each of the activities [774] that arises from the difference of the faculties is likely to make their forms, too, differ in many ways. This, then, we must examine and investigate and find out by method. Now I think I discern at once, from the very essence of the things themselves, a very great difference between all the psychic functions and the vital ones. For over the former, choice has authority over their coming-to-be, and is able at times, even if the need calls, the faculty is in good condition and each of the organs is fit for the activity, nevertheless to hold them back and keep them from motion. And where it can restrain them, so great a thing as that, surely moving them slowly or quickly, and raising them to a greater or a lesser extent, and over a longer or a shorter time, is very easy for it. With the vital functions it is not so: when the need calls, the faculty being strong and the organs being fit for their motions, it is not possible for the activity to become either slow or small.

At any rate, in the case of the pulses in inflamed parts it is seen most clearly that, on account of the motion of the arteries in them, violent pain supervenes, because it is not in our power to make the motion smaller in magnitude or slower in speed. [775] And yet, if it were in our power to render it smaller and slower, we should have counted nothing of greater importance, since by this means we would be going to soothe the pain. For everything that is inflamed requires complete rest. When the parts in them are moved and rubbed against one another, it is compressed, becomes the seat of a flux, and is pained in every way. But if at some time it should be compelled by the urgency of need, it bears the smaller and slower motion more easily than the larger and quicker. So too the leg, when some part in it is inflamed, longs above all to rest; but if we are compelled to move it because some need is pressing, we walk less and more slowly. But it is not possible to do this in the case of the arteries. For their motion is not in our power, neither so as to stop it while it is taking place, nor so as to make it slower instead of quicker or smaller instead of larger; rather, we must of necessity put up with the one that is present, whether it be quick, or large, or in whatever way violent.

For this reason, when the arteries move in inflamed parts, we feel pain, but we can make the movement neither [776] fainter nor smaller nor slower. Yet in the case of the activities that are according to choice, we either rest the leg altogether or make its movement quite small and slow. When we speak of small and large movement, it is surely plain to everyone that we say so not in the strict sense, but from the distances over which the thing in motion is carried. Since, then, the thorax too, being one of the parts of the animal, is an instrument of respiration, as the artery is of pulses and the leg of walking, it follows that if respiration is one of the vital functions, the thorax will move analogously to the arteries, and if one of the psychic functions, similarly to the legs. But respiration is in fact one of the psychic functions, as has been demonstrated elsewhere; it is clear, therefore, that the thorax will move similarly to the legs. If, then, it should be inflamed and be compelled to move, it will expand more slowly and much less than it ought. But if it does this, it will breathe deficiently.

And if it does this same thing a second and still a third time as well, the deficit in each [breath], having at length become one considerable sum total, will bring the animal close to [777] suffocating. So that this may not happen, it makes its activities more frequent, no longer resting as long as when it was in its natural state, doing something like those who, because they cannot take in sufficient nourishment all at once, feed continually on a little. But in this case the breathing as a whole must become small, slow and frequent, and indeed smaller than is proper to a greater degree than it is slower. For the pain to the thorax is not so severe on account of the speed of the movement as on account of the magnitude of the expansion. For speed, even if it is painful during the activity itself, nevertheless, by making the whole movement short in duration, distresses the thorax less; for it arrives quickly at that toward which it hastens; and it hastens, of course, toward rest, and longs to attain this as quickly as possible, since this alone soothes for it the pain arising from the inflammation. But the magnitude of the expansion is altogether troublesome, both through the very violence of the movement and through at once compressing and stretching the inflamed parts, and paining the thorax in all manner of ways.

For this reason, then, it takes away more from the size than from the speed; and when [778] this alone is the affection, namely a pain of the parts about the thorax, and the demands of the need do not press, the heat in the heart evidently remaining within its natural limits, the movement of the thorax manifestly becomes slower. But when some fiery heat arises in it, the speed is not relaxed, for the reasons we stated earlier; here too the size is considerably reduced, but in its place frequency is produced, because of the urgency of the need. So from what has already been said it is plain that pain by itself, arising about one of the respiratory organs, will make the breath small, slow and frequent. With burning heat it will still be small now, in the same way, but more frequent than that which is due to pain alone, and already somewhat quicker. The difficulty of breathing that arises from fiery heat alone was shown earlier to make the breath large, quick and frequent. So each of the simple kinds, and the kind compounded from both, is clear and easily distinguished.

For the one arising from excess of heat alone, even if it makes the breathing [779] frequent, much as does the one due to pain alone, is nevertheless clearly distinguished by size and speed; while the one arising from both causes coming together differs from the one due to fiery heat (phlogōsis) by smallness alone, and from the one due to pain by size and speed. Moreover, the dyspnoea due to the chilling of the natural heat is also distinguished from all of these by certain clear signs. For this one, as was shown, makes the breathing small, slow and infrequent; and in none of the others do slowness and infrequency occur together. But to the extent that, owing to deficiencies and excesses of heat, the form of the respiration departs from its natural rhythm, these things hold in the same way for the pulses as well; whereas those owing to painful conditions of the organs no longer hold in the same way, but where they differ has, I think, been clearly shown. The remaining conditions of the organs, however, all those that arise without pain from obstructions or scirrhous indurations or compressions or, in general, from certain narrowings, produce the alterations similarly in both activities, the psychic and the vital.

For in these the breath becomes small, rapid and frequent [780]: small, because, owing to the narrowness of the parts that receive it, less than is required is drawn in; frequent, because the requirements of the need are not fulfilled; and for the same cause rapid as well. It has been shown in the commentaries on pulses that the magnitude of the dilatation, when it adequately fulfils the need, requires no rapidity, but when it falls short in some respect, then the shift is made to rapidity as well, provided the faculty is strong; and when not even this is sufficient, then to frequency as well. For these reasons, then, the breath becomes small, rapid and frequent, in the pulses and in the breathing, in the conditions mentioned before. It was said in the work on pulses that it is also irregular, and that this is above all their proper sign, and the reasoning about the cause has been stated there. It was also said that in the very parts that have the obstructions, and in those that share with them, the features of irregularity are most evident, and smallness of the pulses accompanies them either always or for the most part, whereas in the other parts it is rather largeness.

But if the affection is near the source, it thus becomes common [781] to all the arteries. These things, then, have been both stated and demonstrated in that work. But we shall now go through what is peculiar to the respiratory organs, so that nothing may be lacking to the account. When, then, because unconcocted tumours have formed in them, or viscous and thick humours have occupied the passages of the breath, or some scirrhous swelling has grown up in them, or one of the bodies adjoining them has, in some manner whatsoever, been raised into a swelling of excessive size, the breath is drawn in to a lesser extent than is needed on account of lack of space, there necessarily accrues to it, for the reasons stated, speed and frequency. And several forms come to be within the genus of this difficulty of breathing, different parts in the respiratory organs being straitened for space at different times.

For the swellings contrary to nature that arise in the stomach and liver, and also in the spleen and the colon and the parts connected with these, make the breath small, quick and frequent through the constriction of the diaphragm. In the same way, in the dropsical, in pregnant women, [782] in those who are overfilled, and in those with a protruding belly, this form of respiration comes about. In the so-called orthopnoeas it comes about when viscous and thick fluids collect in the rough arteries in the lung. So too, if something in the lung should become scirrhous, or a growth should form there, compressing and constricting the class of the rough arteries (for it is these that receive the inhaled air), the breath will be small, frequent and quick. In the same way, if such a growth should form in the thorax as well, of the kind by which the parts along the spine often become humped backward, bowed forward and twisted sideways, the breath will become small, frequent and quick, evidently because the swelling contrary to nature occupies the space of the lung into which it used to extend when it dilated. And often such conditions have rendered the whole thorax itself narrower, either befalling them straight away while they were being carried in the womb, or else occurring later, afterwards.

It makes no difference, at least as regards the lung's being unable, when constricted, to draw in a sufficient quantity of air, whether the whole thorax has become narrow through some condition or other, [783] or the lung has lost the intervening space because it has been occupied by certain bodies formed contrary to nature within the thorax, or whether the lung itself has become scirrhous or obstructed or swollen, as happens in the so-called pneumonic and peripneumonic affections. For in all cases there is this one containing cause of the inspiration's becoming small: the constriction of the rough arteries. And because the inspiration is small, for this reason, as has often been said, frequency and speed are added to it. But when the affection occurs in the lung itself, then, even though the thorax is able to dilate to the greatest extent, they nevertheless inspire little; and so too when the spaces between the organs have been occupied. When, however, the whole thorax becomes small and narrow, either in those still being carried in the womb or in some other way, it is clear that, by producing a dilation that is likewise small in proportion to itself, it becomes for the lung the cause of the speed of the inspiration. So too when the diaphragm is compressed by something, specifically at the lower boundary itself of the thorax, as in the painless affections.

[784] For this above all must be remembered: that sometimes the condition of the thorax alone, sometimes that of the lung, and sometimes that of the space between both, brings about the change of the breathing towards smallness, and on this account towards quickness and frequency, provided at least that the faculty is strong. For this too must be remembered, though it has already been said many times before.

Let us therefore no longer, in this discussion, make mention of those with pleurisy, or of those who have certain abscessions or, in general, painful swellings in the thorax. The whole of the foregoing discussion was carried through concerning the painless affections, those which, by compressing the lung and constricting the rough arteries within it, make the inspiration smaller. Those others, rather, let us assign to the affections of the thorax written about before these, in the case of which we said that the thorax, being less expanded on account of the pain, makes the breath small. But the condition of those who are called empyematous, even though its genesis very often comes about from pleurisy, let us count together with those just now mentioned, which, producing constriction [785] in the lung without pain, render the breathing small. For the pus contained in it in such conditions becomes the cause of the smallness in the expansion. Since, then, it is itself no longer dilating according to nature, neither does it make an equal drawing-in of the breath. In what way, then, will these affections of the respiratory organs without pain be distinguished from those with pain (for this still remains for the present discussion), if indeed in both alike the breath becomes small and frequent? Or is it by the speed of the movement? For in the affections with pain they breathe little and frequently, but not quickly, at least whenever such an affection occurs without fever. With fever, however, even if they breathe in a similar way as to smallness and speed, they are nevertheless distinguished by frequency.

For their breath becomes frequent to no moderate degree; but this is not the case in those who have difficulty of breathing on account of narrowness of the respiratory organs: rather, even if their breath should become more frequent, it undergoes this only moderately, and far below the extreme [786] frequency. Moreover, in those who are feverish the expiration is at once both larger and hotter, which was not the case in those who breathe out small and frequent on account of narrowness. How one must diagnose precisely the smallness and largeness of each of the two parts of the whole respiration will be stated a little later, once we have first completed the entire account concerning the organs. For that the difficulties of breathing of these organs which are without pain differ from those with pain has indeed already been said. But just as we declared without qualification that the narrowness must extend to the lung, and above all to its rough arteries, for the animal to have difficulty of breathing, must we likewise say that the pain must arise in the respiratory organs, and above all in the thorax (for the lung is all but insensible)? Or must we seek some other declaration concerning difficulties of breathing of this kind?

For he who says that this kind of difficulty of breathing follows only upon the pains of the respiratory organs would not, I think, seem to have understood the whole matter concerning them rightly, nor to remember the earlier [787] reasonings, in which it was shown that the breath becomes small and frequent not because of the affection, but because of the faculty of the activity, which is psychic. The kind of difficulty of breathing that follows upon narrowings of the lung, however, needs no further contribution from the faculty for its coming-to-be; hence in this case we made our declaration rightly, framing the account universally for the whole matter. But concerning painful affections one ought not to have spoken without qualification, at any rate when they arise in the respiratory parts. For it was not on account of the nature of the parts themselves, specifically, but because a psychic faculty had charge of their motion, that the respiration came to be turned towards smallness, so that the animal should not be pained more greatly, the faculty dilating the thorax less than is fitting. And this forethought against being pained more greatly exists, surely, for all the other parts as well that are moved together with the respiratory organs when these move: the gullet, the stomach, the liver, the spleen, the peritoneum, the colon, the upper parts of the small intestines, and the muscles at the hypochondrium.

[788] For these move together with the movements of the thorax, and especially if those movements are greater. It is therefore evident that they suffer more pain with the large movements of the thorax and less with the small ones. For this reason the breath will be small and frequent not only in pleuritics but also in those whose gullet or stomach is in a painful condition, though less so, because in these the sensation too is less. Those who suffer pain in the liver or the spleen, or in any other of the parts mentioned before, are, however, similarly short of breath. For all such parts, some suspended from the respiratory organs and others grown together with them, are shaken along with them when they move, and for this reason they are distressed when [the patients] breathe. And so let our account now concern not, as before, the respiratory parts only, but all the parts that move at all in breathing, and let us venture to declare universally that small and frequent breath is a sign of pain in any of the parts of the animal that move in the course of breathing.

Is it, then, only in this respect that the pulses differ from the breathing, or is it possible to find some difference also with regard to the cause itself, taken on its own, that [789] arises from the faculty, apart from its being interwoven with the organs? For the natural faculties all devote themselves continually to the works that are necessary to them, and are never slack or neglectful; but whatever comes under the authority of choice is often accomplished rather neglectfully when choice is occupied with other actions. At any rate, when we are sometimes walking briskly towards some business, and then in the meantime, on the way, think of something, and next go on to examine it and to ponder about it, we slacken much of the intensity of our walk. Yet we do not perceive or recognise this very fact for as long as we attend to the object of our thought

[our] mind; but whenever we stop, and no longer have our thought on anything except walking alone, then, as if roused from some sleep, we both recognize how far our present activity falls short of our original impulse, and rouse ourselves again to the task. So too those who are delirious, having their mind, I suppose, on their phantasms [790] as though on certain preoccupations, neglect the psychic activities: they neither urinate unless someone reminds them, nor defecate, nor ask to drink or to eat, nor anything else of the kind; and if they do happen to ask at some time, they have forgotten in the interval while it is being brought, and need reminders once more. At any rate we know a great many who asked for a chamber pot, and when it was given no longer urinated, but held it idly in their two hands; and others who got up as if to defecate, but when they had sat down forgot completely and did nothing, until those present reminded them. And just as all these perform their activities at long intervals, so also they perform them on a large scale: at any rate they urinate a very great quantity all at once, and drink at a single go beyond the due measure, and do each of the other things in the same way. And this is nothing surprising, I think: for what they ought to have done often, at the proper times, they are compelled to fulfil all at once when the need presses, and especially when it is necessary for life.

For someone who drinks less than is needed is able to hold out not [791] for days only, but even for whole months, whereas someone who breathes less could not last even for the smallest part of a day. Hence, even if the delirious drink a very great amount at one time, yet, because it is taken at long intervals, the whole of their drink falls far short of the moderate amount; but the need of respiration, when it is not fulfilled, because it carries a danger at once imminent and distressing, rouses them to the activity and does not allow them to be slack even for a very short time, and at once recovers all that it has been deprived of through the time of rest; and thus [the breath] becomes not only infrequent but also large, and larger than is proper by as much as it is also more infrequent, which does not happen in the case of drink: for they drink much more infrequently, but only a little more, whence Hippocrates called them 'drinkers of little' (brachypotai). This argument, then, demonstrates that in the delirious the breathing turns to infrequency and largeness; and not least does direct observation also bear witness to it, at least for those who wish to examine the theory upon the very works of the art.

But those who, in their lectures with the young, sit lofty and conspicuous upon lofty chairs, [792] who have neglected the works of the art and babble whatever comes to their tongue: to these, things attested by what is clearly apparent are no more credible than they are to people who do not know in the first place even whether this or that thing appears at all. Indeed, one of these sophists once disputed with me about the breath becoming large and sparse in those who are deranged. For he supposed respiration to be one of the vital functions, but what appears did not agree with such a hypothesis; and so he decided that he must meet it head-on. For he said that this kind of respiration does not appear at all in deliria. For the things that the sophists have never undertaken to observe closely in the sick themselves, about these they shamelessly insist as if they had seen them ten thousand times, and they do not hesitate to profess long experience of things they have not seen even in a dream. But those who do observe closely what appears and what befalls the sick write just as Hippocrates also does.

For they have seen, I think, many patients similar to those he wrote about, bearing witness to the [793] argument stated before. I would already have set out the patients recorded by him in the Epidemics, had I not proposed, as I said earlier too, to give over the whole of my next book, the second, to their exposition, and to bring this book to a conclusion by itself, together with its proper demonstrations. So then, let the account of those who are delirious end here. Now let it be stated how one might best discern large and small breathing, for I know that I deferred this too in what preceded. It would have been ready to hand to say that it makes no difference whether large inspiration is discerned by the magnitude of the expansion of the respiratory organs or by the quantity of the substance inhaled. This is indeed what some say, holding that the quantity of the inspiration must always be proportional to the quantity [sc. of the expansion] of the organs. Such a thing, however, is not true universally; it requires some qualification.

For when the organs are in their natural state, the quantity of the pneuma is always proportional to the dilatations [794] of them; but not, indeed, when they are also disposed contrary to nature: rather, it is possible at times for the thorax to be distended to the greatest extent, and yet for only a little of the outside air to be inhaled. For there are many conditions, if we remember anything of what was said before, by which the lung, being constricted, is unable to receive a sufficient quantity of air. Inspirations, therefore, do not come about in proportion to the states of all the respiratory organs, but only of the rough arteries. But it is not possible to discern the dilatation of these by any one of the senses. Therefore one ought not even to direct one's attention to the respiratory organs whenever we wish to discern the quantity of the inspiration. For it suffices to examine the air alone: how much is inhaled, and how much, in turn, is exhaled. For neither do we infer anything about the amount of foods from the bulk of the belly; here too it suffices to examine only the quantity of what is eaten.

Since in expirations the muscles are sometimes entirely idle, allowing the thorax, as it collapses, to regain its proper state, and sometimes, being active, contract it further [795] (for this has been demonstrated by us many times), contractions of the thorax without the intensity of these muscles would never produce a large expiration, whereas those accompanied by it, which are in fact also blowings-out, as this too was shown, are the producers of largeness. But not even in these cases do I think it right to strip the person and look at the tension of the muscles; it is enough to take the form of expiration accompanied by blowing out as the most important sign. At any rate, when the need presses, we are compelled to breathe out all at once, just as also, when the need for inspiration presses, we draw in the outside air in large quantity and all at once. And since we have now gone through these matters sufficiently as well, let us recapitulate the chief points of what has been said from the beginning and then turn to what remains.

The chief points were, I think, these: having discovered the simple dyspnoeas, to connect them with the sustaining causes of respiration, and to show for each of them the cause that produces it, and again, for each of the causes, the dyspnoea that follows upon it; and in doing this we were compelled also to [796] mention compound dyspnoeas. Further, in some respects what pertains to the pulses agrees with the respirations, while in others it differs, and this too was no small chief point among those we went through. Since all these have been completed, let us next consider the compound dyspnoeas, for these still remain, at least for the first of the books we set ourselves. Once the simple ones have been discovered, it is no longer at all difficult to discover these as well, since they are compounded from those. For since there is a large inspiration, and likewise a quick one, and their opposites, the small and the slow, there must necessarily be four compound dyspnoeas in all with respect to inspiration: the large and at the same time slow, the large and quick, the small and quick, and fourth the small and slow. In the same way, with respect to expiration too, the same four combinations must necessarily exist: two large and two small, divided by quickness and slowness. In the pauses, however, it is not possible for a compound form of dyspnoea to arise.

[797] For they did not have two antitheses, as the movements did, but only one, consisting in frequency and infrequency. Moreover, when the movements themselves are compared with one another (I mean inspiration with expiration, just as in the pulses diastole with systole), there will be certain forms of rhythm of the whole respiration. For it is possible for the inspiration to be large and the expiration small; or conversely the inspiration small and the expiration large; or both small, or both large. So too both may be quick, or both slow, or the one quick and the other slow. Moreover, there is also an uneven respiration, just as there is an uneven pulse, both that in a collection of movements and that within a single movement. Likewise respiration may also be ordered and disordered, just as the pulse may. As many as are the differences of uneven pulses, both of those within a single movement and of those consisting in several, so many are there also of respirations.

[798] But, as I said right at the very beginning of the discussion, all have treated respiration altogether negligently; and I might state the cause of their indolence concerning it as the discussion proceeds. For now we must carry through what lies before us, beginning from the irregularity within a single motion, since this would also seem by its nature to be ranked between the strictly simple kinds and those that are admittedly compound. At any rate, someone once disputed with us about it, holding that it is not compound; and he would not have been led into this view had it not lain close to the simple kinds. But that it is compound is clear from the following. If someone, on beginning to breathe in, draws in the air quickly but at the end slowly, or conversely passes from a slow beginning to a quick end, we would not say that this inspiration is simply either quick or slow, but evidently compound, having one part of itself swift and another slow.

In the same way also the expiration, if it is altered in every way (the motion changing either from slowness to speed or, conversely, from speed to [799] slowness), we shall say is composed of parts that stand in a contrary relation to one another, and for this reason is not simple but compound. Likewise also, when some rest splits and cuts through one of the two motions, either the inspiration or the expiration, we shall say that then too the divided one, whichever it may be, is compound. And it has sometimes, though rarely, been seen that not only one of the two, but both parts of the whole respiration are so disposed in the same person; and that such a thing occurs especially when a quantity of fluids collected in the rough arteries is choking the person, as a result of a deadly pleuritis, or of a peripneumonia that has not been cleared out, or of an empyema formed there, so that in this respect the respirations agree with the pulses. For in the case of those too the unevenness was shown to arise from obstructions of the organs and compressions and, in general, narrowings. And so anyone who has learned what was said about the other arteries, those throughout the whole animal, in the second book On the Causes in Pulses would be better equipped to say similar things about the so-called rough [arteries] in the lung.

For the former [arteries] must be constricted [800] for the pulse to become irregular, and the rough arteries for the breathing. It was said in that work that irregularity of the pulses can also arise through weakness of the faculty, when it is unable to dilate the arteries completely at one go. For they stop in between and take rests, just as old men do when travelling on foot. Sometimes there may also arise in the breathing a certain irregularity, both the one within a single activity alone and the one called systematic, through some weakness of the faculty that produces it. Since this faculty is psychic, whereas a vital faculty produces the pulses, there may be some difference in the prognoses drawn from them: the pulses always indicate the weakness of the faculty in proportion to their own impairment, but the breathings no longer do so in the same way, unless one further takes into account the patient's choice.

For if Hippocrates says that from an orderly person even a bold reply is a bad sign, then in those who are bold by nature you should consider that not only such a reply, but not even delirium itself, signifies anything [801] of great moment. So it is also with respiration. For those who are unaccustomed to hardship and soft breathe irregularly at every task, even if nothing great is forcing them; but those who are fond of toil and noble in disposition would never breathe irregularly before their faculty has arrived at extreme weakness. In the case of irregularity of the pulses, however, the prognosis of the condition is the same both in those of better disposition and in those of worse. For, to speak generally, wherever choice contributes nothing at all to the activity, there what is indicated is the same for all; but in those cases where it contributes either the whole or the greatest part, in these one must additionally consider the character of the patient. And just as the difference of the faculties that produce the activities makes the prognoses from the pulses and from the respirations differ, so also from the very nature of the organs there will be a certain difference of indication. For the pulses come about through the smooth arteries, whereas respirations come about not through the rough arteries alone, but no less than through them, if indeed not even more, through the muscular kind.

[802] For this is what the psychic faculty first moves for the generation of breathing; and the thorax, moved as a whole by this, in its turn itself moves the lung along with it, in the manner we demonstrated in our reasonings about these things. The rough arteries are part of the lung, and it is into them that the inhaled air first comes. Just as, then, the affections of these often render the whole breathing irregular, so too do those of the muscles: the former because they are the spaces of the pneuma, the muscles because they are the first instrument of the motion. But it is not the same affection in each of the two kinds of organs that renders the breathing irregular, because their uses are not alike either. If, then, each of the organs, when diseased, harms the function in precisely those respects in which, when healthy, it benefits it, the damage of the rough arteries is a kind of narrowness, while that of the muscles is a faulty and disorderly motion; for the damage is to the former as places of the pneuma, to the latter as organs of motion.

Now, for the constriction in the rough (arteries) I blamed the swellings contrary to nature; of the faulty movements in the muscles [803] we shall now state the causes. Spasms, palpitations and tremors, then, are affections peculiar to muscles, as has been demonstrated in other works; and that they are faulty movements needs no argument. If both of these belong to these affections, so that they are both faulty movements and movements of muscles, and if these are the very things being sought, then this discussion too would already have reached its end; for breathing will sometimes be irregular through one of these as well. For just as walking becomes irregular when the muscles in the legs either tremble or palpitate or are in spasm, so breathing too might sometimes become irregular because the muscles that move the thorax are, as has been said, impaired. So for all the irregularities, both those within a single activity and those that arise across many successive activities, the cause will be either constriction of the rough arteries, or faulty movement of the muscles of the thorax, or weakness of the faculty that produces it.

It has been written, as I said, at very great length concerning [804] all the anomalies in the second book of On the Causes in Pulses. For this reason we pass over everything that is common to that account, merely reminding the reader of it; but whatever is peculiar to respiration we shall go through in this treatise. Now the factors pertaining to the need (χρεία), as was also said before, are common, and those of the rough arteries are analogous to those of the smooth; but what belongs peculiarly and exclusively to respirations, as distinct from pulses, is the class of the muscles. The faculties that produce them are in one respect analogous and in another respect not so. Insofar as they are efficient causes, in this respect they are analogous; but insofar as choice (προαίρεσις) governs the respiratory faculty, whereas the vital faculty has no higher master but is perfectly free, in this respect they differ. And so respiration will have something additional, compared with the pulses, towards the generation of anomaly, and let us not pass over this either.

It is twofold: the one proceeding from the psychic faculty itself alone, the other from its combination with pains. That which comes from the [805] faculty alone is slight and hard to recognise; that which comes about through pains is greater, clearer and more varied. For in deliria infrequency and largeness predominate, but a certain irregularity and disorder shows itself both over several breaths and sometimes within a single one alone. This is, I think, because the phantasms at one time more, at another less, displace the reasoning from its natural state. For in such impressions it is reasonable that respiration too should undergo some change and variation, towards the generation of irregularity and disorder, and contrary to the quantity of the need. For so long as each of its activities falls only a little short, the departure from the natural state is small. But when the deficiency relative to the natural state becomes considerable, then it is already necessary that the quantity of the rests be altered, and that in the movements not only the quantity but also the quality be altered, and in this way the whole respiration becomes irregular and disordered. This same thing must necessarily happen also in pains.

For in those cases, too, the need is not fulfilled in each activity; for they are able to dilate the thorax neither [806] quickly nor frequently nor to the greatest extent. For all these things are painful to them: most of all the size, second the speed, and then also the frequency; for it is less distressing for those in pain to be moved over a longer time than over a shorter. For this reason, then, they take away a very great deal from the size, very little from the speed, and from the frequency they take away nothing, but even add something to it, correcting the deficiency, relative to the natural state, that results from the smallness. Yet what is added is not so much as to make up the whole shortfall. Whatever portion of the need, then, is left unfulfilled, this, accumulating over many successive activities, when the animal has now come close to being choked, then compels the choice as well, at least for some time, to make the breathing larger, much quicker, and more frequent than before.

But in the activities of this [breathing], while the need is being fulfilled but the animal is being worn out by the pains, choice once again takes away from the size, the speed and the frequency, at one time more from one, at another time more from another, as though it were at a loss [807] and neither able to stop the activity, for fear of suffocation, nor finding any cure for the pain. At any rate it passes at one time to one thing and at another time to another: to the one as something that will fulfil the need, to the other as something that will soothe the pain. And since, of all these, those that fulfil the need exacerbate the pains, while those that relieve these increase the need, and no remedy common to both is found, it passes in many ways to all of them through perplexity, always dissatisfied with what is present. And from this arises both the irregularity in each breath taken by itself and in all the breaths in succession, and the manifold disorder. For in the destruction of equality lies the genesis of all the irregularities and of the disorders. For this too was shown in the work on the differences of pulses: that consecutive equality is regularity, while periodic equality is order; and that when consecutive equality is destroyed, irregularity arises, and when periodic equality is destroyed, disorder.

Nevertheless, although much unevenness and much disorder occur in such conditions [808], the class of difficulty of breathing that consists in smallness and frequency prevails. For even if at some point they should take a large breath (reading ἀπαπνεύσειαν as 'breathe') all at once, as if making trial of such breathing, they immediately desist because of the pain, and for a very long time they breathe very small, until, compelled by the pressing need, they turn once more to another attempt at a large breath. The continuity of their unevenness and disordered change, then, consists chiefly in speed and slowness and in the variations of frequency. Because of the urgency of the need, the breathing never becomes simply infrequent; it becomes more and less frequent, and in this it acquires its unevenness. So in those who are so disposed the breath is always frequent, rarely large, and no more slow than fast, because of its quick-tipping transition into either of these.

It was therefore rightly said earlier that, when any of the organs moved in respiration is in pain, small and frequent breathing follows; and, by the same reasoning, that in deliria the breathing becomes large and infrequent, even though some irregularity very much [809] attends these too. For in them infrequency and largeness predominate: in those who are delirious the breathing becomes more or less infrequent and more or less large, but never small and frequent. This much seems to me sufficient to know about the irregularities, both those in a single activity and those that arise in several. For about the latter too what was fitting has been said, through what the account has in common. And indeed these latter are clearly compound, since they require a great many activities both for their generation and for their diagnosis; whereas those in a single activity, as was also said before, might perhaps seem to someone to be simple. In the same discussion we went through not only the systematic irregularities but also the instances of disorder. For these are a kind of irregularity, as was shown also in the works on pulses. Let us then return again to the remaining compound difficulties of breathing, and let us first take up those of them that arise in any one single activity.

A large and at the same time fast inspiration occurs when the need is pressing, the instruments are compliant, and the [810] faculty either is strong with its own proper strength or has been only slightly altered. The argument needs no demonstration for those who remember what was said earlier. The inspiration that is large but slow, on the other hand, occurs only in those who are deranged, and not always in them. Here too the reasoning about the cause is plain from what was said before, just as it is also when they breathe in small and slowly, in whom the innate heat has been considerably cooled. The remaining, fourth pairing was smallness together with speed. It does not invariably arise upon any simple condition, just as the inspiration that is large and at the same time slow does not either, which we said sometimes befalls those who are deranged. It does, however, follow, if not continually, at least for the most part, when pain and an increase of the need come together in the same person. For in pains they of necessity breathe small. Since the need remains unfulfilled, both because of this very smallness and because it was assumed to be in excess on its own account, it is not enough that the activities merely be made frequent; they are often compelled to breathe in spasmodically.

Analogously [811] to what has been said, one must also discover the conditions underlying the combinations that concern expirations. For in these too we shall find either the faculty, or one of the organs, affected, or the measure of the heat altered. For the residues that we call, as it were, sooty, fuliginous and smoky in the class of heat are all earthy, and, so to speak, half-concocted by the innate heat, just as smoke is by fire. For in the case of fire it is plainly evident that all the smoky residues of the material are acrid and hot, which indicates that they have received into themselves the power of the fire, yet have not been wholly mastered by it; for in that case flame would have come into being, and no longer smoke.

So that if someone were to say that, when smoky heat predominates in the bodies of animals, the expiration becomes at once large and fast, he would not be wrong; but it is clear that at that time the faculty must also be strong, and none of the organs must be affected. In the same way he would not be wrong in saying that the expiration which is at once large and slow occurs in some of those who are delirious, just as was the case with inspiration; and likewise the small and at the same time slow expiration in those in whom no smoky residue had [812] accumulated, and the small and fast in those in whom it had accumulated and in whom those of the parts that are, evidently, moved in respiration are in pain. For one must always bear these things in mind, even if they are sometimes omitted in the wording. These, then, are the four combinations of the dyspnoeas that are constituted in each part of the whole respiration separately; but there are others according to what is, as it were, its rhythm, not in each part separately: when we compare inspiration with expiration, just as in the pulses diastole with systole, we call such a thing rhythm. It is clear that this topic will admit the same theory as the one written by Herophilus on the rhythms in the pulses. We have, then, said what is needed about them in the treatises on the pulses as well; but they will be stated now also, as briefly as possible: the points to which one must direct one's attention, as to certain marks, in order readily to discover the causes of the lack of rhythm in respirations.

For the very things I just set out concerning each [813] part of the whole respiration (I mean inspiration and expiration), which we have already stated in the preceding discussion, these same things I think it right to consider now also with respect to their arrhythmias. For example (there is nothing wrong with demonstrating what is being said on some one case, as an example), let inspiration be slower and smaller than the natural, and expiration quicker and larger: we shall say that in those so disposed the natural heat has been diminished and the smoky has been increased. Again, in another arrhythmia that is the reverse, such that inspiration is large and quick and expiration small and slow, we shall say that the natural heat has been increased and that there is no smoky residue. For one must always conceive of heat as twofold in kind: the one proper and innate to the body, the other acquired and spurious. It is clear, then, that such a combination alters nothing of what belongs to each of the two on its own.

For if the inspiration happens to become small and slow, it indicates a chilling of the natural heat, however the expiration may be; and if the expiration is [814] disposed in the same way, it will indicate the same thing. For again, if it should at some time become large and quick, it will indicate a heat that is excessive and contrary to nature, however matters stand with the inspiration. Hence such a combination teaches nothing more towards prognoses than what is already known about each of them on its own. We must, then, turn our attention only to those compound difficulties of breathing in which the simple ones are common to several conditions, and for this reason indicate nothing clear, but, when coupled with certain others, arrive at a secure distinction. For largeness of breathing, taken in and by itself, is a simple difficulty of breathing; but it is a sure sign of nothing, since it occurs both when the need is urgent and when the mind is impaired. But if it is joined with frequency, it indicates urgency of the need; if with infrequency, derangement.

In the same way smallness too, taken by itself, indicates either that some part is in pain or that the need is slackened, so that it too indicates nothing clear; but when it becomes compound, with frequency it indicates pain, and with infrequency a slackening of the [815] need. And if you take up frequency on its own, or infrequency, you would find that neither of these, too, indicates anything clear unless it is distinguished by being combined with some other kind of difficulty of breathing. For frequent and at the same time large indicates an increase of the faculty; frequent and at the same time small, pain of one of the organs that move together with the respirations; and the infrequent, which accompanies deliria and chillings, if it is with largeness, indicates the first of the things mentioned; if with smallness, the second. And for this reason, of all the compound difficulties of breathing, such pairings are the most useful, since each indicates a single condition clearly and securely: frequency together with smallness, pain; but if it occurs with largeness, an increase of the need; infrequency with largeness, delirium, and with smallness, a slackening of the need. These pairings come to be four, the differences in the activities according to largeness and smallness being combined with the differences of the rests.

For two antitheses [816], interchanged with one another, produce four conjunctions. So here too it has already become clear that neither more nor fewer combinations can arise from these antitheses. But in the case of the rests there is only one antithesis, that according to frequency and infrequency, whereas in the case of the activities there is not only that according to largeness and smallness, but also that according to speed and slowness. And clearly four pairings will likewise arise from the interchanges of these: first, frequent and fast; second, frequent and at the same time slow; third, infrequent and at the same time fast; and fourth, slow and at the same time infrequent. But these make nothing known simply and of necessity, as the former four do; rather one must make distinctions as follows: when the change towards frequency is great, but that towards speed slight, there is an increase both of pain and of need; but if, conversely, it departs from the natural state more towards speed and less towards frequency, it will show that the need alone has been intensified.

With a difficulty of breathing of this kind, largeness will in every case also concur, [817] and with the other one, mentioned before it, smallness, so that we shall have no need to mention speed. For if the combination of speed and frequency, when left undistinguished, shows us nothing clear, but, once brought to a distinction, comes about straightaway together with largeness when speed predominates, and necessarily has smallness following upon it when frequency prevails, then it will be frequent and at the same time large according to the one distinction, and frequent and at the same time small according to the other. In this way the frequent and slow combination will also be explained. For when frequency predominates, it will indicate pain alone; but when it departs from the natural state as far as it also does in slowness, it will be a sign of a compound condition. For it will show both that the faculty has been diminished and that some part is in pain. So too, if slowness predominates over frequency, it will be a sign of the condition already stated, but it will show that those so affected are in less pain, and that their faculty has been diminished to a greater degree. Accordingly, we have no need of this combination either for prognoses.

For in the first four that were mentioned, which [818] we said were the most useful, we have great signs both of pain and of a diminution of the need. And the third combination mentioned, the one that is sparse and at the same time fast, will indicate nothing of necessity, but it accompanies either certain deliria, or deliria together with the very increases of the need. It has also been said before that in those who are delirious the breathing is in every case sparse and large, but not in every case fast, just as it is not in every case slow either; for each of these occurs irregularly and unevenly. When, however, the increase of the need also concurs, they are then compelled to breathe both much larger than if they were only delirious, and now also faster. So we have no need of this combination either for the prognoses, since we already have what is indicated through it, together with the distinction, in the first four combinations. There remained the fourth of the compound dyspnoeas of this genus, the one that is slow and at the same time sparse, which likewise accompanies both certain deliria and diminutions of the need. Therefore we no longer need this one either; for we recognised both delirium and diminished need from the first four combinations.

[819] It is not only from having shown that the difference with respect to quickness and slowness is not necessary for prognoses, whether you take it alone or combine it with the others, that the usefulness of those [other combinations] becomes clearly evident; it also appears from the very nature of the matter. For since there are three primary genera of the causes of respiration, the need, the faculty and the instruments, it is clear that, if we find from which and from how many dyspnoeas we shall recognise the conditions in these, these will be the most useful to us for prognoses, while all the others we shall examine as something over and above [what is needed]. But it was found that the large and frequent [breathing] indicates an increase of the need, and the opposite one, the small and sparse, its decrease; that the large and sparse is peculiar to delirium, and the small and frequent to pain. In addition the irregular ones came in from outside, indicating sometimes the conditions of the muscular class, sometimes also the narrowings of the rough arteries.

When the faculty is weak, in the first place no sign of difficulty of breathing is necessarily found, since those who shrink from hardship shape their [820] breathing in one way and the hardy in another; and if there should indeed be something uneven and disorderly, it is obscure, and the inequalities in frequency and infrequency and smallness and size produce the unevennesses and the disorders themselves. Besides, weakness of the psychic faculty is recognised through countless other things as well, and we have no need at all of the breathing. Hippocrates taught the most important and the most numerous of these in his Prognostic book, and if anything has been omitted, it is very easy to find from what has been said. But if someone should wish to have specific signs when the respiratory faculty itself is weak, and in common the whole psychic faculty, and especially when it has been chilled, he will have the movement of the alae of the nose, the activity of all the muscles about the shoulder blades, and the sudden collapse of the thorax.

For whenever this is moved more feebly than is fitting, during inspirations the wings of the nose come to the aid of the rush of the breath, themselves too in a way drawing in the outside air along with it, in the same manner as we draw the lips together when we intend to draw something in through the mouth; and again during expirations there occurs a sudden, all-at-once [821] collapse of the thorax, not a gradual subsidence. It has been stated at greater length in the books On the Movement of Muscles in what way the collapse of a part differs from its lowering and relaxation: the former occurs when the faculty is weak, the latter when it is strong. Further, in those who are weak in the respiratory faculty something of the following kind also happens during expirations. The tension which the thorax, together with the diaphragm, had until then possessed during inspirations, it lays aside all at once, as if it were suddenly dying. It was said in the commentaries On Respiration that the diaphragm merely relaxes its tension when people breathe out; but to relax it gradually is not the same as to lay it all aside at once. The intercostal muscles contribute a little to such expirations; we have shown that forcible exhalations occur when these are active. Such, then, and from these causes, is the form of respiration in those whose faculty is weak. What seems to me still lacking to complete this first book will now be stated.

[822] Since there are two rests in respiration, one before inspiration and the other before expiration, whichever of the two movements is harmed also displaces the rest that precedes it from its natural state. Since, then, there is a twofold harm in the movements and a twofold harm in the rests as well, deficiencies of the need always produce long-lasting pauses, and excesses short-lasting ones. So when we say that respiration becomes frequent and large from an abundance of heat, the statement is true for each of the two movements. For excesses of the natural heat, which make inspiration large, at once also render the rest that precedes it short in duration. Excesses of the unnatural and smoky heat, just as they make expiration large, so also make the pause before it brief. So the breath certainly becomes large and frequent whenever a kind of heat is in excess; yet it is not the same part of respiration that this changes towards largeness, nor the same rest that it changes towards frequency.

In the same way, too, if the demands of the need are reduced because the heat has been diminished, then, when the innate [823] heat has been impaired and the inspiration becomes small, a long rest precedes it; and when the preternatural heat is being destroyed, the expiration becomes small and the quiescence before it long. Often, however, the preternatural heat has increased while the natural heat has diminished; and in this way the quiescence before the expiration becomes long in duration, and the other short in duration. For whichever of the movements the need presses for, it does not allow the aforementioned quiescence to be prolonged. As much, then, as is useful for present purposes has now been said about these matters. If anyone is in difficulty about the difference among the heats, this would not now be the occasion to instruct him; rather, it is the occasion to refer him to the treatises On Innate Heat. For I think that, unless he is altogether contentious, he will find in them remedies for all his difficulties. What, then, remains? To add nothing that has not also been said before, but to recall what has been said, so that we may easily follow what is to be said next, having the complete synopsis of it in brief compass.

The summary sets out from the very substance of the matter. [824] For one must recognise the dispositions of the faculty, those of the instruments, and those of the need. We have shown how many dispositions there are of each of the things mentioned, which of them are made known by which difficulties of breathing, and that the four combinations are necessary, and in addition to these the irregularity as a fifth. As for all the other things that befall respirations, both the simple and the compound, one must train oneself in what causes they follow upon; but it was not proper to think that they of necessity indicate some one particular thing.
