Rather, one obtains from them something extra towards prognosis, while the only most careful and secure prognosis is that based on the four combinations so often mentioned, and further on the difference of the difficulty of breathing according to the irregularity.

[825] GALEN, ON DIFFICULTY OF BREATHING, BOOK TWO. The present discourse is an exegesis of what was said by Hippocrates about difficulty of breathing. He said a great deal on it in many places, some in his treatises (syngrammata) and some also in his notes (hypomnemata). For indeed most of the Epidemics, if not in fact all of them, one might justly consider to be notes.

Now exegesis is, as one of the ancients somewhere said, the unfolding of an obscure expression; but we, it seems, shall do not only this, but shall also bear witness that everything written by [826] him about difficulty of breathing is true. We shall not, however, demonstrate any of it in this treatise, but shall refer back to the book preceding this one, in which nothing has been said without demonstration. And so that no one should be overawed by the reputation of Hippocrates and so trust what is said too readily, before being compelled by the demonstrations, we wrote the first book separately and on its own. But since that book has been completed with the appropriate syllogisms, in this treatise we shall honour the discoverer and, as it were, father of the doctrines. This honour is at once just and fitting for those who have discovered any good thing whatever: that their discoveries be neither hidden away nor unknown to men, but that the discoveries themselves be made manifest and the method that discovered them be recognised. For in this way they will also come to be admired according to their worth.

First, then, there is that which we hold ought always to be preserved by those who are in earnest about truth, namely that none of the things which evidently appear be concealed, not even if the reasoning about the [827] cause is in the highest degree perplexing. For this it is right to praise Hippocrates, both in all his other writings and not least in his discussions of difficulty of breathing. For sparse and large breath is seen every day to occur in countless persons who are deranged; but those of the sophists who are unable to state its cause (and these are, as we showed earlier, the ones who have supposed breathing to be an unwilled and natural function) say that such a kind of difficulty of breathing never even occurs at all. On the basis of the things about whose cause they are at a loss, they dare to overturn the reality of the thing itself, when they ought to have overturned not this but their own faulty supposition, and to watch carefully the very things that befall the sick, as Hippocrates did. 'For this man,' he says, 'breath throughout, as of one recollecting, sparse and large.' 'This man,' that is, Philiscus, the first patient written up after the three constitutions in the first book of the Epidemics. Was it, then, in this man alone that the breath was large and sparse, or did Hippocrates observe it occurring in certain others as well?

Not to him alone, but also to many others, and in particular to the one written up after these, [828] Silenus by name. For having gone through, in his case too, everything that befell him while he was ill, at the very end of the account he writes this: 'From the beginning and throughout, this man had breathing sparse, large.' Again, among the patients that follow, 'The wife of Dromeades,' he says, 'having given birth, and everything else having gone as it should, on the second day was seized by rigor.' Then, going on a little further, he says: 'Breathing sparse, large.' This, then, he wrote thus right on the first of the days; and again, discussing the sixth, he writes as follows: 'On the sixth, early in the morning, she had a renewed rigor; quickly became warm throughout; sweated all over. Extremities cold. She wandered in her mind. Breathing sparse, large.' In the first book of the Epidemics Hippocrates, having written up sixteen patients in all, is seen to mention sparse and large breathing four times. Yet these noble sophists of ours say that they have never at all seen anyone breathing large and sparse. (Or) but perhaps in this they are to be believed.

For they have not seen any distinction either of this or of any other difficulty of breathing, since they do not even [829] look at the sick themselves, but sit indoors, putting together wicked sophisms. Must we, then, go on to mention also the other patients whom he recorded in the other books of the Epidemics as breathing large and sparse? Or are these sufficient for the proof of what is now under discussion? For Hippocrates, who is acknowledged by all physicians to have been most diligent in the observation of what befalls the sick, evidently saw many breathing in this way. In the following book, however, we shall need to mention also certain other patients who breathed large and sparse, whom Hippocrates recorded in the subsequent books. That will not be for the proof of what is now under discussion, for this is already clear, but for the explanation of certain other questions contained in the account of them; and incidentally the proof that many breathe in this way will also be strengthened. Of what condition, then, is such difficulty of breathing indicative? Of none other than derangement.

[830] For what reason, has been clearly shown in the previous book; but for the sake of reminder it will be stated now too, briefly. For in truth it is a symptom peculiar to derangement to make the breathing large and sparse, that is, at long intervals of time. For why should one breathe in more when one does not need more? Or why at long intervals of time, when it is possible at shorter ones? That those who breathe in large and sparse do not need more air, the infrequency itself proves. For they would certainly hasten to breathe in more continuously if they needed more; but remaining at rest for a long time is a sign of not needing much. Rather, both of these seem to be affections of one who, as it were, forgets the activity. For to make the drawing of the breath immoderate, and the rest immoderate, belongs to one who knows neither at what point he must stop the activity nor when he must begin it again, but who in both exceeds the measure through ignorance of what is fitting.

Just as, then, the delirious, having often asked for a chamber pot in order to urinate, forget it in the meantime, and then would not urinate unless [831] someone reminds them, so, since breathing too is a psychic function, and their reasoning has been damaged, they become rather forgetful both about the activities themselves and about the intervals between them. Doing both, then, over a long time, both the activities and the rests, they thus bring about largeness and infrequency in the breathing as a whole. Do we, then, say this, while Hippocrates thought otherwise? Or did he too write in the Prognostic in this way: 'Breathing that is large and at long intervals of time signifies delirium'? For what in the first book of the Epidemics he called 'infrequent', this in the Prognostic he has called 'at long intervals', changing the name into a phrase. And indeed in the case of those patients in whom he says the breath becomes large and infrequent, in addition to the other symptoms he also records delirium; in the case of the very first of all, Philiscus, in this way: 'Night uncomfortable; he did not sleep; he was wholly out of his wits.' So it is in the account of the third day. And again in that of the fifth: 'Short sleeps; talking; raving.'

In the case of the second [832] of the patients, whose name was Silenus, in the account of the second day he says, 'he wandered slightly,' and in that of the third, 'much talk, laughter, singing; he could not be restrained.' Then, continuing, he will say, 'Fourth day: the same symptoms.' That Philiscus and Silenus were deranged, then, he recorded in this way. In the case of the wife of Dromeades (for of her too he says that she breathed sparse and large) he wrote as follows: 'Around midday she wandered much, and again quickly had slight understanding.' So he writes on the fifth of the days. Then he adds: 'At night she dozed a little; she wandered.' And in the same way, writing of what happened during the sixth day, he says roughly this: 'extremities cold; she wandered.' Thus in the first book of the Epidemics, wherever he mentions large and sparse breathing, there he also mentions derangement. In the same way, throughout the following books he reminds us of it, nowhere mentioning large and sparse breathing where he does not also mention great derangement.

[833] That Hippocrates, then, often observed in the sick this kind of difficulty of breathing occurring with delirium, and that he made a general declaration about it in the Prognostic, I consider sufficiently shown; but it will be confirmed no less by what is to be said next. And indeed it would have been right not to say very much about it. But because of those who have gone astray in their reasonings about the nature of respiration, and who then, out of love of contention, behave shamelessly, we too have been compelled to say more than is fitting, in the hope that we might somehow be able, even now at least, to bring them over to the better. There is, it seems, no dye so indelible as the attachment of those without reasoning to bad doctrines. For it is not possible to persuade otherwise those who have been reared in them, since they are neither trained in the demonstrative methods nor have provided themselves at all with any criterion of what is true and what is false. Indeed, most of them do not even wish there to be one, and they hate this wisdom.

Of such men, one once showed us a patient who was delirious, yet breathed neither large nor [834] sparse; laughing at us, or rather guffawing shamelessly, and mocking Hippocrates and us, he went off, neither allowing us a word nor bearing to listen to anything at all, although we offered to teach him that the phenomenon conflicts neither with what is said by us nor with what Hippocrates wrote. For Hippocrates says that large and sparse breathing is a sign of delirium, not, however, that if someone is delirious, he necessarily breathes sparse and large. What is said by us declares this very same thing, since we neither falsify nor alter anything of what he wrote, but add only the exegeses and the demonstrations. 'But if you have now discovered, you there,' I said, 'that in all the delirious the breathing becomes sparse and large, you plainly show that you have read nothing of Hippocrates' works, although you make a show of condemning them, as though, presumably, you had read them beforehand.'

But that man went away before learning anything useful. You, however, who engage with these writings, if you truly love the truth, listen to Hippocrates in the third book of the Epidemics, writing about a certain patient, [835] Pythion by name, as follows in the account of the seventh day: 'At night much disturbance; he talked deliriously; he did not sleep at all.' Then next, for the eighth day, as follows: 'Late in the day he grew warm again; he was deranged.' And after this again, for the ninth: 'Around sunset he was in distress; he talked deliriously.' As you have listened to these, so listen again to what kind of dyspnoea occurred in this Pythion. For you will learn that he breathed neither large nor rare, although he was delirious. Hippocrates, then, mentioned the dyspnoea that befell him twice in all in the whole account, on the second day and on the eighth. But I shall first cite the passage on the eighth, on which he says the man both went off his head and had difficulty in breathing, writing as follows: 'On the eighth, early in the morning he slept a little, but suddenly coldness, loss of voice, breath fine and diminished; late in the day he grew warm again; he was deranged.' Here, then, he has written one right after the other that his breath was fine and diminished and that he was deranged, on one and the same day, this eighth.

Is it not then, by Zeus, already clear that Hippocrates does not say that the breath becomes sparse and large in every [836] derangement? Unless, you there, you think that the diminished (μινυθῶδες) does not differ at all from the large. For if that is so, it is plain that you do not even know what 'to diminish' (μινύθειν) is, and you think it the same as 'to increase'. Do not, then, learn such things from us at any rate, but go to those who teach the first letters. But just as the man who does not know 'to diminish' did not learn these things, so neither has he read the treatises of Hippocrates. For he would certainly have found in them countless times 'to diminish' (μινύθειν), 'to have been diminished' (μινυθῆναι) and 'diminution' (μινύθησις), inflected everywhere in almost all numbers, genders and cases, signifying the opposite of increase and of increasing, so that 'diminished' too would be the opposite of 'increased'. If, then, the increased is large, the diminished is small. So too, accordingly, when he was narrating the second day of Pythion, he called him short-breathed. For short-breathing indicates that both the activity itself and the rest become short, just as long-breathing, conversely, indicates that both have been lengthened.

And yet, even if only one of the two [837] had been indicated, it would in this way too have been agreed that the breath does not become large and sparse in all who are delirious. For the sparse and large breath is long in both respects, both in the activity and in the rest; whereas short breathing is in any case short in at least one of the two, just as the fine and the diminished breath is in any case short. Hippocrates himself, then, clearly knows that the large and sparse breath is not of necessity present in all who are delirious; yet this does not conflict with his pronouncement concerning this kind of difficulty of breathing. For the sparse and large breath is proper to derangement, and for this reason it will of necessity indicate it; but if someone is deranged, it does not follow that he of necessity breathes large and sparse.

For we said that sparse and large breathing is not inseparable from derangement but proper to it, just as are geometrising, carpentering, philosophising, practising oratory and countless other things. Each of these belongs to none of the other animals, but to man alone, and for this reason is called a property of him, yet it is [838] not something inseparable from him, as being rational is. For not every property is thereby also inseparable. And just as dialectic, which is reviled by them, taught us these things, so it also taught us that such a proposition, 'if he breathes large and sparse, he is deranged', is neither the same as 'if he is deranged, he breathes large and sparse', nor is it necessary that they be true together. For these do not convert with one another, but are only inverted. So, as no one can win at Olympia without having trained for a long time beforehand, so no one can become a defender of truth in arguments without having learned the wrestling holds in these as well.

And just as those who are wholly ignorant of wrestling holds do not even know how to fall in a seemly manner, but sometimes, lying on their backs on the ground, keep their grip, choke, and do not let go, in the same way, I think, those who are ignorant of the art in arguments, though they have often plainly fallen a most shameful fall, are so far from being ashamed that they even think they have won. Such is the man who points to a delirious patient breathing small, and then thinks that through this [839] phenomenon Hippocrates' pronouncement has been refuted. This man, at any rate, though he had fallen a most shameful fall, supposed that he had thrown his opponent. For how is it not most shameful, on the one hand to be found to have read nothing of Hippocrates, and for that reason to think that what was written by him in turn was said idly; and on the other hand not even to understand what is said, but to mishear it and to think that 'large and rare breath is a sign of delirium' is the same as 'the said difficulty of breathing invariably follows delirium'? What wonder is it, then, that those who do not know even such small things are blind in their reasonings about cures? But plainly these small things depend upon other things, themselves also small, but neglected by them. For not knowing what faculty governs the respiratory activity is the origin of such errors; and that was not known because it had not been known beforehand from where one must procure the premisses for demonstrations.

For it is because some have remained unexercised in this hold, and others are utterly ignorant of it, that they take falls of such magnitude. We have also shown elsewhere, and especially in the second book On the Movement of [840] Muscles, that those who said that respiration is an unwilled function came to err because they were unable to procure the premisses for the demonstration from the very essence of the thing itself, and instead followed the other things, what is accidental. But Hippocrates, who saw the very nature of things and disregarded the rest as accidental, declared firmly in the universal, in the Prognostic: 'Breath drawn large and at long intervals signifies delirium.' In the particular, however, he tested the statement against the phenomena that appear in diseases, with tests carried to the utmost precision, which, I think, anyone would admire if he were willing to apply his mind to what is said. For he will learn that large and rare breath follows all deliria according to their own proper account, yet not all who are delirious, but only those who do not have their respiration altered in some other way through some other condition greater than the delirium.

But let me first be permitted to add the account of one sick woman, written in the third book of the Epidemics, both as a demonstration of what has already been said and at the same time for the discovery [841] of what is now before us. He begins the account of her in this way: 'In Thasos the wife of Dealces, who lay sick on the Leion, was seized after grief by an acute, shivering fever. From the beginning she kept herself wrapped up, and throughout, always silent, she groped about, plucked, scratched, picked at hairs; tears and again laughter; she did not sleep; irritation from the bowels, nothing passed through; she drank little when reminded; urine scanty, thin, without sediment; fevers slight to the touch; coldness of the extremities. On the ninth day she talked much wanderingly, and again settled down in silence.' So then, that this woman was deranged both from the beginning and throughout, we have learned; for not merely some single form of derangement befell her, nor an ordinary one, but many and severe ones, some while she was silent, others while she was uttering sounds, and some with tears, others indeed with laughter. Let us next hear Hippocrates too, as to what sort of form of difficulty of breathing he says arose in her. He writes as follows: 'On the fourteenth day breathing rare, large, at long intervals; and again she was short-breathed.'

Here, at any rate, the short-breathed woman is again clearly spoken of [842] by antithesis to the woman who has large and sparse breath. No one any longer, not even if he were altogether the most obtuse of men, could be in doubt that Hippocrates does not say that the breathing becomes sparse and large in all who are deranged. At any rate, in the case of one and the same woman he mentions both kinds of difficulty of breathing in succession. Going on a little further, he writes something like this: 'On the twentieth, much talk, and again she settled down, voiceless, short-breathed.' Then, having said 'on the twenty-first she died', at the end of the whole account he has added the following: 'In this woman, throughout, breath sparse, large; she was insensible of everything; she was always wrapping herself up.' From all the passages we have cited, then, it is clear that Hippocrates knew that in the deranged the large and sparse breath sometimes occurs, sometimes its opposite, and sometimes both befall the same person in turn. And I think I shall show you, if you pay attention and do not listen to what is said cursorily, that in the very patients about whom he wrote the cause of each of the aforementioned differences is indicated by him.

I shall begin from the illness of the wife of Dealces, the last [843] cited by us. In her case, having completed the whole account, he then, as is his custom, briefly recapitulates the chief points that hold it together and writes as follows: 'In this woman, throughout, the breath was sparse, large; she was insensible of everything.' For the need for respiration too is one of 'everything', and this too she neglected for a considerable time, because she perceived nothing. And since in the meantime a long pause was produced, the breath became sparse, the choice setting out towards the activity for the first time only when it comes near to destruction and suffocation. And just as this woman did not drink sufficiently ('for she drank little,' he says, 'when people reminded her'), so neither did she breathe until she was reminded by the violence that goes with being suffocated, which pricks and goads her and rouses her to the activity far more vehemently than those reminding her to drink. And once she had begun to breathe, she nonetheless recovered the whole preceding deficit by the magnitude of the activity, like those who sigh in griefs and in weeping.

But those persons suffer this from a twofold cause: first, because they are wholly absorbed in the thing they are anxious about, over which they grieve, [844] and for this reason, having breathed more rarely and smaller over many successive activities, they are then forced by the deficit and compelled to make it all up at once; and further, because in griefs both the pneuma and the heat move inward, and in such conditions, when the abundant heat that collects in the depth imperceptibly and little by little first distresses the person, he must breathe larger. In the conditions of those who are delirious, the necessity arising from the first cause is similar, but that arising from the second no longer exists. For in them the heat does not move inward rather than outward, unless some other symptom happens by chance to be added. Those who are deranged also differ from those who grieve for other reasons in that they are feverish. And indeed Hippocrates himself is found using the term 'recall' (anaklēsis), as elsewhere too when he says of Philiscus: 'in him the breath was throughout as of one recalling it.' What, then, is meant by 'at intervals' (dia chronou)? It is right to explain this as well.

For if 'long' were missing, 'at intervals' would mean the same as what is said in the Prognostic: 'breathing that is large and at [845] long intervals of time signifies delirium.' But if this is so, the same thing would be said twice in succession in the cases of both the wife of Dealces and the young man at Meliboea. For he writes in the same way for both: 'breath sparse, large, at intervals'. If 'long' were added, what is said would become: 'breath sparse, large, at long intervals', and 'sparse' would be said twice. Must we then hold that 'long' is not missing, or that it is missing not in the way we have just stated but otherwise and after a different manner, so that what is said is this: 'breath large and sparse, not continuously nor in succession, but at a longer interval'? For if all the breaths happened to be large and sparse continuously and in succession, he would not add 'at intervals' to such breaths but would write simply 'breath large and sparse'. But if most of the breaths were not large and sparse, and only a few such breaths fell in among them, then he would no longer say simply 'sparse and large' but would add 'at intervals'.

Or does what is said about the wife of Dealces at the end of the whole account also conflict with this? For he says this: 'breath throughout sparse and large'; and yet higher up he said, at the fourteenth day: 'breath sparse and large, at intervals.' For clearly what he here called 'at intervals', this in what follows he has called 'throughout'. What, then, is 'throughout' (διὰ τέλεος)? Plainly, that which occurs up to the end, through the whole [846] of the disease. But what was said at the fourteenth day would seem to conflict with this: 'breath sparse and large at intervals, and again short-breathed.' For how, if the breath was large and sparse through the whole time, has 'and again short-breathed' been added? For if there was some whole period of time when she was short-breathed, she was not long-breathed throughout. And indeed that he meant her to have been long-breathed throughout is clearly shown, if not by this phrase at the fourteenth day, at least at the end, when he said 'throughout'; and this will be agreed by all who are accustomed to hearing the diction of Hippocrates.

For not once or twice, but very often, the expression 'throughout' (διὰ τέλεος) is found in him, and it is not applied [847] to any one other thing than when he wishes to indicate 'through the whole time'. So this point remains wholly perplexing, whether we suppose that 'throughout' (διὰ τέλεος) itself signifies 'for a time' (διὰ χρόνου) or something else. Perhaps, then, it is not even perplexing, and we are harassing ourselves in vain. For what rarely intrudes does not, in any statement made in this manner, break up the assertion that is made in general terms; it is just as if we were to say: in this woman the breathing was large and rare through the whole time, but occasionally, as a rare event, short breathing intruded. That such a usage is customary for Hippocrates himself can be shown both from his other books and from the third book of the Epidemics itself, in which this patient too has been recorded. For in setting out the pestilential constitution he began roughly thus: 'A southerly year, rainy, windlessness throughout (διὰ τέλεος).' And having gone on a little, he says: 'The etesian winds blew slight and intermittent.'

But he called the year windless for this very reason: that neither any other winds nor those called the etesians blew continuously and to any considerable degree, but only slightly and intermittently. [848] And when writing of Apollonius in Abdera, the thirteenth case after this constitution, once he had gone through all the days of his illness, he added at the end of the whole account: 'delirious throughout'. Yet a little above he had written about him in these very words: 'About the twenty-fourth, by way of soothing treatment (διὰ παρηγορίης): the rest in the same state, but he understood a little.' But his understanding a little was not enough to overturn the pronouncement made about the patient as a whole, and for this reason he rightly said 'delirious throughout', that is, 'until the end', which amounts to the same as 'through the whole of the disease'. Therefore (for it is now necessary to put a head on the argument) 'at intervals' (διὰ χρόνου) is not the same as 'throughout' (διὰ τέλεος).

And since this has been shown, let us next state the cause on account of which, in some of those who are deranged, the breath becomes sparse and large throughout the whole disease, and in some never; and in some it is so for the greater part of the time, with something infrequently intervening that is either simply different or even contrary, while in others, conversely, the large and sparse breath occurs infrequently [849], but frequently either the contrary or what is different in any way whatsoever; and in others each equally. Here too let us again recall what was demonstrated in the previous book concerning the simple conditions. For pain alone, arising in one of the parts that are moved in breathing, was shown to make the whole breathing small and frequent; derangement alone to make the opposite of this, sparse and large; increase of the heat to make it large and frequent; and cooling, the opposite of that, small and sparse. If, then, the order of the breathing were confounded by derangement alone, the breath will be large and sparse throughout; if by pain alone, small and frequent; and if both come together, then when the pain prevails strongly, the alteration arising from the derangement is entirely imperceptible; but when it is moderate, it will happen that the breathing is altered either more by the pain and less by the derangement, or the reverse, or equally by both.

For delirium is not altogether able to obliterate completely the alteration arising from the pain, unless it should itself be [850] great and exceedingly violent, and the pain small and faint; the pain, however, when it is strong, completely overcomes the difficulty of breathing arising from the delirium, so that it does not show itself at all. In the same way, if delirium is combined with any of the other conditions, it will produce now one form of breathing and now another, according as it prevails, or is prevailed over, or is of equal strength, or at one time, as it may happen, prevails, and again at another moment of the disease is prevailed over. We shall show, then, that in the books of the Epidemics too he teaches this very thing through the patients written up in them. It will be shown clearly and plainly once we have first said a little about the purpose of Hippocrates. For the ancients suppose that he writes down everything that befalls the sick, just as Thucydides does; but this is not so; rather, this very point is that in which the writings of Hippocrates are most opposed to those of Thucydides.

For the one, Thucydides, writes everything that is familiar even to laymen, leaving out none of it at all, whereas Hippocrates writes few of these things, only those that bear upon the whole condition in which the patient was in danger, [851] but a great many other things which are overlooked by laymen, yet which furnish a thoroughly technical and precise diagnosis, and which can often escape the notice even of the best physicians themselves. And he, being swift in expression, and thinking fit to write nothing that will not also be of great benefit, will on the other hand seem to you to have departed from his own wits when he writes things that did not happen to the patient at all, making clear this very point, that it did not happen. For would not one who leaves out most even of the things that happened seem to be deranged in spending time on things that did not happen? But if you understood that it is for the same reason that he both leaves out those things and writes these, then, I think, you would admire him. For he wrote nothing chance, nothing that could occur to just any physician. This too has been demonstrated by us both in many other works and in particular in the books On the Anatomy of Hippocrates, and not least in those On the Plague in Thucydides. Keeping these things in mind, then, you will without difficulty perceive what is being said.

For I am going to show, even if it will seem paradoxical to someone, that many of those written up in the Epidemics suffered difficulty of breathing, and yet Hippocrates said nothing about their [852] difficulty of breathing, because it was clear and evident to all physicians. For if it happened that someone's sternum, or ribs, or the parts about the collarbones and the pharynx became inflamed, and that on this account he necessarily breathed small and frequent, as was shown in the preceding book, Hippocrates would not have thought it worth writing down either the form of the difficulty of breathing or at all the fact that the patient had become dyspnoeic. For this form of difficulty of breathing is common, being seen almost every day in peripneumonic, pleuritic and synanchic patients, and, in a word, in all those in whom something in the thorax and the lung is inflamed. This form of difficulty of breathing also follows inflammations of the liver, especially those in its convex parts, and those of the spleen, and those at its head, and those of the peritoneum.

But also those whose stomach is inflamed, and the more so if it is its mouth and its stomachos, and those in whom one of the membranes or of the muscles in the hypochondrium, or the diaphragm itself, is inflamed: in all of these the breath becomes small and frequent. [853] And often also one of the thin intestines, especially those at the jejunum, and the upper parts of the colon, when more severely inflamed, has compelled the person to have difficulty in breathing in this way. By 'inflammation' (phlegmonē) is here understood the hard, hot and painful swelling, as Erasistratus and all the more recent physicians are accustomed to call it, since almost no one is unaware that the ancients gave this name to fiery heat (phlogōsis). It was shown in the book before this one also why the breath becomes small and frequent in the dropsical, in those overfilled with either drink or food, in pregnant women and in the pot-bellied, and, to speak generally, in all in whom any one of the respiratory organs is confined in space. For so too the asthmatic, those with affections of the lung, the empyematous, those whose spine is greatly distorted, those in whom there is a formation of unconcocted growths (phymata) either in the thorax or in the lung, and in general all who have a scirrhus or some other considerable swelling of any one at all of the parts mentioned before, must of necessity breathe small and frequent.

Neither, then, can these patients escape the notice [854] even of any chance physician, nor can their conditions, upon which difficulty of breathing follows of necessity. For the conditions are clear, and the form of the difficulty of breathing is evident, and it occurs in many people very nearly every day. But it has been shown many times that Hippocrates writes nothing of things so clear. For Thucydides wrote down what befell the sick as a layman for laymen, but Hippocrates as a practitioner of the art for practitioners of the art. Let us now, then, speak of the very patients who suffered difficulty of breathing, in whose case he did not see fit to state, I do not say the form of the difficulty of breathing, but not even simply this alone, that they had difficulty in breathing.

Since there are seven books of the Epidemics in all, and of these the seventh seems to everyone clearly to be spurious, both later and reworked, and the fifth to be not by the great Hippocrates, the son of Heraclides, but by the younger, the son of Draco; while the second, the fourth and the sixth seemed to some to be by the son of Hippocrates, and to others by Hippocrates himself, yet not to be treatises, nor such as were intended to be published to the Greeks, but rather to be notes [855]; and some, who also seem to me to have grasped the character of the books more exactly, think that the five were written by Thessalus, and that two are by the great Hippocrates, and that it is for this reason that the heading 'the things from the little tablet' was written somewhere, evidently because Thessalus was eager to gather together into one all that his father happened to have written, so that nothing should be lost; and it is agreed by nearly everyone that the only remaining ones of these seven books that are by the great Hippocrates are the first and the third: it seemed reasonable to me first to take up the patients written of in these books, and after this, joining directly to them according to the affinity of the texts, both those in the other books of the Epidemics and whatever he has said about difficulty of breathing in his other treatises. And so let us first of all recall Anaxion, whom, as he himself says, an acute fever seized; continuous pain of the right side; he coughed dry, and did not spit up in the first days.

And first let us show this very thing: why on earth Hippocrates, although he is concise, and although it was possible to say it [856] by a single word, namely that Anaxion was pleuritic, instead stated in this way the symptoms belonging to this disease, and thought fit to give his account of him through those rather than through the name. For such a thing is not his custom; quite the opposite: he always reduces the particulars to one name and heading. Nor, indeed, is it possible that on this occasion a man who writes nothing at random wrote in this way by chance. What, then, is the cause? Of the symptoms belonging to each of the diseases, some are present of necessity, others for the most part. Among those that are present of necessity there are several differentiae. Some are seen very often, and for this reason are believed to be proper to the nature of the disease. Others are seen quite rarely, and are exceptional on account of some particular circumstance that has supervened.

Hippocrates, then, when the forms of the symptoms are the usual ones, is content at that point with the general name of the disease alone; but when one of the rare ones occurs, then right after the general and common designation of the whole disease he immediately specifies that one; and if he should ever observe several forms of affections beyond the common and customary nature, each requiring its own distinction, [857] he then passes over the general name and immediately describes each of the particulars, on the understanding that from these that general one too is made plain. Now in pleuritics there necessarily occur pain of the side, and that together with fever, and difficulty of breathing, and cough; for it is not possible for someone to be pleuritic and yet not have all of these present. But that something of the products of the inflammation should be brought up together with the coughing is not necessary, though it does happen for the most part. So too the form of what is brought up is reddish, or yellowish, or frothy. And just as among the things mentioned one is customary and another strange, so also among the very things that occur of necessity some forms are seen very often, others rarely. And so Hippocrates, in the case of the patient now before us, Anaxion, since the particular affections required distinction, being of the rarer form, and since he knew that once they were distinguished the pleuritic syndrome would be clearly recognised, considered it superfluous to write what would in any case be understood even without being written down.

For, he says, 'an acute fever seized him, and a pain of the right side, [858] continuous, and he coughed dry ones', meaning, evidently, little coughs. So you have learned not only that there was fever, but also what sort it was, for he says 'acute'; and not only that there was pain of the side, but also what sort, namely that it was continuous; and not only that there were coughs, but also of what sort and which kind, namely dry and without sputum. In this same statement you have also learned that this man was pleuritic; for in no disease of them all is there a concurrence of the affections mentioned except in pleurisy. By a single statement, then, it has been made clear both that the man was wrestling with a pleurisy and of what sort that pleurisy was. But since dyspnoea follows of necessity upon pleurisies, he omitted to write that he was also dyspnoeic. For if he had had anything strange and rare to say about this as well, he would not have kept silent; but since, as it seems, it kept its accustomed form, he reasonably omitted it. And just as he passed over these things, so he added in writing other things which neither belong to pleurisies of necessity, nor for the most part, nor can be understood from what has been said. For what does he say? 'Thirsty, sleepless; urine well-coloured, copious, thin.'

Then he adds: [859] 'On the sixth day delirious, and in response to the warm applications there was no remission at all.' None of these belongs to pleuritics either necessarily or for the most part. And if you also hear him narrating the seventh day, you will recognise the man's purpose more clearly. It runs thus: 'On the seventh, in distress; for the fever intensified, the pains did not abate, the coughs were troublesome, and he had difficulty of breathing.' Here he mentioned difficulty of breathing, when he was drawing the inference that the man was in a bad condition, listing it too among the other things that had befallen him from the beginning but had neither ceased nor abated. For the fevers, he says, even intensified further, while the remaining three (for four were found to be the things that make up the pleuritic syndrome) he says remained as they were: the pains, the coughs, the difficulties of breathing; and from the very substance of the disease he infers that the man was in distress. For if, of the four affections that make up the disease for him, three remained in the same state while the fourth became worse, it is clear to everyone that the man was in a bad way.

You see clearly, then, that it was because he needed it [860] for the prognosis of the condition of the disease that he mentioned the difficulty of breathing, and he would not otherwise have mentioned it. And it is for this reason that I took up this patient first, before the others: to show that, concerning the difficulty of breathing about which he said nothing at the beginning, he did not need it there at all, and that it is not wrongly that he mentions it now. For if you attend to the wording, you will find that it indicates this. 'On the seventh day', he says, 'in distress. For the fever intensified', he says, 'and the pains did not abate, and the coughs were troublesome, and he breathed with difficulty.' For here, as I said, he shows that one thing had intensified while the others remained as they were. For what he made clear by saying 'did not abate' must be understood as applying in common (ἀπὸ κοινοῦ) to the remaining things as well, the coughs and the difficulty of breathing. This kind of expression is most customary not only for Hippocrates but also for nearly all the other ancients. For just as 'the pains did not abate at all', so too 'the coughs were troublesome', clearly in the same way not abating at all, 'and he breathed with difficulty', clearly in the same way with the difficulty of breathing not abating at all.

And the very word 'was' [861] also indicates the same thing as 'as before'. For he did not say 'he became dyspnoeic', although he could have said it, or rather would certainly have said it, if this affection had been added on the seventh day, not having been present before. But clearly it was not added, for it necessarily had to have arisen from the beginning together with the other symptoms; and Hippocrates taught properly, omitting it at the beginning of the account but mentioning it afterwards. In the case of a great many other patients, however, just as he omitted it at the beginning, so too as the narrative proceeds he does not appear to mention difficulty of breathing. I shall set out all of them in order, both those written in the first book of the Epidemics, as I said, and those in the third, having first added what remains of my exposition of the patient described above.

Just as, then, we would have known that he was dyspnoeic from the very nature of the disease, even if it had not been stated by Hippocrates afterwards, so too it is not unclear that the form of his dyspnoea was small and frequent, even if Hippocrates does not write it. For just as it is evident that pleuritics are dyspnoeic, [862] so too it is evident that they breathe small and frequent. We said earlier that Hippocrates writes nothing of the things that are clearly known to others as well. And yet this man was also deranged; at any rate Hippocrates speaks of him thus: 'on the sixth, delirious'. But since this was not a disease by its nature productive of derangement, but an affection supervening upon strong pleurisies, it was surely not going to prevail over the alteration produced by the pain, nor by itself to stamp the form of the dyspnoea. The pain in the side, being strong, was certainly going by itself to alter the respiration. But if, by hypothesis, the pain had been faint and the derangement violent, the derangement would certainly have prevailed over the pain, either completely or for the most part. Thus such a patient would have breathed either large and rare throughout the whole disease, or mostly so but occasionally small and frequent. And this Hippocrates would certainly have indicated beforehand, as in the case of the youth in Meliboea. For he had some tension at the hypochondrium, somewhat soft, but he was also greatly deranged.

At any rate, he writes about the tension as follows: [863] 'tension of the hypochondrium, somewhat flaccid, elongated on both sides'; and about the delirium as follows: 'on the tenth of the days he wandered in his mind quietly, on the fourteenth he spoke much at random, on the twentieth he went raving mad,' he says. Now the word 'he went raving mad' alone would have been sufficient to indicate the magnitude of the delirium; but the fact that the youth was orderly and silent also adds not a little to its magnitude, since in the Prorrhetic too he says that even bold answers, let alone deliria themselves, are bad in those who are orderly. For it was not for any other reason that, in the account of the tenth day, he added the remarks about the youth's character. And so that we should not think, since it is written 'he wandered in his mind quietly', that the delirium was simple and of an ordinary kind, for this reason he adds 'but he was orderly and silent'; and from all these things he indicated the vehemence of the delirium. As for the tension in the hypochondrium on both sides, one might perhaps think that it made the breath small and frequent; for through the very things he wrote about it, he indicated that it was, with good reason, overcome by the delirium.

For he did not simply [864] say, 'there was tension in the hypochondrium', but added 'somewhat slack' (hypolaparos), showing that it was not accompanied by a large swelling; for laparos means 'empty'. And by 'elongated' he indicates the opposite of what he himself often calls the 'drawn-up hypochondrium'. For when it is stretched by the diaphragm, then the whole of it is drawn up and hidden, being pulled into the thorax; but when it is stretched by one of the parts below, then the tension appears elongated, for there is nothing in front of it to hide it, as in the case of the thorax there are the spurious ribs and the sternum. So it is clear not only from these things that the condition in the hypochondrium was altogether slight with respect to producing difficulty of breathing, but also from the very fact that Hippocrates added nothing about pain in it. For he would not have kept silent if it had been painful, since it is his custom to pass over nothing of this kind carelessly.

If, then, these things were altogether slight (for there was neither any great swelling in it nor pain, nor did it compress the diaphragm, but it was stretched out over the whole belly), while the derangement fell short [865] in nothing of being as great and as severe as possible, then it was reasonable that the condition in the hypochondrium was completely overcome by it, so that throughout the whole disease the breathing was sparse and large. For this reason, then, Hippocrates too mentions both together, both the kind of difficulty of breathing and the condition in the hypochondrium. The text runs thus: 'breath sparse, large, at intervals; tension of the hypochondrium, somewhat slack'. He does so in order that no one should pass over the account idly, but, having read in succession two conditions that by nature produce opposite kinds of difficulty of breathing, should investigate the cause why the derangement prevailed completely, while the tension in the hypochondrium was overcome. But we, for our part, have both stated the cause and explained the man's meaning, and we must now move on and go through the remaining part of the discussion proposed.

For when the delirium completely overcomes the opposite condition, it alone alters the breathing according to its own power, as has been written in the case of the young man described above, the one written last in the third book of the Epidemics. Moreover, that when the pain completely [866] prevails, nothing of the dyspnoea that belongs to delirium shows itself alongside it, we demonstrated in the case of Anaxion, who is himself also written up in the third book of the Epidemics, eighth from the pestilential constitution. And again, in the case of the wife of Dealces, whom we also mentioned before, who is written up eighth from him and fifteenth after the pestilential constitution, we showed how for the most part the delirium prevails, but on rare occasions is also itself prevailed over. Now the passages I quoted a little earlier, when I was explaining what 'at intervals' (διὰ χρόνου) signifies; but now I shall state also the conflicting conditions themselves, following here too the words spoken by Hippocrates. No painful condition, then, appears to have befallen this woman, but chilling prevailed, as the innate heat was wasting away. For this is made clear from what is written about her, 'fevers slight to the touch, coldness of the extremities', and from her being kept wrapped up throughout the whole disease. For having said 'and from the beginning she kept herself wrapped up', afterwards, at the end of the whole account, he says 'she was always wrapped up'. And the fact that it began from grief also agrees with these things. For what does he say?

[867] 'A shivery fever took hold of her as a result of grief.' And the shivery fever itself also came about through the same cause. Moreover, the fact that what she drank passed straight through the belly, without being held together (συνιστάμενα) even for a short time, is the strongest evidence that the innate heat was being extinguished. And the skin that is 'parched' is skin that has been dried out, and the innate heat perishes together with such drynesses. That these things did in fact occur in her case is made clear by the following words. 'On the seventeenth,' he says, 'irritations from the bowel, disordered; then the drinks themselves passed through and did not hold together; she was insensible of everything; tension of the skin, parched.' It was therefore with good reason that throughout the whole disease the large and rare breathing prevailed, while at times the short breathing that follows chillings also intervened. I shall now again remind you of the passages, as I have already set them out earlier: 'On the fourteenth, breathing rare, large, at long intervals, and again short-breathed. On the twentieth, much talking; again she settled down (ἱδρύνθη); voiceless, short-breathed. On the twenty-first she died. In her case, breathing throughout rare, large.'

Here, then, the derangement prevailed over the chilling, [868] and for this reason she was observed to be short-breathed only rarely, but long-breathed throughout the whole disease. Conversely, in the case of Pythion, whom I also mentioned earlier, short breathing was present throughout the whole disease, while long breathing occurred only occasionally, and reasonably so. For two conditions that are causes of short breathing were set against the derangement, pain and chilling, both of which are naturally apt to make the respiration small, but pain makes it so with frequency, chilling with infrequency. That he was deranged has been written many times in these very words by Hippocrates himself, so that this would escape no one. Nor would the matter of the pain in the belly, for this too is clearly written thus: 'in the belly, heaviness with pain'. That he had been chilled, and that the innate heat was withering away, is clear from the following: 'on the second day, about midday, coldness of the extremities, especially about the hands and head'. Then next, in the account of the third day: 'late, about sunset, he was slightly chilled'. And for the fourth day it has been added not only that there was coldness, but also that he grew warm again after a time.

And more clearly, [869] in his account of the eighth day, he says: 'early in the morning he slept a little, but quickly there was chilling; late in the day he grew warm again.' And again, on the tenth day, he says: 'much chilling.' From these, then, it is clear that Pythion had chilling as well, and not only pain and derangement. That short breathing prevailed, yet there was also some long breathing, would become clear from the account of the second day. For it is written thus: 'short-breathed for a long time.' This 'for a long time' indicates both that short breathing was not present alone, and also that it predominated over long breathing. This Pythion too is recorded in the third book of the Epidemics, third after the pestilential constitution. So each reader may dwell at greater length, on his own, on the old author's passages, so that we need not make our discourse long by quoting them all. Moreover, anyone who goes to the books themselves would be most fully convinced that we do not deliberately omit any phrase that contradicts what we say.

And for this reason we indicate both in which of the books the patient whom we happen to be discussing on each occasion is written up [870] and what number he is, counting either from the beginning or from a constitution, so that no one should hesitate on this account and, shrinking from the search, either trust us without examination, which we do not wish, or suspect us of quoting in such a way as to alter the text (ὥστε καὶ παραγράφοντας ἡμᾶς), which indeed many of the commentators have done. But they, for this very reason, keep silent about the books and deliberately conceal those from which on each occasion they quote the passages; we, on the other hand, indicate not only the books but also the very places and the chapters, so that what is wanted may be found more easily. For we know that those who have read the whole section of the book from which we quote the saying will have a firmer confidence in what we say. Now, the sequence of the argument compelled us to mention the aforesaid patients, since we wished to make clear in what manner derangement sometimes alone produces the difficulty of breathing, overcoming the opposite condition, and sometimes, being overcome, becomes completely effaced; and sometimes it prevails for the most part, the differing difficulty of breathing occurring only rarely, while at other times it is itself prevailed over, showing itself alongside here and there, as a rare event.

And now there is clear [871] what we were saying at the beginning: that in whom the breath is large and sparse, there is in every case also derangement, but in whom there is derangement, in him the breath is not in every case large and sparse. What still remains of the things proposed, let us add to the account, going through all the patients written up in the first and the third books of the Epidemics, from the first to the very last of all, giving our account the same order that his writing itself has. Now the very first of all, Philiscus: that he was deranged and had a large and sparse breath, we showed in the preceding discussions, citing the statement of Hippocrates himself; but that he had no pain at all in any of the parts in whose affection, as we were saying, breathing becomes small and frequent, we shall now show, here too recalling the very wording of the ancient author, which runs thus: 'the spleen was raised up in a rounded convexity.'

Certainly the spleen is not in any other respect a painful viscus, nor does it compress the diaphragm (phrenes) as the liver and the stomach do, unless at some time it should have a very great swelling at its head, which was not the case with Philiscus; and for this reason the spleen was not able to overcome the difficulty of breathing arising from the [872] delirium, since it was neither painful nor compressing the diaphragm. The one recorded next after him, Silenus, whom we also mentioned in our earlier discussions after Philiscus: that he too had rare and large breathing, and that he became delirious, we showed there; that he had no condition capable of overcoming the delirium will be shown here. For the narrative of the third day of the disease has this too written: 'tension of the hypochondrium, elongated on both sides, somewhat soft towards the navel.' So the tension also gave way towards the navel, and there was neither any pain nor any swelling worth mentioning. Moreover, what is said at the end, 'throbbing of the hypochondrium', is not itself sufficient to alter the difficulty of breathing arising from the delirium either. For it has already been said countless times that either there must be pain in one of the parts moved in respiration, or one of the respiratory organs must be constricted, in order that the breathing become small and frequent. So neither did this Silenus, any more than the earlier one, Philiscus, have any other condition capable of altering the respiration, except delirium.

[873] For there was neither pain nor compression of the respiratory organs, nor indeed was there any chilling, such as we showed, in the third book of the Epidemics, occurring in Pythion and in the wife of Dealces. As for the three recorded next after these, Herophon, the wife of Philinus and the wife of Epicrates, you would find, if you read carefully through the narratives about them, that they had a delirium too slight for the breathing to be altered by it. But in Herophon the spleen was raised up, and there was 'tension of the hypochondrium', he says, without adding any longer 'somewhat soft', nor 'elongated', nor 'towards the navel'; so that in him the parts about the diaphragm were inflamed, and the diaphragm was shown by us in the work On the Causes of Breathing to be its first and most principal organ. The wife of Philinus 'had pain', he says, 'in the cardia and the right hypochondrium'; and the wife of Epicrates had not only pain in the cardia, but also, he says, 'heaviness of the left side with pain'.

For this reason, then, he did not add 'breath small and frequent' in the case of any of these, but kept entirely silent, having the habit, as we have also shown before, of omitting things that are clearly [874] known to all. And most clear and familiar to all, as we have also shown, was the difficulty of breathing by smallness and frequency, with which the three patients described above necessarily had difficulty in breathing. Moreover Cleanactides too, who is described after them, himself likewise necessarily had difficulty in breathing because of the pain of the left side; but in his case too nothing is written about difficulty of breathing, since it could be understood even without being written. This Cleanactides, however, was not delirious. But Meton, who is described after him, had neither a condition capable of causing pain nor one capable of constricting any of the respiratory organs, nor indeed any morbid basis for delirium; rather something paradoxical, and not usually met with, befell him. For on the fifth day, having haemorrhaged and sweated, he reached a complete crisis. He was, then, still haemorrhaging even after the crisis, being sleepless, and moreover he 'talked deliriously' (παρέλεγε), he says, although before the crisis he had not been delirious at all. For this reason, then, we too said that no morbid condition of delirium had arisen in him.

[875] Rather, he talked wildly in the way that happens to those who are drunk, through a filling of the head. For this very reason the word 'he talked wildly' (παρέλεγεν) was written by Hippocrates, indicating the resemblance to drunkenness that arose in him from the filling about the head. For there came to the head, as one may infer from what happened, no small quantity of blood, upon which indeed the whole disease reached its crisis, the head having received the entire affection of it. But of this blood, no small amount was at once, on the fifth day, copiously excreted together with sweat, while a great deal more than what had been evacuated remained in the head, weighing it down and forcing the man to talk wildly. Hence Hippocrates employed bathings over the head, having said: 'he bled frequently after the crisis.' So in this case he not only did not write down any kind of difficulty of breathing, but not even whether he became dyspnoeic at all. For it is not in those who talk wildly in any way whatever, or in those who are drunk, but in those who are deranged alone that the breathing becomes large and sparse.

And for this reason he says in the Prognostic: 'Breathing that is large and at long intervals indicates [876] delirium.' But Erasinus, the patient after him, necessarily had difficulty of breathing, yet the difficulty of breathing has been omitted for the reason that has often been stated. For in general he nowhere appears first to have mentioned any painful condition, or one compressing one of the respiratory organs, and then next to it to have added in writing the difficulty of breathing that follows upon it; rather, he everywhere omits it, as being familiar to all. That there was such a condition in Erasinus he made clear by saying: 'hypochondria raised, tension with pain'; for the magnitude of an inflammation is thereby shown, on account of which the man, although he became delirious, did not have the difficulty of breathing peculiar to delirium, or else Hippocrates would certainly have mentioned this too. For just as he is found always omitting the difficulty that accompanies pains, the small and frequent kind, because it is obvious, so the kind that accompanies deliria, knowing it to be disputed, he nowhere omitted, nor did he pass over it undefined. For the facts concerning Crito, who is written up next after him, have a clear cause.

For since he died on the second day, most contrary to expectation, [877] as one can learn from the account itself, Hippocrates with good reason omitted to say anything about difficulty of breathing, either because he did not observe the difficulty of breathing that occurred, or because he did not think it worth mentioning. For each of these is reasonable. That he did not observe it is reasonable both because of the speed of the death and because of the startling character of the symptoms. For it is no small marvel that a man who was going about and doing his customary things, and who then felt violent pain in the big toe of his foot, should on the first day become slightly heated and on the next day die. Since, then, no interval of time passed in between, but the man died quickly, and was not simply deranged but raving mad, as he says, it was not possible to observe how he breathed. For we cannot bring ourselves even to come near those who are raving mad; we keep away from them by every means, fearing that they may inflict some harm on us.

Either, then, he did not observe it, as we said, or he did not think it worth mentioning the form of the difficulty of breathing, on account of the paradoxical character of the whole syndrome, to which alone it is fitting that we [878] direct our attention, and not be drawn aside towards things that can be discovered through other patients. Next he writes of the man from Clazomenae, who had pain, he says, in the head, neck and loins from the beginning. But these are not sufficient to make the breath small and frequent, unless perhaps the neck; and there is also a place where this will be determined as the discussion proceeds. The hypochondrium, however, raised up with swelling, is sufficient, so that even if this man was deranged, he did not suffer the difficulty of breathing proper to derangement, since the painful affections just mentioned prevailed. The wife of Dromeades, however, who comes after him, and whom I also cited right at the very beginning of this discourse, not only was deranged but also had the breath large and rare, there being no affection either about the thorax or in the hypochondrium of the kind that is naturally apt to make the respiration small and frequent.

This, then, is why Hippocrates too, writing down precisely everything that befell the woman, said: 'she began to suffer first about the hypochondrium, nauseous, restless'; evidently because depraved humours [879] there were biting the mouth of the stomach, though there was certainly no inflammation at all, nor any other affection by which the breath becomes small and frequent. And indeed Hippocrates, having gone on a little further in the account, after writing 'pain of the hypochondrium', added 'nauseous', and then next again, 'thirsty'. So neither was any of the things occurring in the hypochondrium or thorax strong enough to prevail over the delirium, nor was the innate heat being extinguished, as we have shown happened in other cases; so that, with good reason, since none of the conditions opposed to delirium was able to alter the respiration, the breath in her became large and rare. But since the words 'at once drawn up' have been added in the text, I must note this now, so that no one may suppose that we mean to pass it over carelessly.

But now is not the time to explain it; rather, in the discourse that follows it will be examined together with the other things said in like manner. For the present, however, we shall take up the three patients still remaining, who themselves also became delirious, yet did not suffer the [880] difficulty of breathing proper to delirium. For this reason, in the case of the first it is written: 'pain of the right hypochondrium, an inflammation somewhat soft, from the inner part', that is, evidently, the part towards the diaphragm. In the case of the second: 'in the hypochondrium a swelling with pain', and shortly after, 'pain of the hypochondrium', and again next in order, 'and about the left collarbone pain persisted.' In the case of the third of the patients (this was a woman, as was also the one before her): 'strong pain', he says, 'of the head and neck and chest', and shortly after, 'the pains persisted.' These, then, are the fourteen patients from the first book of the Epidemics, written by Hippocrates in sequence in just the order in which we too have mentioned them; and in the third book of the Epidemics there are twelve before the pestilential constitution and sixteen after it, all of them agreeing with what we laid down from the beginning.

And I know clearly that if I pass them over, and leave it to those who wish to examine the agreement in all of them to read through, privately and by themselves, the narratives written by the ancient [881], I shall seem to do this not from a wish to guard against long-windedness, but because I am unable to preserve my initial hypotheses throughout the whole argument; but if I go through all of them in order, I shall seem a sort of babbler and trifler, myself writing out to no purpose things which each person was capable of examining even by himself. Nevertheless, if I must in any case endure one of the two absurdities, either the suspicion that my doctrines are unsound or long-windedness, and I find certain mitigations for long-windedness but none for the suspicion, it is more reasonable to speak about all of them. What, then, are the mitigations of long-windedness? The first is to run through the patients quickly in the account, no longer lingering over each in the same way, but only recalling them to mind; the second is to urge those who cannot bear to listen even to things so brief to pass over them, and to consider them not written at all. For just as at a splendid banquet, when many dishes have been prepared, one person chooses one thing and another another, this one as pleasant, that one as going to be beneficial, so too in discourses the provision ought to be abundant, but the choice left to those who make use of them.

[882] Now the first patient of all, whose name was Pythion, is evident from the account itself as having no basis for difficulty of breathing. The second, Hermocrates, 'began', he says, 'to have pain in the head and loins; tension of the hypochondrium, somewhat soft.' He did not, however, go on to add that the tension inclined downwards and towards the navel, or that it was elongated. From this it is clear that the hypochondrium was being drawn upwards by the inflamed diaphragm, and for this reason it also appeared somewhat soft, as having no inflammation of its own. So even if this man was delirious, the delirium was nevertheless overpowered by another, greater [affection], just as also in the case of the third, fourth, fifth and sixth.

For in the case of the third, a somewhat soft tension of the right hypochondrium is recorded; in the case of the fourth, 'the right hypochondrium was drawn tight, it inclined inwards'; in the case of the fifth, 'he had a painful neck'; and in the case of the sixth of the patients (this was a woman), Hippocrates, having first stated [the preliminaries], [writes]: 'At the beginning of the illness she had pain in the throat, and throughout had redness; uvula [883] drawn up; fluxes many, thin, small, acrid; she coughed, but brought up nothing concocted'; and a little later he will say: 'and there was also something congenitally consumptive'. So in her case too it is clear that the prevailing condition was established in the respiratory organs. The patient after her, however, he begins to describe in this manner: 'The woman with cynanche at Aristion's'; and further on he says: 'breathing elevated', which we shall also explain as the discussion proceeds; for now the matter in hand must be completed. In the case of the eighth patient it is written: 'tension of the hypochondrium, somewhat soft, on both sides'; and in the case of the ninth, 'pains about the hypochondrium'. But she at least was not delirious. The next two women, he says, fared badly as a result of miscarriage, and their conditions, which he describes, are, to state it in general terms, inflammations of the uterus, and in particular, the affections which follow upon these.

Of one more, the remaining one, he says that she had pain at the heart, without adding 'nauseous', but also that she sweated cold sweat, and throughout the whole illness was shivery, and was greatly chilled, and [884] was warmed again with difficulty, or not at all. So it is clear that she too was certainly short-breathed in both conditions, that of the pain and that of the chilling; yet not even in her case did Hippocrates think it worth saying anything about difficulty of breathing, as it was entirely evident.

Next comes the pestilential constitution, after which he again describes first the patient from Paros. In his case, at the end of the account, where he describes what persisted continuously throughout the whole body, this too is added: 'sleepless, with pains'. Second is the man in Thasos, of whom he says: 'coughs continuous, moist, many'. Third is Pythion, whom we have already explained. Fourth is the phrenitic. Fifth is the man who began suddenly to have pain in the right thigh. When the flux went back up to the parts about the head, he at once became delirious and at once also died, like the man in the first book of the Epidemics who began, began from the pain in the great toe, and died on the second day. So in these cases too he wrote nothing whatever about difficulty of breathing, for the reasons which we have already stated [885] in that man's case. The sixth neither became delirious nor had any other condition productive of difficulty of breathing. The seventh patient is the maiden who was troubled in the head on account of the abundance of blood, in the same way as the seventh patient described in the first book of the Epidemics, who had a haemorrhage from the nostrils; so let whatever we have already said about him be transferred here as well. The eighth patient is Anaxion, whom we explained in connection with the preceding one. The ninth had a basis of his whole disease closely similar both to the maiden and to that man from the first book of the Epidemics who had the haemorrhage. The tenth, who is Nicodemus in Abdera, raved once on the sixth day. Then, having reached a crisis on the twentieth day with a sweat and seeming to have become free of fever, he again relapsed into fever and again wandered a little in his mind. Of him he also writes the following: 'the paroxysms and the pains in this man continued to the end'. Pains of what? someone might perhaps ask. He said that he became cardialgic right at the beginning, and a little further on he wrote: 'pains of all parts'.

For this reason, then, the derangement too, being slight [886] and of short duration, did not alter the respiration. Next in order is the woman whose illness began from grief, about whom he writes: 'great, continuous pains'; and moreover, he says, 'many convulsions'. Now in the Aphorisms he writes about convulsions as follows: 'In fevers, breath that is checked (προσκόπτον) is bad, for it signifies convulsion.' And so in this woman too the form of difficulty of breathing arose partly in accordance with the pains and partly in accordance with the convulsions. For this reason, then, although she was deranged, she did not have large and infrequent [breathing], since it was overcome by two other, stronger conditions. After these comes the maiden in Larisa, the twelfth recorded after the pestilential constitution, who fell ill through a plethora of blood and reached her crisis through a haemorrhage from the nostrils, through sweat, and through the menses, which then appeared for the first time; she had no disposition to any difficulty of breathing whatsoever.

Next after these, in the case of Apollonius in Abdera, there was, he says, 'a swelling of the right hypochondrium with pain'; and moreover, that he had at all times had enlarged viscera and that a pain about the hypochondrium was habitual to him, this too is written at the [887] beginning of the account. It is therefore nothing to wonder at if, even though he became deranged, he did not have difficulty of breathing according to the form proper to derangement, since he had acquired so great a painful condition in the hypochondrium. Next after him comes the woman in Cyzicus who gave birth to twin daughters, about whom he wrote somewhat as follows: 'heaviness of the head and neck with pain', so that the difficulty of breathing too was in accordance with this. After her there remain two patients in the third book of the Epidemics, the wife of Dealces and the young man in Meliboea, both of whom became deranged and had their breath large and rare; these were discussed sufficiently earlier. But since this book of ours has already reached a sufficient size, we shall examine in the next one all the remaining things that were said about difficulty of breathing by the ancient.

[888] GALEN, ON DIFFICULTY OF BREATHING, BOOK THREE. Having divided the account of difficulty of breathing into two courses of instruction, in the first of the books we made clear everything that the physician must know about it, together with the proper demonstrations; in the second, which precedes this one, and in this third book itself, we are giving an exegesis of what has been said by Hippocrates about difficulty of breathing in all his treatises. The purpose is this: those who aim only at the works of the art themselves, and who do not think it worth, as they themselves put it, busying themselves at all about what was said by the ancients, may have everything they are eager for sufficiently from the first book; while those who both desire and are able to learn in addition the opinion of Hippocrates may read it in these [889] writings. Now, to desire to know what has been said by the best men is common to all who are by nature lovers of the beautiful; but actually being able to learn it, since that requires a longer time, no longer belongs to all alike; for many, through a great press of affairs, are deprived of leisure for the finest things. Knowing this, then, we on our part went through what is urgent for the works of the art in the first of these books, and next, separately, we are expounding the opinion of Hippocrates in the two remaining books, of which one is the second and the other the third according to the order from the beginning.

And whoever is going to follow what is said in it must first have carefully studied the second book. In that book we first showed the whole intention of Hippocrates: that he does not think fit to write anything commonplace, nor anything that most physicians know. Second, we went through one by one all the patients in the first and third books of the Epidemics. We showed in many cases that, even though the patients must necessarily have had difficulty breathing, he nevertheless did not write it down, just as he did not write down many other things [890] that follow of necessity from what he has written. For what one can learn even without him, finding it out for oneself by starting from what he said, he did not think needed to be written. But in many cases he also adds the form of the difficulty of breathing to the very narratives of the sick, whenever either it does not follow of necessity in the sick, or it is not readily recognisable to those who read his writings. Holding to these aims now as well, since we explained the first and third books of the Epidemics in what preceded, we shall again make our beginning from the second, joining to it the remaining writings of Hippocrates as well. Those who know these matters best think that the first and third books were not only composed by Hippocrates but also joined to one another by the affinity of their theory. Just so, I think, the same holds for the contents of the second, the fourth and the sixth. For it is in fact already agreed that these too were put together by Thessalus, the son of Hippocrates, who found notes of his father himself on certain skins or writing-tablets, and himself added not a few things as well.

The [891] fifth and seventh books of the Epidemics, however, no one, it seems to me, would deem to belong to Hippocrates' own thought; nor, in my opinion, the fourth either, even if some have thought that this too was composed by Thessalus. But the Prognostic and the Aphorisms and the work On Waters, Places and Airs, and further the work On Regimen in Acute Diseases, which some entitle Against the Cnidian Opinions, are not without reason believed to be writings of Hippocrates himself. We shall therefore mention these books wherever need calls for it, together with all the others that people ascribe, some to Hippocrates himself, others to Euryphon, Thessalus and Polybus. We must, then, now begin the exegesis from the passage written in the second book of the Epidemics, which runs thus: 'Breath small, frequent; large, sparse; small, sparse; outward large, inward small; the one extending, the other hastening. A double inward recall, as if they breathe in on top; hot, cold.' This same passage is written more completely in the sixth book.

For in it, to the three combinations of difficulty of breathing the fourth is added, [892] which has clearly been omitted in the second book of the Epidemics, though not, in my opinion, by the writer himself.
