For he is plainly gathering the number of the difficulties of breathing not from some experience and memory but from logical division, and so he was not going to omit any difficulty of breathing. Rather, one of the ancient copyists made a mistake, and then the book, being in this state, was published before the mistake was noticed, and this very error has, understandably, been preserved down to the present. Some people engage carelessly with the books of the ancients, so that they recognise neither whether something is missing nor whether it has been written with a different letter, while others do recognise it but do not dare to add what is missing. For the people of earlier times were not, like those of today, rash or ready to alter an ancient reading written in the same way in all the copies. It was enough for them merely to note that here the division of the difficulties of breathing is written incompletely, but completely in the sixth book of the Epidemics, namely the division according to largeness and smallness and frequency and infrequency.

For indeed it is evident that Hippocrates combines these two antitheses with each other, that according to largeness [893] and smallness and that of infrequency and frequency, and so makes four pairings of difficulty of breathing: one in which the breathing becomes at once smaller and more frequent than the natural; another when it is at once larger and more infrequent; and besides these a third, in which it is smaller and more infrequent; and besides these a fourth, which we say has been omitted in the second book of the Epidemics, in which it becomes at once larger and more frequent. For I have shown many times, even if it is in fact plain to everyone even without being shown, that two antitheses combined with one another produce four pairings. And the passage in the sixth book of the Epidemics differs from that in the second not only in this very respect, but also inasmuch as in what follows, where he compares the magnitude of inspiration with that of expiration, one of the two pairings has been entirely omitted in the second book; here too the copyist clearly displays either the utmost indolence or unscrupulous tampering.

For if he skipped whole phrases, he was utterly careless; but if, in the case of phrases similar to one another, not knowing in what respect they differ, he supposed that both signified one and the same thing, and then [894] removed one of them, he had reached the height of officiousness, making himself out to be a corrector of Hippocrates' writings, not a servant of them. This, then, is useful to remember with regard to many of the unclear passages, in which it is plausible that something has either been omitted or been wrongly written in. For nothing prevents us, in those passages, from making the account complete and true, either by adding what is missing or by correcting what is in error. For just as rewriting the ancient passages is rash, so too it is the work of good interpreters to preserve them as they have been written and to resolve the difficulties by some brief additions or substitutions. But concerning these matters I think I shall show, a little later and through the actual practice, what one ought to do. For it must not be done simply, nor at random, but together with demonstrating both the truth of the facts and, even before that, that the opinion of the ancient himself was such, and that the two agree once the wording has been rearranged. Proceeding now to the matter at hand, and setting out the more complete wording, the one in the sixth book of the Epidemics, let us see what sort of thing its sense is.

For that [895] he attempts to find all the differentiae of difficulties of breathing by logical division, this is the view even of those who have commented on his books, and I think it is altogether easy to grasp. But whether he divides correctly, and whether he omits no species of difficulty of breathing, this is no longer easy for everyone to discover; rather, whoever is to judge these matters must be experienced in the method of division and not unpractised in the doctrines of Hippocrates. Now the method says that one must look to the thing being divided, to what it is like in its nature. For if it is simple, one must examine the things that belong to it according to the account of its substance, how many they are, which they are and of what kind, and divide on the basis of these. But if it is compound, one must divide each of the two, or each of the parts, in the way described, and the whole on the basis of the manner of the composition.

As for Hippocrates' opinion about composition, whatever it may be, it has been stated by us at very great length in other works, and it has also been stated in what precedes, so that nothing prevents us from examining, with our eyes on these aims, the passage of the Epidemics, which runs roughly as follows: 'Breaths small, dense; large, sparse; small, sparse, [896] large, dense; outward large, inward small; inward large, outward small; the one extending, the other pressing hard. A double recall inward, as though they breathe in in addition; hot, cold.' Now, it is easy to see that in the second book of the Epidemics not only the fourth combination, that of dense and large, has been omitted, but also, of the two that follow, in which he compares expiration with inspiration, the second as well: it is written in the passage now taken up, but omitted in the second book of the Epidemics. For in that book 'inward large, outward small' is no longer added; only the other form of difficulty of breathing is indicated, according to which a large breath is breathed out and a small one breathed in. In many places, then, one can find this missing item written in as an addition, but in most of the copies, and the most trustworthy, it is omitted; and this at any rate makes no difference to the present matter. For our purpose is to examine the more complete passage, the one written here.

That the activity of the whole respiration is compounded of the inward and the outward movement of the breath, and that one of its parts is called inspiration and the other expiration, [897] has been stated already in the first book, right at the beginning; but even if it had not been stated by us, hardly anyone is unaware of it. That speed and slowness are proper to nothing else of all things than to motion, this too has been stated before, but let it now also be called back to memory. Magnitude and smallness, however, while they are not proper to motion, are nonetheless inseparable from everything that moves across an extent. And for this reason, in each of the parts of respiration there will arise two oppositions of differences: one according to speed and slowness, the second according to magnitude and smallness. As for the whole respiration, that there is a further opposition constituted according to frequency and infrequency, this too has been stated before, and also that this opposition is composed of intervals, not as belonging to respiration as a motion, but as belonging to a compound thing.

So it is necessary that all the differences of breathing lie in these three genera: in speed and slowness, because these are proper to, and inseparable from, every motion; in largeness and smallness, because the motion of the respiratory organs proceeds through an interval; frequency [898] and infrequency, the third of the genera mentioned, is neither proper to nor inseparable from either of the proper and primary parts of breathing, but becomes a part of breathing as a whole by a kind of accident, since breathing is a compound thing made up of two opposite motions divided by rest. These, then, are the primary differences of breathing as a whole. But because breathing is by nature such as to act and to be acted upon, there would also be another genus of differences in it, according as each of the two parts is carried out evenly or unevenly; and moreover yet another genus belonging to breathing as a whole, as a compound, when the parts are compared with one another. This being so, one must know that the first four differences of difficulties of breathing written in the passage before us belong to breathing as a whole; for frequency and infrequency belong to neither of the parts, if indeed we remember what was said right at the beginning of the first of these commentaries.

And so too the two that follow them; for in these also the two parts of the whole respiration are compared with each other, and for this reason it has been written thus: 'outwards large, inwards small; inwards large, outwards small', meaning, evidently, the breath (pneuma). The two differences that follow next, [899] in which it is said 'the one drawn out, the other hurried', must be held to be peculiar to one of the two parts of respiration, the one which we said belongs most of all to the essence of respiration; for 'drawn out' is the slow, and 'hurried' the fast. And slowness and speed are inseparable from every motion.

What is said next, 'a double recall inwards, as if they breathe in on top', is indicative of an uneven inspiration. It calls for the same antithesis in the case of expiration, and I am persuaded that this was left out by the copyists rather than by Hippocrates himself, since he clearly mentions this kind of dyspnoea too in other treatises, as I shall show plainly in what follows. If anyone thinks it was left out by Hippocrates himself, that person chooses the worse over the better. For to make no mention at all of unevenness in either of the parts of respiration, and to forget and leave it out entirely, would not have been in keeping with Hippocrates' carefulness either. Indeed, even if what is now written about inspiration had not been written at all, [900] I would have ventured to say that this was the copyist's error rather than Hippocrates'; yet it would still have had some plausibility for those who take the worse view. But since he indicated the form of inspiration so clearly, not only saying that a double recall of the breath inwards occurs but also adding 'as if they breathe in on top', how could anyone still suppose that he forgot about expiration? About these matters, then, more later. Next is added another antithesis of dyspnoeas, written at the end of the whole passage roughly thus: 'hot, cold', so that here too we evidently understand 'breath' in addition. For just as the breath is breathed out large and small, and frequent and sparse, so it is also breathed out hot and cold. And yet here too some, misunderstanding on the basis of things they themselves do not comprehend, make 'corrections' and venture to alter the wording. They do not write 'cold and hot' as it now stands, but join these words to what was said before and read thus: 'as if they breathe in cold on top of hot'.

These men, then, besides making the text yield no sense at all, are plainly shown not even to [901] have read the books of the ancient; for they would certainly have remembered what he wrote elsewhere about hot and cold expiration, and they could not say what reason he had either to write of these things in those works or to omit them here. For if he did not consider hot and cold expiration to be among the difficulties of breathing, he did not do well to mention them elsewhere as difficulties of breathing; but if he acted correctly in those works, he did not act correctly in omitting them now. But this is not how these matters stand: for here too they are rightly included in the division of the difficulties of breathing, and what it is in their nature to indicate has been correctly stated elsewhere.

Leaving aside, then, those who so mishear the ancient and who understand anything rather than his meaning, let us ourselves consider by ourselves why on earth in the Prognostic treatise he writes about difficulty of breathing roughly as follows: 'Breath, when it is rapid, indicates pain or inflammation in the regions above the diaphragm; when it is drawn in large and at long intervals, it indicates delirium; and when it is breathed out cold [902] from the nostrils and the mouth, it is already exceedingly deadly.' For in this book he evidently mentions only these three difficulties of breathing. And yet, if there are only so many, why on earth did he himself write of far more in the books of the Epidemics? And if they are so many, why on earth did he mention very few in the Prognostic? Or did he think it useful to know their number, but not useful to know what each of them is of a nature to indicate? Or is it only the ones mentioned that indicate something, and the others nothing? Is it possible that one sometimes breathes contrary to nature, while there is no condition contrary to nature in the animal? Or is this so far from being true that it is altogether necessary that the condition contrary to nature in the animal itself becomes the cause of the difficulty of breathing? If, then, the condition stands in the relation of a cause to the difficulty of breathing, it would accordingly be prior in time, in order and in power. How, then, does Hippocrates evidently pass over so great a number of difficulties of breathing in the Prognostic?

For these reasons I would have wished both to compare the commentators with one another [903] and to investigate and to resolve [the difficulty]; but the matter does not stand so. For of those who are commenting now, who would even make mention of any? And of those before them, at least those whose commentaries have been preserved down to our time, one can find many long pieces of nonsense set down in writing, while points so essential have been left out entirely. But let us at any rate investigate them ourselves, even if we have no path towards their discovery handed down by those men.

It has indeed been stated, both in my writings On the Best Sect and in those of the Therapeutic Method, how one ought both to investigate and to discover all such matters. Moreover, in the first of these present commentaries too I showed a twofold way of discovering such things: one setting out from the differences in difficulty of breathing, the other from the conditions in the respiratory organs, which I said was both easier and clearer. Whoever has read those writings with care will not need many words for the solution of the present questions. But if someone either studied them carelessly, or is otherwise slow to learn, let the careless one read them through again and then come back to these matters; and let the dull one do something else, knowing [904] that a small nature is not able to learn thoroughly the thought of a great man, such as Hippocrates was. At any rate, what no one before me either propounded, or raised as a difficulty, or investigated, or found, I shall propound and raise as a difficulty; I shall say how one ought to investigate it; and with the gods' help I hope to find it. The problem has in fact been stated by me a little earlier: why ever did Hippocrates omit so many kinds of difficulty of breathing in the Prognostic? The difficulty (aporēma) will now be stated, once I have first recalled what was written in the first book. For in those books I reduced all the differences of the difficulties of breathing to five genera in all, both of conditions and of difficulties of breathing, so that the problem becomes still more perplexing, since the only hope still remaining has been taken away.

For in all such cases in which the differences of any existing thing whatsoever are stated as more numerous by one person or one writing, and as fewer by another, there is one sole hope of agreement: if someone could show that the one has remained among the first parts of the division, [905] while the other also cuts it further down. Since, then, this hope has been taken away from us (for it was shown in the first book that neither the genera of the conditions nor those of the dyspnoeas can be reduced to a smaller number), what means could still be found for the solution of the questions now under investigation? For, among other things, besides the omission of some of the primary genera, one might also find fault in the Prognostic with their having been scattered apart, badly contradistinguished from one another, and unclearly expressed, even though it is clear, if ever any other of Hippocrates' books is. And indeed what is said right at the beginning of the text is at once unclear and left undistinguished: 'Breath, when it is frequent, signifies pain or inflammation in the regions above the diaphragm.'

For if frequent breathing were not twofold, the one kind with largeness, the other with smallness, or if each of them were not the offspring of a different condition, Hippocrates would reasonably either have left it undivided or not have indicated the difference in what is signified by each. But since he himself, in the books of the Epidemics, clearly recognises as one thing [906] the frequent and at the same time small, and as another the frequent and large, and we have demonstrated that these belong to the primary differentiae, he did badly in leaving 'frequent' undivided and contenting himself with saying simply this: 'Breathing, when it is frequent, signifies pain or inflammation in the regions above the diaphragm.' This, then, is one perplexing point. Next, he mentioned the third differentia thus: 'When it is drawn in large and at long intervals, it signifies derangement.' Yet, having stated this one alone of the primary differentiae clearly, he made no mention whatever of the difficulty of breathing adjacent to it, the one that shows the breathing as sparse and small. And yet, just as frequent breathing was twofold, divided by largeness and smallness, so sparse breathing too is of necessity twofold, divided by largeness and smallness. But in the Prognostic he mentioned only one of the two, saying: 'When it is drawn in large and at long intervals, it signifies derangement'; the other, the sparse and at the same time small, appears to have been omitted.

So that, of the four combinations which he wrote down in the Epidemics, the first two have been stated without distinction, [907] unclearly and confusedly, and only the third, as we said, has been written clearly, both itself and what is indicated by it, the two alike. And not only in these points would his account seem to be unclear and at the same time lacking in distinctions and to have left out the greater part, but also from what he says next: 'but breath exhaled cold from the nostrils and the mouth is already very deadly.' For why ever, if he had resolved to go through the differences relating to hot and cold, did he mention only the cold one? And further, why ever, in the case of the other two, the one which he calls without distinction 'frequent breath' and the one which, drawing a distinction, he calls 'sparse and large', did he note down only the conditions themselves, but did not indicate in what they will end, saying that pain and inflammation are indicated by the frequent difficulty of breathing, and delirium by the one that is sparse and at the same time large?

In the case of the difference according to cold, however, he does state what it will end in: for he says that such breath is very deadly. But the condition from which people have difficulty in breathing in this way, which is more obscure, he no longer states, although it would have been better, for all the difficulties of breathing, both to state the conditions themselves, [908] whatever they may be, and to add in writing their mode, distinguishing the mild ones from the malignant. He did not, however, do so; rather, for the earlier difficulties of breathing he indicated the conditions, and for the last only the mode. And what is the most inescapable of all the charges, that nothing at all has been said about irregular difficulty of breathing, let this too now be added to the account. For the extended and urgent breath, and the breath that is large outward and small inward, are themselves not mentioned in the Prognostic writing either; yet, from what we went through in the first book, they are found to be contained in the four pairings of difficulties of breathing. But the fifth, the irregular one, half of which he wrote about in the books of the Epidemics, speaking of a double inward recall, but which he omitted entirely in the Prognostic, cannot by any means be found contained under any of the four pairings. Such, then, and so many are the difficulties.

From this point on, however, we must not, like the majority of those who contradict Hippocrates, find the [909] difficulties readily and then be at a loss when it comes to solving them; rather, we must first find some road to their resolution, and then confirm by demonstration what has been found by means of it. What, then, is the road to resolution? For this is where we must begin. One is the brevity of expression that was customary and common to all the ancients; the second is the loftiness of mind of Hippocrates himself. For we have often shown that this man is skilled at passing over whatever is familiar to other physicians as well, as things that could not be unknown to anyone who genuinely practises the art, while explaining carefully and clearly all the things that are unknown to such people. If, then, this is his custom, what wonder is it that the difference of dyspnoea in respect of largeness and infrequency, which is disputed and unclear to most, he both tried to show through his other writings to be peculiar to derangement and in the Prognostic deemed worthy of clear teaching, while the differences in respect of frequency, since these too could not be unknown to physicians, he comprised under a single head and set out quickly?

For in pleurisies and peripneumonias and synanchai and [910] orthopnoeas the breath becomes frequent and small; and even if there is no pleurisy, but only pain is present in the region of the ribs, the breath will be frequent and small, just as also if the pain is about the mouth of the stomach, or the gullet, or the head of the spleen, or the convex parts of the liver. For indeed here too, when some pain is present, the breath must become small and frequent, and much more so if it arises about the diaphragm and that part of it which is joined to the peritoneum, and the muscles that lie around it there. Indeed, even if the peritoneum is affected not only here but also lower down, and more severely, the diaphragm perceives its injury and in this way makes the breath small and frequent. And the more severe conditions of the belly itself, those with pain and swelling, and of the lower parts of the spleen and of the liver, these too no less make the breath frequent and small. In general, whether there is some swelling that presses on and constricts any one of the respiratory organs, or pain about some part that lies so close to the respiratory organs that it is moved together with them when they move, the breath will be frequent and small.

The other causes [911] of these we went through in the first book, just as we also showed that, when much heat has accumulated in the respiratory organs, the breath will become frequent and large. This too is evident almost every day in all burning fevers, so that it could not escape anyone's notice either. Moreover, not only we ourselves but practically all the commentators on Hippocrates have demonstrated that not only Hippocrates but also almost all the others before Erasistratus called burning heat (phlogōsis) contrary to nature 'phlegmonē'. These things being laid down, then, it is no longer surprising that Hippocrates indicated both of the aforementioned differences under a single heading, when he said: 'breath, being frequent, signifies pain or phlegmonē in the regions above the phrenes'. He said this on the assumption that we too are able to understand that the frequent breath with smallness signifies pain, whereas that with largeness indicates phlegmonē, which is to say phlogōsis. He reasonably added 'in the regions above the phrenes', that is, in the respiratory parts, since immoderate heats below the diaphragm are unable to raise the breathing to largeness and frequency.

[912] Such, then, is the path of discovery of the things sought, at least as regards the first differences; but it is necessary also to add some demonstration to the argument. For at present it has been shown that it is not impossible that Hippocrates held this view; it will be shown next that it is entirely so. For why indeed, when in both the books of the Epidemics, the second as well as the sixth, he is found distinguishing these two as the first of all the differences of difficulty of breathing, first the small and frequent breath, second the frequent and large, is he thought to be ignorant of them in the passage before us, in addition to the fact that immediately after this, in the Prognostic, he writes 'sparse and large'? Does he, then, recognise sparse and large breath, yet not know frequent and small?

And even if one of those who are zealous for the worse should say that he was able to know what frequent and small breath itself is, but was unable to know what the condition is that produces it, still, when he says, 'Frequent breath signifies pain or inflammation in the regions above the diaphragm', he is evidently writing of the conditions as well [913] and leaving out neither, but he set them out in the same order that he followed also in the two books of the Epidemics. It is evident, then, that he connects pain with the frequent and small, and fiery heat (phlogōsis) with the frequent and large. Nor can one say this either, that in the two books of the Epidemics he made mention of small and frequent and of large and frequent breath, but nowhere else. For both in those very books, often, and in On Regimen in Acute Diseases, which they entitle On Ptisan, right at the beginning of the treatise, he not only names this form of difficulty of breathing explicitly, but also the condition upon which it arises and the manner in which it naturally does harm; and yet, of those who out of love of contention strike out many books as not genuine works of Hippocrates, none has dared to take this treatise away from the man. For many remove the parts at the end, those after the use of the bath, but everything up to that point all of them preserve. If, then, we show not only in this book, but he is likewise found through many others to know both the differences of frequent breath and the conditions, will anything seem to be lacking for the demonstration?

And if, in the Prognostic itself [914], further down, he should be found neither ignorant of the differences and also knowing the conditions, would you not believe still more that the proposition has been demonstrated? And indeed, that these things are so and that we are saying nothing false, one may examine from the passages themselves. I shall begin with the book On Regimen in Acute Diseases. In this book, right at the beginning, where he discusses the diseases of the lung and thorax, he speaks somewhat as follows: 'For in those in whom food has just been shut in, if one gives the gruel without first evacuating, he would exacerbate the pain if it is present, and if it is not present he would at once produce it, and the breathing would become more frequent; and this is bad, for it is drying to the lung and fatiguing to the hypochondria, the lower belly and the diaphragm.' In this statement he has first shown that frequent breathing also arises through pain, leaving to us, I think, to work out the manner of its generation, which I believe I have clearly gone through in the first of these books.

For just as, when we are in pain in the legs, we cannot take long strides, in the same way, whenever one of the organs that are moved in breathing is in pain, we are compelled to breathe small [915] and we long to stop more quickly. For since the pain is prolonged along with the length of time of the breath, whoever checks the motion of the respiratory organs more quickly will more quickly cease to be in pain. But by as much as he stopped earlier than he should, by so much has the animal had a more deficient enjoyment of inspiration. Just as, then, if someone takes less food than his need requires, he will quickly need more food, so if someone breathes in less than his need requires, he will sooner need a further inspiration, and in this way it will come about that the breathing becomes frequent. For the time during which the organs of breathing used to rest, reposing in the interval between their activities, the animal now does not allow them to rest. For since it breathes deficiently with each breath, it draws ever nearer and nearer to suffocation; and from fear of this very affection it hastens to breathe more quickly, and moves the organs of breathing earlier than it should, not allowing them to rest for as long as they used to rest when it was in its natural state.

When, therefore, Hippocrates says that the breath becomes more frequent on account of the pain, and it is evident that the frequency is generated by way of the smallness as intermediate, [916] it is surely clear to everyone that he also recognises the smallness. For who could know the third from the first while ignorant of the middle, and above all when this middle is the cause of the third's coming into being? And indeed, going on a little further, in his very own words he expressly makes the smallness the cause of the frequency, writing thus: 'For the sputum itself, being held fast, prevents the breath from being carried inwards, and compels it to be carried outwards quickly.' Here again he teaches the other cause of the generation of frequent breathing; he called it in the earlier discussions narrowness of the respiratory organs. What, then, he left to us to work out for ourselves in the case of the pain, this he has here explained himself. And what is this? When much sputum, he says, is contained in the arteries (those of the lung, plainly), and has already occupied the space of the breath itself, the breath is prevented from coming inwards during the activity of inspiration. Is what is now being said, then, anything other than small inspiration?

Not at all, if indeed one must measure the magnitude of breathing by the quantity of the substance inspired, as has been shown in the first [917] book. But if he says that the breath is compelled to be carried outward quickly through some other cause than the smallness of inspiration, not even this can be said, since the text runs thus: 'For the sputum itself, being held fast, prevents the breath from being carried inward, and compels it to be carried outward quickly.' For because it has been deprived of its inward motion, the animal, being in danger of being choked, does not allow it to rest, and in this way it becomes frequent. For to go quickly from inspiration to expiration is nothing other than to breathe frequently. For one ought not to wish to attend to the very syllables of the words when the statements as a whole are clearly expressed, nor to think that rushing quickly to expiration is one thing and breathing frequently another, or that inspiration's being prevented from taking place sufficiently is one thing and breathing's being small another.

But here Hippocrates himself explained clearly how, when the sputum is held back, the breathing becomes frequent by way of the intermediate smallness; in the case of the pain, however, he left it out, since, I think, he himself has said in many places that the functions [918] of the organs are hindered by pain, and since we too are able, even if we had not heard it from him beforehand, to discover it from what plainly appears. Besides, then, teaching us clearly both these things in this passage, namely that pain and narrowness of space alike, by making the breathing small, at once show it to be frequent as well, he further teaches this too: that these are not the only causes of frequent breathing. First, in saying (and it is said thus in the case of the pain), he makes it plain that the breathing is already frequent because of the other cause, when he says that it becomes more frequent because of the pain, since, I think, here too we are able to reason out that the febrile heat in any case makes it frequent. Second, in saying that the sputum, being made viscid by the frequent and copious breathing, as has already been said, prevents its upward passage from taking place, being unconcocted. For of the frequent breathing the pain is the cause, but of the copious breathing it is not this but the febrile heat. And here too he quite clearly said not 'large breathing' but 'copious'.

For 'large' is judged by the quantity in each breath, whereas 'much' can sometimes be accumulated from many small ones [919]. And this is clearly seen to happen in pleuritic patients: they cannot breathe large at a single stroke because of the pain, although they need more air because of the fever, but by the continuity of the activity they accumulate a quantity of breath equal to that of large breaths. For what few large breaths can do, many small ones can do. In the same way, in peripneumonic patients too there is need of much breath, but because of the narrowness little is inhaled; here too, then, the frequency, by making the small breaths many, brings them to equality with the few and large. Shall we then still need to find the syllables of the words written in this book in sequence, thus: 'of small and of large breathing', not being content with the things themselves, so clearly shown?

And yet this was not the question at issue, whether Hippocrates knows the name of small and large breathing; for it is found written both in the books of the Epidemics and again in the Prognostic, in the words where he said: 'breath drawn large and at long [920] intervals signifies derangement'. The question was rather whether he knows that frequent breath is twofold, and says that one kind of it arises from pain, the other from much heat collecting in the respiratory organs. Since, then, these things have been demonstrated, it is superfluous still to long to hear the syllables of the names. For even in respect of this very statement in the Prognostic, which he wrote about derangement, it will be open to someone to say that it is not sparse and large breath that has been stated to indicate it, and to put forward the passage as running in the following way: 'breath drawn large and at long intervals signifies derangement', as though it were not one and the same thing to say either 'sparse' or 'at long intervals', or as though we were now hunting for names and not seeking the things themselves. But since some have come to such a pitch of perversity as to want to hear even the names themselves, let us remind them too, from the very book On Regimen in Acute Diseases, of two passages that run roughly as follows: 'breath stumbling in its upward course, frequent or large.'

Here, if you desire it, you have the word 'large'; and 'small', in turn, where he says: 'and the breath [921] small, and a frequent and violent counter-drawing of the breath supervenes.' Again, in the Prognostic itself he speaks of bearing the disease with difficulty and of the breath being large and frequent. This, then, he wrote outright in the very words, 'large and frequent'; and 'small and frequent', in turn, in his account of synanche, saying: 'they cause very great pain and orthopnoea.' For I do not know whether anyone is unaware that in orthopnoeas the breath becomes small and frequent because of the narrowness of the respiratory organs. And yet, if we wish to learn such things from Hippocrates himself, in On Regimen in Acute Diseases, in the passages I wrote out a little earlier, he taught us how small and frequent breath arises with the retention of the sputa.

And in On Joints, right at the beginning of his section on the spine, where he describes the kyphoses that arise from swellings or diseases in the regions above the diaphragm, he speaks somewhat as follows (for I think it seems better to transcribe the whole passage): "In those in whom the hump is above the diaphragm, the ribs will not grow into breadth, [922] but forwards, and the chest becomes pointed, but not broad, and they themselves become dyspnoeic and wheezy; for the cavities that receive the breath and send it onwards have less of a straight course. And indeed they are also compelled to hold the neck bent backwards (lordotic) at the great vertebra, so that the head may not be pitched forward for them. This, then, produces much narrowness for the throat; and this also contributes to its inclining inwards. For even in those who are naturally upright this bone, if it inclines inwards, produces dyspnoea until it is pressed back up. On account of such a condition, then, people of this kind appear to have protruding windpipes rather than to be healthy, and such people are for the most part tuberculous in the lung, with hard and unconcocted tumours. For indeed the cause of the hump and of the contraction in most cases comes about through such concretions, in which the tensed [cords] come to share." In this whole passage he says that the kyphosis arises from the unconcocted and hard tumours in the lung, and the dyspnoea from the narrowness; and he has called this sort of variety of it 'wheezy'.

And in the [923] On Regimen in Acute Diseases, when he made mention of those whose breathing turns to smallness and frequency, he both added this very name of orthopnoea and said that they rattle in the throat; so that also when, in the Prognostic, treating of synanche, he said 'they cause very great distress and orthopnoea', he calls by this name no other kind of difficulty of breathing than that of small and frequent breath. For all who, through narrowness of space, are unable to breathe in sufficiently are in danger of choking if they lie down. And for this reason they need to keep both the whole thorax and the neck upright, since no small help comes to them from such a posture. For all the organs of respiration together become at once wider and longer, on the one hand being straightened out by the upright postures, on the other being hindered so that they collapse less into themselves.

Hippocrates himself also clearly held this view of them, just as we are now saying, as appears from what he says in On Joints: "they themselves become dyspnoeic and wheezing, for the cavities that receive the breath and send [924] it onward have less straightness." In all, then, who breathe with difficulty because of narrowness, the breath becomes small, and two symptoms follow of necessity: the wheezing kind of respiration, which is also called rattling, and the one mentioned a little earlier, orthopnoea. And indeed, as if dividing them on purpose, he writes the one in the Prognostic, saying that it attends deadly synanchai, and the second in On Joints: in the Prognostic orthopnoea, in On Joints the wheezing. But in On Regimen in Acute Diseases Hippocrates brought both together, writing thus: "those who were choked by orthopnoea and rattle." For what in On Joints he called wheeze (kerchnos), here he named rattle (rhenchos). Elsewhere in his writings too he uses both names as able to signify the same thing. Since, then, he himself in On Regimen went through so carefully every origin of frequent breath, it is no wonder if in the Prognostic he wrote only the sum total itself of the whole account.

That he went [925] carefully through the whole account of rapid breathing, I need say nothing further; instead, having recalled only this, that breathing becomes rapid either on account of pain, or narrowness of space, or an abundance of heat, I shall next set out the whole passage, which runs as follows: “For those in whom food has just been shut up within, if one gives the gruel without first evacuating from below, it would further exacerbate the pain if it is present, and if it is not present would at once produce it, and the breathing would become more rapid; and this is bad, for it is drying to the lung, and fatiguing to the hypochondrium, the lower belly and the diaphragm. And if, while the pain of the side is continuous and does not relax under the warm applications, and the sputum does not come away but even becomes viscid without being concocted, one does not resolve the pain, either by softening the bowel or by cutting a vein, whichever of these is indicated, but gives the ptisans to those in this state, the deaths of such patients come swiftly.”

For these reasons, then, and others of the same kind, those who use whole ptisans die even more often on the seventh day or within fewer days, some having also suffered some damage to their judgement [926], others choked by orthopnoea and by rattling. The ancients were especially wont to call such persons 'struck' (blētoi), chiefly for this reason, and not least because, when they have died, the side is found livid, something like a blow. The cause of this is that they die before the pain has been resolved. For they quickly become short of breath (pneumatiai), and, as has already been said, by the frequent and copious breathing the sputum, becoming viscid without concoction, prevents its upward passage from taking place, but, being held fast in the bronchi of the lung, produces the rattle. When it comes to this, it is for the most part deadly. For the sputum itself, being held fast, prevents the breath from being carried inward and compels it to be carried outward quickly, and so they assist one another toward the bad outcome. For the sputum, being held fast, makes the breathing frequent, and the breathing, being frequent, makes the sputum more viscid and prevents it from slipping away. If anyone attends carefully to this passage and reads it over many times, I hope that he will easily be persuaded by what has been said.

For since the division of frequent breathing into the [927] differences within it did not require great wisdom, and since he had already written it out completely in this book, for this reason he ran over it very quickly in the Prognostic, as though addressing those who already knew the whole, making a sort of epitome of the account. Three combinations of difficulties of breathing have thus already been found by us; the fourth remains, in which the breathing is small and sparse. Why then did he pass this over and write 'cold expiration'? Is it not because the breathing that is at once small and sparse is not one thing and the cold another? This is clear. For we showed that its opposite, the breathing that is at once large and frequent, is the offspring of immoderate heat collected in the respiratory organs. Of necessity, then, the small and sparse breathing will belong to these same organs when they have been chilled; and two difficulties are resolved for us, in that neither the fourth combination of difficulty of breathing, the small and sparse, has been omitted, nor the hot.

For we shall find that one comprised in one of the two parts of the dense breathing spoken of at the beginning, since it is the same as the dense and [928] large; and the sparse and small, in turn, in the cold, since this too does not differ from the cold. Why then did he write of it not as sparse and small but as cold? Because, first, he wished to indicate it by the more readily apparent symptom; second, he wished to point to the cause on account of which he calls it deadly; and third, because he supposed that in this way we would most quickly understand both that this very breathing differs in no way from the sparse and small, and that its opposite, the hot, differs in no way from the dense and large. For cold breathing is in every case sparse and small, as was also shown in the second book; and the dense and large breathing, which is indicative of fiery heat (phlogōsis) of the respiratory organs, one could not even rightly call so unless it were also exhaled hot. Moreover, by adding to the cold breathing alone that it 'is then very deadly', he clearly shows what opinion he holds about the three difficulties of breathing spoken of before. For if he had considered any of those also deadly, he would surely have added it somewhere. Did he then suppose them to be without danger? By no means; rather, not deadly, but no longer without danger either.

For it is downright deadly that the respiratory [929] organs should be chilled, since the heart, which we know to be the origin and source of the innate heat, is situated right there; but that there should be either much fiery heat (phlogōsis) in them, or pain, or delirium, is not in every case deadly. For such heat attends many of the acute fevers, and how many and which diseases involve pain has been stated before. Moreover, delirium too is among the things that are not of necessity deadly. That he thinks thus about them he showed clearly in the passage that follows, where he says: 'One must consider that easy breathing has very great power towards recovery in all acute diseases that are accompanied by fevers and reach their crisis within forty days.' For if he considered that easy breathing has great power towards recovery, he evidently supposed that difficulties of breathing are not always without danger. So the other difficulties of breathing are this alone, namely not without danger (?), whereas the one mentioned last of all, besides being dangerous and deadly, indicates that the person will die before long.

For this reason, therefore, he did not say simply that it is deadly, but also added 'very', and, again not content even with this, he appended 'already', as though this difficulty of breathing alone indicates that death is imminent. For it is so deadly that it seems to me that Hippocrates would not have written anything about it at all, had he not been going through the whole manner [of the subject] in speaking about the difficulties of breathing. For the things that already occur in the dying have no great value in prognoses. The task of good physicians is not to foreknow what is already apparent to laymen, but whatever escapes their notice and appears while the patient seems to have nothing bad. But because he wished to write down all the kinds of difficulty of breathing in order, he seems to me to have mentioned this one too, and moreover on account of its antithesis to the large and frequent [breathing]. Let these matters, then, end here.

Why did he write nothing in the Prognostic about the uneven difficulty of breathing, although he knew of it not only in the second and the sixth books of the Epidemics, [931] but also in the first and third, and moreover in On Regimen in Acute Diseases and in the Aphorisms, and in many other places of his writings? For in the second and the sixth he mentioned it in the passage quoted above, saying: 'double recall inwards, as if they breathe in on top of a breath.' And moreover in the second of the Epidemics, in narrating what befell Lycia, he added: 'and the breath was doubled.' For this differs in no way from 'double recall inwards, as if they breathe in on top of a breath.' And in the sixth he says: 'if breath is left behind.' For this too is the same as what is said in On Regimen: 'breath stumbling in its upward course.' For just as some, when breathing in, do not do this all at once, but cut the activity short with a pause, like little children whimpering, so also when breathing out. But also in what follows the discussion of baths he has spoken of 'forward-stretchings of breaths', indicating the interrupted activity.

And in the first book of the Epidemics, in the case of Philiscus, he spoke in this manner: 'In this man [932] the breath throughout was as of one recalling [it].' For here too 'recalling' is used in the same sense as in 'double recall inward'. Again, in the case of the wife of Dromeades, he said: 'breath sparse, large, at once drawn back'. For this too is said in the same sense. In the Aphorisms, moreover, he also teaches what such breath signifies, writing as follows: 'In fevers, breath that stumbles is bad, for it signifies convulsion.' It is consistent, then, that in the Epidemics as well he says that the wife of Dromeades was convulsed and died, she of whom he had said earlier: 'breath sparse, large, at once drawn back'. Here indeed one may most of all marvel at how each of the two difficulties of breathing revealed the condition proper to itself. For this woman was not only convulsed but also became deranged, as one who had had not only the difficulty of breathing peculiar to convulsions but also that peculiar to derangement.

So it has been clearly demonstrated that Hippocrates recognised this irregular dyspnoea; but that he reasonably passed it over in the Prognostic as well, just as [933] he did most of the prognostic signs too, is what we should state next, after first recalling by chief points that he wrote nothing in the Prognostic about the things relating to ages, or regions, or seasons, or the epidemic constitutions, although a whole book, On Airs, Places and Waters, was written by him, and in the Aphorisms all these things were stated in epitome. Nor did he go over in the Prognostic as well the points on the diagnosis from urines that he included in the Aphorisms. Nor indeed did he transfer into the Prognostic the points about women that he wrote in the Aphorisms. And yet both these and many other things stated in the Aphorisms belong to the prognostic part of medicine, as he himself shows through his own words. For both in saying: 'If it is northerly, coughs, sore throats, dry bowels, shivery dysurias, pains of the sides and of the chest; when this prevails, expect such things in the illnesses' —

and in saying: 'When summer turns out like spring, expect copious sweats in fevers,' [934] it is evident that he is indicating that such things belong to the prognostic part of the art. For 'to expect', 'to anticipate' and 'to hope', and all verbs of this sort, are proper to prognosis. Moreover, in saying: 'If the winter turns out dry and northerly, and the spring rainy and southerly, in the summer acute fevers, ophthalmias and dysenteries must necessarily occur,' he plainly indicates this very same thing, and much more so when he writes somewhat as follows about the urines: 'In those who have thick, clotted, scanty urines, not without fever, a copious quantity of thin urine coming after these is beneficial; and such urines come chiefly in those who from the beginning, quickly, have a sediment.' And again: 'In those whose urines are stirred up, like that of a beast of burden, headaches are either present or will be present.' And again: 'In those who reach a crisis on the seventh day, the urine has a red cloud on the fourth day, and the other things accordingly.'

In the same way as these, the things that reveal the conditions of the bladder and the kidneys are also written in the Aphorisms, while a great many other things have been omitted in the Prognostic, [935] such as the following: 'In whatever diseases black bile passes off, either upwards or downwards, at their beginning, it is fatal.' 'Dysentery, if it begins from black bile, is fatal.' 'In those who in fevers have a copious haemorrhage from any place whatever, in the recoveries of such persons the bowels become moist.' And a great many such things, belonging to the prognostic part of the art, can be found written in the Aphorisms. Why, then, did he go through none of these in the Prognostic treatise? Because in that work he set out to teach about acute diseases, as he himself explained both when beginning and when completing the book: at the beginning he said, 'One must examine thus in acute diseases'; and at the end he added the following: 'I say these things about acute diseases and those that arise from them.' What the things arising from these are, Hippocrates himself again goes through in the same book: 'The dropsies that arise from acute diseases are all bad.'

And again this: 'One must consider that easy breathing has a very great power towards survival in all acute [936] diseases that are accompanied by fevers and come to a crisis within forty days.' Here too he is referring to the acute diseases that arise by transition, as we have also shown in our work On Critical Days. In many other places of the treatise as well he has indicated that his discussion concerns either acute diseases or the diseases that arise from them, as in these words: 'Sweats are best in all acute diseases when they occur on critical days.' And why need one say much? For he himself clearly shows that he deliberately omits many of the prognostic signs in that book, at one point speaking roughly as follows: 'Let it not deceive you if the bladder itself, having some disease, passes any of these urines; for it is a sign not of the whole body, but of the bladder itself by itself.' Yet he does not add the distinguishing marks in the Prognostic, but writes them in the Aphorisms.

And again he says: 'One must also consider the differences of the swift diseases that are epidemic, and the constitution of the season must not escape notice'; yet he teaches us nothing about this either in the [937] Prognostic. For he set out, as I said, to go through only what is peculiar to acute diseases, and to leave aside everything peculiar to chronic ones. So it was reasonable that he also left aside here the irregular difficulty of breathing, since it belongs to another genus of disease. For if it does arise when the respiratory organs are convulsed, the affection would also accompany chronic diseases, and in this respect it would be peculiar to neither the acute nor the chronic. It would also occur without fever, as convulsions themselves do. But his purpose in the Prognostic is to discourse about the diseases properly called acute. These are the ones that occur with fevers that are, for the most part, continuous, as he himself made clear in On Regimen in Acute Diseases, writing more or less as follows: 'These, then, are acute: such as the ancients named pleuritis and peripneumonia and phrenitis and causus, and the others connected with these, in which the fevers are for the most part continuous.'

Convulsions, then, do not belong to this class of diseases; and for this reason he did not go through the difficulty of breathing peculiar to them together [938] with these, just as he did not go through urines either, or stools, or any of the other things that he wrote about in the Aphorisms, because they were not peculiar to acute diseases. As for why he taught nothing in the Prognostic about such difficulties of breathing either, those in which either only the inspiration or only the expiration is large, I think it superfluous to go into it now. I showed clearly in the first of these commentaries that it is sufficient to refer the other differences back to these five difficulties of breathing, about which I have just finished speaking. Nor, indeed, did he make mention of either rapid or slow breathing in the Prognostic. By the same reasoning we showed that all the other differences turn out to be contained in those previously mentioned. Hippocrates, then, evidently did each of these things correctly: in the books of the Epidemics he set out the division into all the particular difficulties of breathing, and in the Prognostic and the Aphorisms he set out what is pressing for practical use.

[939] Since, then, these things have been sufficiently demonstrated by us, it would still remain to explain the remaining passages from all of his writings, beginning again from the second and the sixth books of the Epidemics. For in both these books, immediately after the passage stated first of all, the one that teaches the differences of all difficulty of breathing, it is written somewhat as follows: 'A remedy for continual yawnings: long-breathed. In those who do not drink and who drink with difficulty, short-breathed.' Here, whether he so named the person long-breathed or the difficulty of breathing itself, it has been shown in the second book that what occurs at a long interval of time, that is, sparse breath and moreover copious breath, is indicated by this designation; and likewise that what occurs at a short interval, that is, frequent breath and moreover small breath, is indicated by 'short-breathed'.

Healing, then, whether as sign or as cause (for it is possible to demonstrate each), of continuous yawnings is the large and rare breathing: a sign, inasmuch as the condition is changing over into its opposite; a cause, because the remedies of opposites are opposites. [940] For people yawn and stretch continuously when some vaporous and thick pneuma is trapped in the muscular kind of tissue, as has been shown elsewhere; and those to whom this has happened at once also breathe out continuously, as though such pneuma were being cleared out and evacuated in the expirations. But if someone no longer makes his expirations continuously, but now at long intervals of time, it is clear that the conditions previously present in him have ceased, and thus long breathing will be a healing sign of the yawning. Moreover, that it is also possible to understand long breathing as a cause that cures the continuous yawnings, this too, it seems to me, no longer needs a long account. For holding back respiration for as long as possible, which is called retention of breath, will cure yawnings on the same principle by which it cures hiccups. And indeed all athletes do this after their exercises, striving to force out by violence everything that is held in the fine pores in the skin, whether of moistures or of vapours.

For these reasons, then, long breathing is a sign, or a healing cause, of continuous yawnings. 'And again, in those who do not drink and drink with difficulty, short breathing': but this is no longer said clearly, but now rather more enigmatically. For are we to consider that he now means the phrenitic, because elsewhere too he said: 'the phrenitic are short drinkers, catching at noise, tremulous'? Or rather those in whom the parts about the lung and the heart have been chilled, so that they at once breathe in at long intervals and breathe out cold [breath]? For short breathing, when it is introduced in both, is a healing sign; but in the chilled it is not only a sign but also a cause. For just as the holding of the breath was able to evacuate the superfluities, and for this reason we [941] employed it in those who hiccup and yawn much and stretch, and who have exercised strenuously, so continuous breathing will be able at once to fan and to heat thoroughly the parts that have been chilled.

In accordance with this reasoning, then, in the second book of the Epidemics too he advised that one make a practice of inducing irascibility (ὀξυθυμίη), both for the sake of the recovery of colour and for the sake of ecchymosis (ἐκχύμωσις), since irascibility too is able to rouse the innate [942] heat. And that irascibility in any case makes the breathing more frequent, no one is unaware. We shall therefore employ it in those who are chilled, colourless and lean, at certain intervals and at the appropriate times. It is certainly not to be used so continuously as to do great harm to the faculty. Just as we do not bid that the exercises which strengthen the innate heat be performed without measure, but employ them at the right time and in due measure, so too short breathing, whether we practise it on its own or together with irascibility, we shall not employ without regard to the right time and measure. Here, however, one must attend to the argument and not suppose that the condition now being described by us is the same as the one in the Prognostic, concerning which he said: 'cold breath exhaled from the nostrils and the mouth is already very deadly.'

For in those who are in acute diseases, about which he speaks in that book, such difficulty of breathing signifies death; but in the other diseases, those that are without fever, coldness seizes the whole condition of the [943] animal. Even in these it does not occur without danger, yet not fatally in every case. To these belong also the so-called hysterical suffocation and, in general, all the apnoeas, which befall women frequently, and especially barren women, but rarely and only at times men also. For in all such conditions the innate heat is weighed down by an abundance of cold matter, like a flame being choked by many wet logs, so that it is sometimes possible for one who has mastered the matter to kindle it again. In those, however, in whom the matter has been consumed and the heat is of necessity extinguished along with it, as in those who in acute diseases breathe out in this way, no hope of recovery remains.

These things, then, must be remembered, and also that in apnoeas it is neither possible to suppose that all breathing has been entirely lost, nor does what happens appear to be so to those who examine it carefully. Rather, the breath in them becomes at once very small and drawn at very long intervals, and in this way it escapes the notice of most people. But if someone attends carefully with his [944] mind, or even places one of his fingers in front of the patient's nose, he will perceive the breathing. And if he also hangs a hair in front of it, or fine wool, thoroughly carded, he will see these too being stirred. In such conditions, then, short breathing, that is, the movement of the respiratory organs at a short interval, which we also call dense breath, is at once both a cause and a sign, a remedy (ἰητήριον). In the same way, in the case of continuous yawnings, not only the breathing at a long interval, that is, the sparse breathing, is at once both a sign and a cause, a remedy, but also the large breathing. For this too is called, in a secondary sense, long breathing. For primarily it is the breathing that takes place at a long interval of time, that is, the sparse breathing, that has acquired this name, and secondarily the large breathing as well. So much, then, for these matters. Let us now set out also all the other things written by him about difficulty of breathing.

In the second book of the Epidemics, in the case of the wife of Antigenes, having first said that she became asthmatic before childbirth, he then adds: 'then [945] together with childbirth she vomited up pus.' So this too agrees with what has been demonstrated by us: for those who breathe frequently and at the same time dilate the thorax to a great extent are asthmatic. This happens sometimes in conditions that require much inspiration. Indeed, such a thing befalls those who have run, or have exercised vigorously in any other way, and occurs in all burning fevers. It happens also, as was shown, whenever there is some obstruction, or compression, or narrowness in the respiratory organs. Something of this kind appears to have befallen the wife of Antigenes as well, as the pus made clear. This, then, is the first difficulty of breathing he mentions in the second book of the Epidemics. After it he mentions the one that befell Lycia, about whom, as I was saying before, he wrote: 'the breath was doubled, but not large in proportion.' For the nervous kind of her organs had been affected, so that there was also a complete retention of urine. It was for this reason, then, that the breath became doubled. But why was it not large? Was it because she had been chilled?

At any rate he says, 'she was contracted'; and it has been shown [946] that he uses this word of those whose innate heat is being chilled. Next, discussing also the patients with cynanche who occurred at that time, he writes as follows: 'In these the breathing was not very elevated', implying, evidently, that in patients with cynanche the breathing is for the most part elevated. It is his custom to call by this name the small breathing, the kind that, as it might seem to someone, enters only somewhere thereabouts, as far as the pharynx, and does not descend into the depth of the thorax. That the breathing must be of this kind in those who feel pain in any of the respiratory organs whatsoever has been said before. What, then, is the cause why in these patients with cynanche the breathing was not very elevated? Is it because the form of the cynanche did not arise in them in the usual way either? For first he says: 'the pharynx not inflamed, but lying still'; then he says this: 'most of them not choking, unless they tried to swallow'. And in general the whole account of the cynanche that occurred at that time showed that the pharynx remained unaffected, whereas the parts neighbouring it, those continuous with the vertebrae of the neck, were affected.

And indeed he says that the vertebrae themselves were also displaced, [947] some only inwards, others also to the sides. Since, then, neither was any other of the respiratory organs affected, nor even the throat itself in its own right, except insofar as, through the community of position, it shared in the affections, the breathing in them was, as was to be expected, not very elevated. For if the throat had not been troubled at all, the breathing would not have been elevated in any way; but since it was troubled through its sympathetic affection with the adjacent parts, the breathing acquired the state intermediate between those mentioned, having become moderately frequent. Next after this constitution he mentions another which occurred in Perinthus, beginning the account in this manner: 'We came to Perinthus about the summer solstice, a little [before it]'. Then he relates the whole character of the diseases, which began from causus, but became emetic and persisted for a very long time. But he also added this: that the causi occurred in these people without vomiting, and that their belly passed a great deal.

So that from these and from all the other things it is clearly evident that the basis of the constitution lay in putrefying phlegms, the respiratory organs [948] remaining unaffected, and also the mouth of the stomach, while the causus in turn arose from the lower parts. Reasonably, then, their breathing neither became large, as in those in whose lung and heart an abundance of fiery heat had collected, nor was it altogether small, since they were neither in pain nor chilled. If, then, 'elevated' signifies something not at all different from 'small', it is with reason that he says their breaths became elevated, though not very much so. After this constitution Hippocrates does not mention any difficulty of breathing in what follows, up to that passage which I cited first of all at the beginning of this book, which begins thus: 'Breaths frequent and small, large and rare.' This I have already explained in its entirety. It would now be the time to mention the difficulty of breathing that he wrote next, in a certain patient whose name was Scopus. The words of the ancient run thus: 'Breathing somewhat frequent; the hypochondria were painful, both when he breathed and when he turned.'

[949] This patient, too, evidently bears witness to what we have often said before: for since the hypochondria are connected to the respiratory organs, for this reason, when they were in pain, the breathing was somewhat dense. These, then, are the kinds of difficulty of breathing that he wrote of in the second book of the Epidemics. In the fourth he first mentions the wife of Nicostratus, the one in Crannon, who had small and dense breathing; and second the wife of Antigenes, who was asthmatic, not having become so recently at that time but having been so from the beginning, so that she also coughed constantly. About this woman, then, there would be no question at all; but concerning the woman in Crannon, the wife of Nicostratus, he seems to me to have added the small and dense breathing for this reason, because she became deranged. For it has already been said many times that, on the contrary, sparse and large breathing is peculiar to derangement; so it is worth inquiring why this did not occur, but rather its opposite, the one peculiar to pains, the small and dense.

For in his account of the illness he did not add that any pain arose in any of the parts, nor any notable swelling [950] either in the hypochondrium or in the chest. What, then, is it that took place? It seems to me that a twofold form of disease was established in the woman from a twofold origin. From her being delirious and having her neck, mouth and nose drawn aside by spasm, it is clear that she had some basis of disease in the head. But from the food being shut in until the tenth day, and from the sediment in the urine becoming like bitter vetch, I think that no small inflammation arose in the liver. Under this inflammation the condition from above was overcome and could not by itself give its stamp to the respiration. For it has already been said many times before that the form of the difficulty of breathing is shaped according to the prevailing condition. Not least, the ancient's own wording shows that the delirium was slight. At any rate he said that she 'talked somewhat at random' (παραλέγειν). He is accustomed to use such a verb when he wishes to indicate a slight impairment, as this too has been demonstrated many times.

It is therefore nothing to wonder at that, since she was delirious only briefly but was strongly inflamed in the liver, the difficulty of breathing that befell her was not [951] the one proper to the delirium but the one proper to the inflammation. So, then, matters stand with these things too. But what ought we to understand when he says that someone became 'full of pneuma' (pneumatōdēs)? Is it the person whom in On Regimen in Acute Diseases he called a pneumatias? Or the person whose belly is inflated with pneuma? What the pneumatias is, he himself explained most clearly in On Regimen in Acute Diseases. For having first said that they quickly become pneumatiai, he at once adds, joining it on: 'and by much and frequent breathing.' This I explained right at the beginning of this book. But the passage in the fourth book of the Epidemics must be examined, once we have written out the text itself, which runs thus: 'The man from the mines: right hypochondrium distended, spleen large, belly distended, somewhat hard, full of pneuma, colourless.' For either is possible: both that he had become dyspnoic, on account of the affections in the hypochondria, and that his belly had become inflated with pneuma.

[952] Much more unclear still is the next patient, recorded thus: 'The (son) of Timaineos had something of pneuma, so as to be sallow.' For in this man too there was quite certainly some malfunction of the liver, on account of which it was possible both that he was short of breath and that his belly was inflated with pneuma; for a sallow colour is a sign of a malfunctioning liver. What is said next, thus: 'The husband of the woman in childbed, the one at Sitodokos' house, jaundiced, whom I visited on the seventh day, died on the eighth, passing neither urine nor stools; hypochondria large and hard, and breathing frequent', presents no problem at all. For when the hypochondria have become immoderately hard and large, it is reasonable that his breathing was frequent. But entirely unclear is what is said immediately after this about the woman in childbed, thus: 'When the fever remitted, the breathing was not resolved.' For what kind of difficulty of breathing she had he neither stated clearly himself, nor did he record any other such symptom from which one might infer the condition that had arisen in her.

And indeed after this one, having gone on not a little further, [953] he begins his account in this manner: 'The woman of Timaenes, full of pneuma.' For this can be understood as 'dyspnoeic', but it can also be taken to be said, as most of the commentators think, of one inflated with pneuma in the hypochondria. Yet it seems to me better, and perhaps necessary, that she be said to be inflated in the hypochondria rather than dyspnoeic. Having gone on a little further in the account, then, he says 'and somewhat easier of breathing', as though he had already said of her that she was dyspnoeic. That he is accustomed to call 'full of pneuma' those whose breathing is frequent has been stated in what precedes as well, but it is clear now too: for the symptoms of this woman had turned again for the worse, and he says that she died on the sixteenth day, having frequent breathing.

And as for the patient written up after her, that he too breathed rapidly on account of the condition of the hypochondria, the text itself will make clear, which runs as follows: 'The boy who belonged to the woman, the sister of Apoimantus: hypochondria [954] large, and spleen; breath; evacuation bilious.' For just as he sometimes calls those who breathe rapidly 'full of pneuma' (pneumatōdeis), so too he sometimes writes simply 'breath' (pneuma). And it is no wonder that, the hypochondria being large, the breath became rapid. For further on he will again say of him: 'the hypochondria were distended, and there was also a slight dry cough, gently.' For in general, as we have said, whenever either a swelling or some pain arises in the parts at the hypochondria, they of necessity breathe small and rapid. So it is no wonder either when, in what follows, having first said 'hypochondrium somewhat soft', he adds 'but not very full of pneuma'. For if 'soft' (laparon) means empty and 'somewhat soft' (hypolaparon) somewhat empty, they will have difficulty in breathing to the same extent as the parts at the hypochondrium are in a bad state with them.

When, therefore, these [parts] are moderately affected, they will have a moderate difficulty of breathing; just as again, in the later parts of the book, he writes somewhat as follows: 'In the household slave-woman, whom I saw when she had been newly bought, [955] in whom there was a large hardening in the right-hand parts, not very painful'; and he reasonably adds: 'and not very dyspnoeic.' For if the hardening was not very painful, it was likely that the woman was not very dyspnoeic either. So too, at the very end of the book, in his account of the older man, after first saying 'he was deranged in an orderly manner', he added: 'not very dyspnoeic.' For the magnitude of the difficulty of breathing always corresponds to the magnitude of the cause producing the difficulty of breathing. But these things too are written in the fourth book of the Epidemics, and they agree with what we have demonstrated concerning difficulty of breathing.

Again, in the fifth book of the Epidemics the fourteenth patient is written up in this way: 'In Larissa Hipposthenes seemed to the physicians to be gripped by peripneumonia, but it was not so at all. At the beginning, while wrestling, he fell on his back on hard ground, and [his opponent] fell on top of him; and he bathed in cold water, and stayed [in it], and seemed to become heavier. On the next day he was feverish, and had a rather dry cough, and his [956] breathing was frequent.' Then, a little further on: 'whenever he coughed,' he says, 'he had pain in the chest and the back.' It is therefore nothing surprising that, with the parts of the thorax in this condition, the breathing became frequent. What is added at the end of the account, 'nor did he have rattling,' is said as a proof that the man had not become peripneumonic; but it also agrees with what we said right at the beginning of this treatise, when we were expounding this phrase in On Regimen in Acute Diseases: 'those who are choked by orthopnoea and rattling.' The thirty-ninth patient in the fifth book of the Epidemics is written up as also having frequent breathing. Here too I shall set down the passage itself, which runs roughly as follows: 'A child was struck by a mule in the belly and the liver; it died on the fourth day; it had frequent breathing, and did not comprehend, and fever held it.' It is not unclear in this case that the peritoneum and the diaphragm became inflamed together with the belly and liver, and that for this reason the child was also delirious.

But it was not in accordance with the delirium [957] that he had difficulty of breathing; for the greater affection, the one in the hypochondrium, stamped the form of the respiration in accordance with itself, while the lesser was overcome. These, then, are the cases in the fifth book. Passing over once more to the sixth, of which we have already explained earlier the passage it shares with the second, let us come to the remaining passages. Nearly all of them are by now clear because of what has been said before. For it was shown that when, in the concurrences of symptoms of diseases, he writes simply 'breath' (pneuma) on its own in this way, he means the difficulty of breathing from which the breath becomes rapid; and this same thing, when it is made rapid to a still greater degree, it is his custom to call panting (asthma). So in the sixth book of the Epidemics, when he says 'breath is left behind' (pneuma enkataleipētai), we shall understand the difficulty of breathing accompanied by rapidity. Likewise also in the case of the woman in Crannon, about whom he writes thus: 'spleen naturally large, ardent fever, very red, breath', we must understand the aforementioned difficulty of breathing, in which the breath is made rapid, as also in the case of the daughter of Agisias.

That rapid breathing differs [958] from asthma he showed clearly. The passage runs thus: 'The daughter of Agisias, while still a girl, was rapid-breathing; having become a woman, and being in distress from a childbirth not long before, she lifted a great load carelessly, and at once she seemed to feel a crack in her chest; on the next day she had asthma and pain in the right hip.' Then next 'she spat up frothy matter', he says, 'and at the beginning she was florid.' And it is evident from the whole concurrence of symptoms that she spat these up when an old and hard-to-concoct tumour in the respiratory organs had ruptured, and that she was rapid-breathing because of these tumours. Again, in the later parts of the book, in the constitution which he began in this way: 'Coughs began about the winter solstice; and in those in whom the breathing was also raised up along with them', he says (and that 'raised' breathing is breathing that is small and rapid we have gone through in what precedes), he also said, of course, that synanchai occurred in that constitution.

Wrong, then, are those who think that 'elevated' has been said in place of 'large', on the ground that it elevates the thorax, distending it to the utmost. [959] A little further on he names certain people pneumatiai; this too has been discussed earlier, namely that he so calls either those who are inflated with pneuma or those who are asthmatic. What is said in what follows, 'indistinct breathing', is small and for that reason imperceptible, such as also attends the so-called apnoeas and uterine suffocations. He means to indicate something of this kind, as appears from the wording itself, which runs thus: 'And indistinct breathings in the consumptive are bad, and in the childless; and all other such things from the same constitution.' For childless women (and these are for the most part those who are not properly purged) are most of all seized by apnoeas, as indeed are also those who remain widowed for a very long time. So the breathings that are not clearly distinct and are not plainly evident to us, these he has called indistinct. Setting out from these, one could find even without me all the other things said about difficulty of breathing in both the genuine and the spurious books, although we have gone through nearly all the genuine ones in this treatise.

But since the writings of Thessalus his son and [960] those of Polybus his son-in-law also belong to the art of Hippocrates, and not far from them are those which are thought to be by Euryphon but are transmitted among the works of Hippocrates, if ever I should come to have more leisure, I shall add another, fourth book, explaining what has been said about difficulty of breathing in the remaining writings that bear the title of Hippocrates. But now, since other matters are pressing, I shall not pass on to those.
